## Housekeeping — Groovy 6.0.0-RC-3  *(shipped)*

`gradle.properties` moves `groovyVersion` from RC-2 to `org.apache.groovy:6.0.0-RC-3`, resolved from its
release-vote staging repository (`orgapachegroovy-1123` — the TEMPORARY `maven { url … }` entry in
`build.gradle`, `examples-dsl/build.gradle` and `ci/consumer-smoke/build.gradle`, repointed from RC-2's
now-deleted `…1122`). Built-against wording refreshed in README, BUILD.md, the `build.gradle` comment and the
consumer-smoke fallback.

**RC-3 has since been RELEASED, and the temporary entries are gone** — all six modules the build uses
(`groovy`, `groovy-contracts`, `groovy-test`, `groovy-typecheckers`, `groovy-macro`, `groovy-callsite`) answer
from Central, and the staging repository `…1123` was already deleted, so the entries were by then pointing at
nothing rather than merely being redundant. That is the second vote repo in a row to be removed only after it
had gone (RC-2's `…1122` was found 404 as well): a staging entry is dead the moment the vote closes, not when
someone remembers it. The build now resolves from `mavenCentral()` alone, verified with
`--refresh-dependencies` rather than against a warm cache.

Gates re-run on the released artifacts, from Central: suite 2149/2149; `check` green end to end (2207 tests,
runtime rung 674/681 clean with the same 2 allowlisted spec-throw divergences, 0 needing review); docLint 0
drift; all four TLA+ models "No error has been found"; `frayCheck` green; nuscr 5 protocols ok.

**Unlike RC-2, this one needed code**, and finding out why took three layers.

**The change.** A switch EXPRESSION used as a method's IMPLICIT return is now compiled as a plain
`SwitchStatement`; RC-2 and earlier wrapped it as `ExpressionStatement(SwitchExpression)`. `return switch (…)`
still carries a first-class `SwitchExpression` in both. Confirmed INTENDED upstream. Runtime semantics are
unchanged — both forms still yield their value — so this is an AST-consumer change, not a user-visible one.

**Three layers, because each fix exposed the next.** The first symptom was `unsupported statement
SwitchStatement`: `BodyEncoder` never saw a value, because the body was a statement rather than a tail
expression. Reading a tail `SwitchStatement` back as the `SwitchExpression` it stands for (same three parts)
moved the failure to `return expression … is outside fragment` — the encoder's `caseValueExpr` requires one
statement per arm, and RC-3's arms are break-terminated (`Block[Expr(e), Break]`) where a first-class
`SwitchExpression` carries `Block(Yield(e))`. Dropping a trailing `break` (it ends the arm, it does not change
its value) moved the failure again, to the arms arriving ALREADY WOVEN —
`Block[Expr(result = 'a'), If, Return(result)]`.

**That third layer is the one worth recording**, because it is the load-bearing invariant of the whole design.
`ContractExpansionTransform.copyBody` deliberately rebuilds only the containers groovy-contracts restructures
IN PLACE — `BlockStatement`, `IfStatement`, `TryCatchStatement` — and shares everything else so that STC's
later metadata stays visible. RC-3 promoted `SwitchStatement` into that set: with the switch in return
position, groovy-contracts injects `result = …; if (!post) …; return result` into each ARM, and a shared node
leaked that weaving into the clean-body snapshot. The encoder was reading the instrumented arm instead of the
author's value. `SwitchStatement` is now owned by `copyBody` for exactly the reason an `IfStatement`'s branches
are.

Also: Groovy's parser now reports `Unexpected ','` where it reported `Unexpected input` for a bare brace array
initializer. The P-java-fragment case pins that the form does not PARSE, not the wording for why, so the
expectation narrows to the stable part — the same treatment the hardware-dependent FizzBuzz slot got.

**A defect of our own, found by the fuller run.** `ActorTimerSemanticsTest` failed with a
`ConcurrentModificationException`, not a timing threshold: the Phase 292–297 semantics tests collect actor
output into `Collections.synchronizedList`, which guards individual operations but NOT iteration — and the test
thread runs `count {}` / `any {}` / a copy constructor while the actor thread is still appending. Latent since
those tests were written and exposed once a replay was still in flight. All 13 shared lists across the three
files are now `CopyOnWriteArrayList`, whose iteration has snapshot semantics, which removes the hazard class
rather than guarding each site.

Gates on the RC-3 artifacts, all green: suite 2143/2143; `:test` 2201 tests, 0 failures; docLint 0 drift
(191 case links, 37 pinned diagnostics); nuscr 5 protocols ok. The P291 double-monoid solver timeout seen on
CI is unrelated to this bump — it predates it, does not reproduce locally (~190ms against an 8000ms budget),
and is tracked as the FP model-search variance item.

## Phase 304 — a switch is an n-way `if`/`else`: the rule GROOVY-12399 settled, adopted  *(shipped)*

The RC-3 housekeeping above adapted to the new switch shape in three layers, each a patch for the symptom in
front of it. Then the upstream rationale arrived, and it names a RULE rather than a shape:

> position, not arm shape, decides whether a switch produces a value

GROOVY-12399 restored Java's rule and removed a carve-out that had kept a switch in implicit-return position an
expression. The carve-out had made one piece of syntax mean two things — under `@CompileStatic` a
declared-`Object` case label resolved statically in that position and dynamically once any statement followed
the switch, so adding a trailing line changed how labels matched — and cost ~110 lines in `AstBuilder`
duplicating what `ReturnAdder` already knew. Three things fall out of that reading for the checker.

**The model gets simpler, and wider.** If POSITION decides, then in implicit-return position `ReturnAdder`
makes each arm a return, and everywhere else the arms are plain branches. Either way a switch in STATEMENT form
is an n-way `if`/`else` on the subject — so `BodyEncoder` walks it as one, with the path splitting an
`IfStatement` already gets: a guard `subject == label` per arm, the earlier labels negated ahead of it, and a
no-match path carrying the default's arm or, with none, `null` in return position (measured). That replaces the
RC-3 stopgap, which synthesised a `SwitchExpression` from the statement's parts and pushed it through the
ite-chain lowering — a lowering that requires each arm to be ONE expression. Two shapes it could never reach
now verify: **an arm that does real work before yielding** (`case 1 -> { int t = 2; yield t * 3 }`) and **a
switch that is not the method's last statement**. Both carry refute twins, because "compiles cleanly" is what a
silent skip looks like too. A switch in EXPRESSION position (`return switch (…)`) is still a first-class
`SwitchExpression` and keeps the ite-chain.

**A boundary the branch model makes speakable.** Fall-through was never modelled and never could be by an
ite-chain, which simply had no way to say so. As branches it is a precise condition — every arm must LEAVE, by
the arrow form's implicit break or an explicit break/return/throw — and a colon-form arm that runs on into the
next is now refused with `switch case falls through to the next (line N) — only arms that leave are modelled`
instead of being lumped in with "outside fragment".

**A soundness assumption checked rather than assumed.** The removed carve-out is what GUARANTEED an unmatched
implicit-return switch yields `null`, and the encoder's no-default model — an unconstrained result, a sound
conservative refute — rests on exactly that. Measured on RC-3: an unmatched switch still yields `null`, and the
checker still refutes a non-trivial postcondition on that path. The behaviour is now incidental rather than
specified, so it is pinned as a case instead of left as an assumption.

Also of note, and requiring nothing: the `@CompileStatic` inconsistency the carve-out caused is gone, so label
matching no longer depends on what follows the switch — one less piece of context the verifier would have had
to model.

Cases (G144, 12 — was 6): the existing six unchanged; the unmatched-yields-null pin; a working arm and its
refute twin; a statement-position switch and its refute twin; and the fall-through refusal. Suite 2149/2149;
`:test` 2207 tests, 0 failures; docLint 0 drift.

## Phase 305 — the witness fast path: an FP law refutation that is not a lottery  *(shipped)*

The `double` sum monoid's associativity refutation had been failing intermittently on CI with
`Could not decide … (solver: timeout)` while passing locally in ~190ms against an 8000ms budget. The diagnosis
took two wrong turns worth recording, because each was cheap to believe and measurement killed both.

**The first wrong turn: blaming the recent work.** Measured at the parent of the commit that had touched that
case: identical, ~190ms. Exonerated, and the mechanism was absent anyway (the change moved line numbers, which
do not reach SMT symbol names).

**The second wrong turn, which was nearly shipped.** With no seed pinned in `Z3Backend`, the obvious reading
was "search roulette, pin the seed". The whole corpus stayed green with `random_seed = 1`, which looked like
validation. It was not: the seed was never measured against THIS query. It costs **3600ms under seed 1** where
the unpinned run costs 188ms. Varying only the seed:

| seed | 0 | 2 | 1 | 42 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| cost | 188ms | 2021ms | 3600ms | **6845ms** |

A **36x spread on identical input**, with seed 42 at 85% of the CI budget on a 12-core laptop — so the fix
being proposed would have made the failure MORE likely, and the "40x headroom" reported from the local run was
a lucky draw rather than headroom. It also means the dev default of 2000ms is calibrated to that luck: a bad
draw fails locally too.

**What it actually is.** Refuting a law over IEEE floats is a MODEL SEARCH, which Z3 bit-blasts — 3 x 64 bits
of it. That is the lottery. But the refutation never needed a search: the witness is textbook, and checking a
law at fixed values is evaluation.

**The fix.** Before the general check, ask the law once with every parameter pinned to its position in
`(1e16, -1e16, 1.0)` — the triple where `(a+b)+c` loses the `1.0` that `a+(b+c)` keeps. A REFUTED answer there
refutes the law outright and the model names the values; anything else falls through to the ordinary check, so
nothing that proves today stops proving, and the path can only ever turn a lottery into a decision. Gated on a
law lemma (`REDUCER_LAW_KEY`) whose parameters are all floating-point, so every other law is untouched.

**Two things the measurements settled about the implementation.**

* **A disjunction is not enough.** Constraining each parameter to a CHOICE of witness values leaves a finite
  search (125 combinations for a three-parameter law) and measured no better than the original. Pinning each
  parameter to one value outright is what turns it into evaluation.
* **Asking FIRST matters, not just asking.** Run as a fallback after an UNKNOWN, the witness check inherits a
  solver carrying state from the failed search and times out too. Run first, it costs ~35ms.

Result, against the seeds that provoked it: **39ms / 34ms / 40ms / 39ms for seeds 0 / 1 / 2 / 42** — seed
independent, 175x faster than the worst draw, and the case still refutes with the budget turned down to 60ms.
The P291 group's solver time fell from 201ms to 63ms, because the refutation no longer searches at all.

Gates: suite 2149/2149; `:test` 2207 tests, 0 failures; docLint 0 drift. **No seed is pinned** — the point is
that the answer no longer depends on one.

**Open:** the same treatment for a floating-point law whose counterexample is NOT at this witness (a `double`
product monoid, say) still falls through to the search and keeps the lottery; a second witness triple chosen
for multiplication would cover it, and the fall-through is already the mechanism for adding one.

## Phase 306 — Fray on a Kerridge deadlock: the refutation exhibited  *(shipped — rung 3 for the channel gallery)*

The gallery's most striking refutations are DEADLOCKS — the deadlock exercise (two processes each reading from
the other before writing), the forgotten `close()`, the send-send knot on rendezvous channels — and every one
of them was a compile-time claim with no runtime counterpart. The three-rung stance says a proof is one rung of
a concurrency argument; the channel gallery had been standing on one.

`ChannelCycleFrayTest` adds the third. `aPrimedCycleIsDeadlockFree` drives the repaired network over 200
controlled schedules, clean; `aMutualReceiveCycleDeadlocks` (`@Disabled`, like its bank-transfer sibling)
reports a `DeadlockException` with both threads parked in the channel receive —
`Unsafe.park → LockSupport.park → DefaultGroovyMethods.first` — one waiting on `bToA`, the other on `aToB`.

**Why it belongs at this rung rather than duplicating one.** `CONCURRENCY.md` sets the bar itself: Fray "earns
its place only where it's DISTINCT — deadlock / lock-ordering on hand-threaded code". The bank transfer is a
cycle over two MONITORS repaired by a global lock order; this is a cycle over two CHANNELS repaired by a
PRIMING SEND — a different mechanism and a different fix, which is exactly the pairing the books teach and the
gallery's primed-ring case verifies at rung 1.

Feasibility was checked before writing anything, since it is what decides whether Fray can see the hang at all:
`groovy.concurrent` runs on PLATFORM threads (`Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor`, ForkJoinPool — no virtual
threads, whose carrier scheduling a controlled scheduler would have to intercept). So the substrate is the one
Fray already handles here, and the two Groovy-specific settings the bank transfer needed
(`-Dgroovy.indy.callsite.cleaner.inline=true`, `ignoreTimedBlock = true`) carried over unchanged — the scenario
was the only new cost. Both processes drive the real `AsyncChannel`, hand-threaded rather than run as
`async {}` tasks so Fray schedules the application threads directly.

The disabled twin was ENABLED and run before being committed as disabled: a deadlock-free half that passes
proves nothing on its own if the deadlocking half cannot be found. It is found, in 61s of search.

`frayCheck`: 3 classes, 3 enabled tests, 0 failures (3 skipped by design). The task description, which still
named only the bank transfer, now says what it runs.

**Tried and rejected: Fray on the actor mailbox knot.** This was written up above as "the same shape, one
increment". It is not, and the reason is worth more than the test would have been. Phase 289's knot was ported
(a burst into a `BLOCK`-bounded mailbox whose handler waits on a gate fed only afterwards) along with its
untied twin, and the twin FAILED: Fray reported a `DeadlockException` on the scenario that is deadlock-free,
with only the MAIN thread in the report and the actor's dispatch thread absent from it entirely. The same
scenario run as a plain JUnit test terminates immediately, and a trivial actor round-trip passes under Fray —
so Fray can drive an actor, but not one whose sender is parked on a bounded mailbox.

Two things follow. The mechanical one: the actor's dispatch thread is created INTERNALLY by the library rather
than by the test, and Fray's view of it is not good enough to schedule a mailbox-blocking scenario — a second,
deeper Groovy-runtime interaction than the `PIC-Cleaner` one the bank transfer documents. The conceptual one
matters more: "a sender blocked on a full mailbox is released when the handler drains" is a LIVENESS property
under a fair scheduler, not deadlock-freedom. A controlled scheduler exploring adversarial interleavings may
simply never run the handler, and no amount of tuning makes that a deadlock — it makes it starvation. Fray is a
deadlock oracle; this property is not a deadlock property. Cost said the same thing more bluntly: ~10-35s per
ITERATION against ~0.1s for the channel cycle.

So the actor mailbox belongs at rung 2, not rung 3 — TLA+ can state weak fairness (`WF_vars`) and ask the
question the property actually poses. Recorded here rather than left as an open invitation to retry it.

**Open (the rungs for the rest):** TLC on a channel network — deadlock-freedom is proved STRUCTURALLY at
rung 1, so an exhaustive check is a genuinely independent oracle, and TLA+'s `WF_vars` is the native vocabulary
for Phase 255's weak-fairness assumption (SHIPPED as Phase 307 below); and TLC on an actor with several
concurrent senders, which is precisely what Phase 300 withholds. Lincheck is the weak fit for both — an actor
is serialized by construction, so linearizability is close to definitional, and Lincheck-ing `AsyncChannel`
would test Groovy's library rather than these proofs.

---

## Phase 307 — TLC on a channel network: rung 2 for the Kerridge gallery  *(shipped)*

The third rung-2 artifact, beside the Smith buffer and Leino's ticket lock: `src/tlc/Network.tla`, the
gallery's **deadlock exercise** as a state machine — channels by OCCUPANCY (content is irrelevant to
blocking), each process by its position in its own two-step program, and a `Primed` constant selecting
between the student mistake and the repair the books teach.

**The pairing is not the same argument twice, which is the test for whether a rung is worth adding.** Rung 1
refutes the cycle STRUCTURALLY — it builds the wait-for order and shows it is not well-founded, naming the
cycle. "No interleaving reaches a stuck state" is a different claim, and TLC decides it by enumerating them.
The second property is stronger still: Phase 255 certifies liveness UNDER WEAK FAIRNESS, an assumption written
in prose at rung 1 and as `WF_vars` here, which is TLA+'s own vocabulary for it — so the assumption is checked
rather than declared.

`Network.cfg` (`Primed = TRUE`) completes clean: 5 distinct states, no deadlock, `Progress` holds.
`NetworkCycle.cfg` (`Primed = FALSE`) reports `Deadlock reached` in the INITIAL state — both processes at
their first step, both channels empty, neither receive enabled — which is the rung-2 counterpart of the
compile-time *"Process-network deadlock: circular wait"* and of the `DeadlockException` Fray exhibits for the
same network at rung 3. **One example, argued three ways**, which is what the three-rung stance claims is
possible and had not been demonstrated end to end before.

One modelling note worth keeping: TLC calls ANY state with no successor a deadlock, so a network that simply
finishes would be reported as one. The spec stutters once both processes are done, so only a state where a
process still has work to do but nothing is enabled counts.

`tlcNetwork` runs it; CI's rung-2 step now runs all three models. Gates unchanged elsewhere (this touches no
checker code): docLint 0 drift.

**Open:** nothing named for the channel gallery. The actor mailbox followed as Phase 308 below.

---

## Phase 308 — TLC on the actor mailbox: the property Fray could not pose  *(shipped — the rungs closed)*

`src/tlc/Mailbox.tla`, the fourth rung-2 artifact. Phase 289's knot — a `BLOCK`-bounded mailbox filled by a
burst while the handler is blocked on a channel the burst only feeds afterwards — as a state machine.

**It is at this rung because rung 3 was tried and was the wrong one**, and that is the more useful half of the
result. The property is "a sender blocked on a full mailbox is eventually released, because the handler drains
it": a LIVENESS property under a fair scheduler, not deadlock-freedom. A controlled scheduler exploring
adversarial interleavings may simply never run the handler — starvation, not deadlock — so no amount of tuning
would have made Fray the right oracle. It also misfired empirically (a `DeadlockException` on the
deadlock-FREE scenario, the actor's internally-created dispatch thread missing from the report, ~10-35s per
iteration). `WF_vars` states the property directly, so it can be posed rather than approximated.

**Two open items closed by one spec.** `Mailbox.cfg` runs the repair with TWO CONCURRENT SENDERS — which is
what Phase 300 declines to claim at rung 1, since once more than one method can send to the actor "this
method's sends are not the whole count". Here the siblings interleave exhaustively: 35 distinct states,
`Bounds` (the mailbox never exceeds its cap) holds throughout, `Progress` holds. `MailboxKnot.cfg` reports
`Deadlock reached`, and the trace is the mechanism rather than a verdict:

```
State 1  box = 0, busy = FALSE, gate = 0, sent = 0
State 2  <Send>  box = 1,                 sent = 1
State 3  <Take>  box = 0, busy = TRUE          ← handler now blocked on the gate
State 4  <Send>  box = 1,                 sent = 2
         ← stuck: box full, handler waiting on an empty gate, and the feed that would
           release it comes after the send that is stuck
```

One message in flight ON TOP of the `Cap` the box holds is exactly why the (Cap+2)-th send is the one that
waits — the arithmetic rung 1 does symbolically, here enumerated.

`tlcMailbox` runs it; CI's rung-2 step now runs all four models. This touches no checker code; docLint 0 drift.

**Where the three rungs now stand.** The Kerridge deadlock exercise is argued three ways (structural refutation,
exhaustive model, Fray exhibiting the hang). The actor mailbox is argued twice, at the two rungs where its
property can actually be stated. Lincheck remains the weak fit for both and is recorded as such rather than
attempted: an actor is serialized by construction so linearizability is close to definitional, and
Lincheck-ing `AsyncChannel` would test Groovy's library rather than these proofs.

## Housekeeping — Groovy 6.0.0  *(shipped)*

`gradle.properties` moves `groovyVersion` from RC-3 to the GA release, `org.apache.groovy:6.0.0`. All six modules
the build uses (`groovy`, `groovy-contracts`, `groovy-test`, `groovy-typecheckers`, `groovy-macro`,
`groovy-callsite`) were on Central at once, so this time there was no staging repository to add and later remove.
Built-against wording refreshed in README, BUILD.md (including the consumer dependency snippet), the
`build.gradle` comment and the consumer-smoke fallback. No code changes.

Gates on the released artifacts, resolved with `--refresh-dependencies`, all green: suite 2149/2149; `check` green
end to end (2207 tests, 0 failures; runtime rung 674/681 clean with the same 2 allowlisted spec-throw divergences,
0 needing review; docLint clean); all four TLA+ models "No error has been found"; `frayCheck` green; nuscr 5
protocols ok; the CI consumer-smoke step, run locally, against Groovy 6.0.0 on the JDK 17 floor.

**Two 6.0.0 compiler features were assessed and left out of the build.** `groovyc --check` stops at
`CLASS_GENERATION`, so every check runs but no class files are written. `--error-format=short`
(`CompilerConfiguration.errorFormat`, GROOVY-12312) prints one `file:line:column: severity: message` line per
diagnostic. Neither changes anything here. The harness compiles in memory and reads each error with `toString()`,
while the format is applied only when `ErrorCollector.write` prints the whole report, so the `@ line L, column C.`
anchors the cases check for are unaffected. Both do work for consumers without changes: `--check` runs verification
like a linter (exit 0 when everything proves, 1 on a refutation), and the short format keeps the counterexample and
`fails on:` call on its single line. In Gradle the short format is set through `groovyOptions.configurationScript`
(checked in a real `compileGroovy`). One rough edge: the one-line join puts no separator before each label
(`…return path ensured: …`).

**Classic-codegen sweep on 6.0.0** (`VERIFY_RUNG_INDY=false`, fresh daemon per run): 674/681 clean, the same 2
allowlisted divergences, report byte-identical to the indy run. The first attempt raised a gap: the report never
said which codegen it ran, so a matching pair could not rule out the knob failing to reach the forked rung JVM.
`RuntimeRung.codegenProbe()` now compiles a one-method class with the rung's own configuration, reads the mode off
the bytecode (classic call sites leave a synthetic `$getCallSiteArray`; indy does not), prints it as the header's
`codegen:` line, and exits 2 when it disagrees with what was asked for. Re-run with the probe: `invokedynamic
(default)` and `classic call sites (VERIFY_RUNG_INDY=false)`, reports otherwise identical.

## Phase 309 — call results as arguments, and the LemmaScript port  *(shipped — engine change)*

Porting LemmaScript's examples (TypeScript with `//@` contracts, proved through Dafny) surfaced a gap in the
inter-procedural core: a contracted call's result could not reach **another call's `@Requires`**. Minimised:

```groovy
@Ensures({ result >= 0 }) static int f(int n) { n >= 0 ? n : 0 }
@Requires({ z >= 0 })      static int g(int z) { z }
static int h(int n) { int c = f(n); return g(c) }   // refuted: c = -1, n = Integer.MIN_VALUE
```

Three shapes, three routes, one cause. The call-site precondition check (Phase 24) replays the straight-line
prefix to the call. A scalar local bound from a call was **havoc'd** there, so `f`'s `result >= 0` never reached
`g`'s check. The postcondition path had always assumed the callee's `@Ensures` for the same local (Phase 7), which
is why `@Ensures({ result >= 0 }) h` proved while `g(c)` refuted. The direct form `g(f(n))` didn't get that far:
the actual argument didn't translate, so the precondition was skipped as outside the fragment. And on the
postcondition side, `return decode(encode(n))` skipped too: the Phase 206 return-position hoist tried the outer
call first and gave up because its argument was a call. Sound throughout (havoc and skip lose facts, never invent
them), but the counterexample sat exactly where the havoc left the value open, which made it look meaningful.

**The fix (`VerifyChecker`):**

1. **`replayScalarCall`**, the scalar twin of Phase 144's `replayCarrierCall`: in the prefix replay, an
   int-like, boolean or String local declared or assigned from a contracted call gets a fresh handle constrained
   by the callee's `@Ensures` (`assumeCalleeEnsures`, `result` bound to the handle). No usable `@Ensures` → false
   → the old havoc. List- and tuple-valued locals keep their own oracle routes.
2. **Nested call arguments.** In the call-site check, an actual that is itself a contracted call is bound
   through the same helper, so `g(f(n))` discharges like `int c = f(n); g(c)`.
3. **Inside-out return hoist.** The Phase 206 hoist now rewrites a call's *arguments* first, so `decode(encode(n))`
   hoists `encode(n)` and then `decode(…)` over the temp. Arguments only; a call receiver (`a.f().g()`) keeps
   its carrier-chain route.

The hoist's temporaries were named `ret$call$k` and showed up in counterexamples; they are now `ret$call#k`,
hidden by the existing `#` filter (a case pins the absence).

**Shipped tests (group `P309 call results as arguments`, 9 cases):** the local, reassigned-local, nested-argument
and boolean forms prove; a too-weak callee `@Ensures` still refutes in both the local and the nested form; an
uncontracted callee whose body can go negative refutes (an uncontracted body that can't — `n >= 0 ? n : 0` —
correctly proves, since such bodies are read); the nested return proves, and a wrong claim over it **refutes**
rather than skips, which pins that the return expression is really reasoned about.

**The LemmaScript port** — `examples/lemmascript.md`, group `LemmaScript port` (15 cases, 14 linked). The
front page's binary search, and from LemmaScript's `examples/` folder clamp, linear search, max, isSorted, sum,
swap, leftPad, duplicate detection, zigzag encoding, a bounded counter and `Math.max(...)`. LemmaScript's
`//@ contract` sentence is carried as a groovydoc comment until `@Spec` lands. Zigzag is the instructive one:
its round-trip laws prove over mathematical integers (LemmaScript's `number` model), and `@CheckOverflow`
refutes the same `encode` on Java's 32-bit `int` (`encode(Integer.MIN_VALUE)` is really `-1`). Zigzag also needs
`decode` to state what it computes — Dafny sees through a function body at a call site, groovy-verify reasons
through the callee's contract — and that need is what exposed this phase's gap.

**Open (recorded in the doc's "Not ported yet"):** `break` in a verified loop (every LemmaScript `break` +
`done_with` became an early `return`); prefix counts (`arr[0..<i].count(x)`, LemmaScript's `occOf`), which
block Boyer–Moore majority; list building (`findAll`, list recursion, element facts after `add` — `pruneWindow`
proves only its size bound); nonlinear arithmetic (the front page's money-splitting `allocate`). Also met on the
way: a loop that writes a local's *contents* forgets facts the loop can't change (`r != null`, `r.length`, and
`leftPad`'s `n == len - str.length()`), so ports restate them as invariants where Dafny frames them for free. (Closed by
Phase 318. `break` was closed by Phase 312.)

**Perf ceilings re-based.** `test` reached 7,093 solver checks against the 7,000 ceiling (distinct VCs 4,239
of 4,500). The engine change is not the cause: the corpus before this phase measured 6,818 checks in `verify`,
and adding the first seven P309 cases took it to 6,838 — about three checks a case, with the existing corpus
unchanged. The ceiling was simply within 200 of the corpus at 6.0.0. Re-based to 8,000 checks and 5,000 distinct
VCs.

## Phase 310 — early exits and the fall-through path: a soundness fix  *(shipped — engine change)*

**A soundness fix to Phase 49/49b, found while checking how GROOVY-12126 (non-local control flow for closures)
would interact with the `break` work.** On the natural path out of a loop, `checkUse` assumed **every**
early-return guard false — in the state *after* the loop. A guard is a fact about the state it was evaluated in,
and the post-loop state is not that state:

- **An in-body guard ran against earlier iterations' values.** `while (i < n) { if (i == 3) return 0; i++ }`
  never evaluates the guard at `i == 3` when `n == 3`; the loop stops first and returns `i == 3`. Assuming
  `i != 3` at exit ruled that run out, so `@Ensures({ result != 3 })` "proved". `f(3)` fails at runtime.
- **A zero-iteration loop never evaluates its in-body guard at all**, even one over an unchanging parameter.
- **A prefix guard over a variable the loop changes** was assumed in the post-loop state. `int j = k; if (j == 0)
  return 2; while (j > 0) j--` drives `j` to 0, so assuming `j != 0` after the loop made the path contradictory
  and *any* postcondition proved.
- **A `return` inside a `.each` closure** (the GROOVY-12126 route) ends only that element's call: the iteration
  continues. The `.each` → for-in modelling kept it as a `return`, which Phase 49b then read as a *method* return.
  `a.each { if (n == 0) return 2 }; return n == 0 ? 5 : 2` "proved" `result == 2`, though `f(new int[0], 0)` returns
  5. In the other direction it refuted true claims (`result = 8`).

All four were confirmed against groovy-contracts at runtime (`PostconditionViolation`). The runtime rung missed
them because no corpus case had these shapes — every early-exit proof in the corpus gets its natural-path facts
from its invariant, which is also why no existing case changed when the assumption was dropped.

**The fix (`VerifyChecker`):**

1. `checkUse` never assumes an **in-body** guard false on the fall-through path.
2. A **prefix** guard is assumed false only when nothing after it can change what it reads (`prefixGuardStable`):
   every variable in it is a parameter or local of a value type (primitive, boxed, String — nothing can mutate it
   in place), and no assignment form (`=`, `op=`, `++`/`--`) targets it in the rest of the prefix or the loop.
   This deliberately doesn't reuse `modifiedLocations`, which misses compound assignment, `++`/`--` and most mutators.
3. When a prefix guard *isn't* stable, a plain `while`/`for` loop gets the precise context
   (`assumePrefixThenSummary`): replay the prefix, assert each prefix guard false where it was evaluated, then
   summarise the loop with the nested-loop summary (`LoopEncoder.summarizeInner`: havoc its writes, assume
   `inv ∧ ¬guard`). Without it the refutation was right but the reproduction wasn't: the post-loop symbols floated
   free of the prefix, and `fails on: f(0)` named a call that takes the early exit. Other loop shapes, and loops
   whose writes the summary can't frame, keep the coarse context, which is still sound.
4. A `.each`/`.eachWithIndex`-derived loop (`LoopSpec.fromEach`) whose closure body contains a `return` outside
   nested closures skips loudly — "acts like `continue`" — until `continue` is modelled. The skip also covers
   preservation: those iterations would otherwise be excluded from the preservation check.

**Shipped tests (group `P310 early exits and the fall-through path`, 6 cases):** the counter guard refutes with
`fails on: f(3)`; the zero-iteration loop refutes; a prefix guard on an unchanged parameter still carries (proves);
a prefix guard on a variable the loop changes refutes with the real failing call `f(1)`; `.each` and
`.eachWithIndex` closure returns skip loudly.

**Seen on the way, not fixed:** a counterexample over a *reassigned parameter* shows its post-loop value as the
argument (`k = 0`, `fails on: f(0)`, where the failing call is `f(1)`). The P310 case uses a local copy so its
pinned reproduction is the true one; the reproduction builder should read a parameter's entry value.

**GROOVY-12126, when it lands:** plain loop `break`/`continue` are untouched (the rewriter only touches statements
inside closures passed to a call). Inside `.each`, `break`/`continue` would reach the checker as
`throw LoopControl.BREAK` / `CONTINUE`, since the rewriter runs at CANONICALIZATION and edits in place the closure
statements this project's CONVERSION-time `.each` modelling shares. The `break` slice will recognise
`LoopControl.BREAK` as a break in `.each`-derived loops; `CONTINUE` joins the closure `return` as `continue`.

## Phase 311 — replaying to an obligation: a soundness fix  *(shipped — engine change)*

**Found while designing `break` support, whose after-loop checks replay the body up to each `break`.** An
implicit obligation inside a loop body (an index, a divisor) is discharged by `dischargeSeeded`: assert the
region's entry facts (`assumePos`, e.g. invariant ∧ guard), replay the statements before the obligation
(`preceding`), check. Two holes, both confirmed at runtime and both missed:

- **R1 — stale values after an early-exit `if`.** `while (i < a.length) { if (a[i] == 7) return 1; i = i + 1;
  int x = a[i] }` — `f([1] as int[])` throws `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`. The replay reached the exit `if`,
  `LoopEncoder.symExec` threw on the `return`, and the exception was swallowed with the comment "leave those vars
  havoc". They weren't havoc'd: every write after the throw point simply never applied, so `a[i]` was checked
  against the `i` from before `i = i + 1`.
- **R2 — a branch condition assumed in the wrong state.** `while (i < n) { i = i + 1; if (i > 0) { x =
  10.intdiv(i - 1) } }` — `f(1)` divides by zero. The branch condition was added to `assumePos`, which is asserted
  in the region's *entry* state, before `preceding` is replayed. So it assumed "the old `i` > 0", which makes the
  divisor look non-zero. The same shape applied to the early-exit narrowing (`if (c) return` → the rest of the
  region runs under `¬c`) and to `&&` / `||` / ternary guards.

Also fixed on the way: **R3** — the straight-line call-site replay havocs a statement it can't model using
`modifiedLocations`, which saw only `=` (not `op=`, `++`/`--`); `int i = 0; i++; g(i)` checked `g`'s
precondition against `i == 0`. And an **assignment's value** (`ok = l && r`, `boolean b = c ? x : y`) was one leaf
for the short-circuit discharge, so its guards were ignored entirely — a false positive that also meant a
short-circuit refute proved nothing about the state fix until it was handled.

**The fix:**

1. **Conditions are assumed where they're evaluated.** A branch, ternary or `&&`/`||` condition is no longer an
   `assumePos` fact; it becomes an assume marker (a synthetic `AssertStatement` tagged `REPLAY_ASSUME_KEY`,
   `withAssume`) at the end of `preceding`, so it is asserted after the replay reaches its point. Entry facts
   (precondition, invariant, guard) stay in `assumePos`. Markers still feed the index-site quantifier stripping
   and the NIA monotonicity-lemma context, as the `assumePos` conditions did.
2. **An exit-aware replay** (`LoopEncoder.replay`): an `if` whose branch always leaves (return / throw / break /
   continue) asserts the condition false (or the else-branch's condition true) and replays the other branch as
   straight-line code; both leaving makes the rest unreachable. This replaces the region-level narrowing. The loop
   VCs keep the strict `symExec`, so an exit shape they don't recognise still loud-skips.
3. **Nothing stale when a replay fails** (`replaySafely`): a statement that can't be replayed havocs everything it
   and every later statement may write (`havocWritesOf` — every assignment form, element and field stores, call
   receivers, reference arguments, all instance fields for an implicit-this call), and only the markers after the
   last real statement are still assumed. Used by `dischargeSeeded` and the call-site check's in-loop prefix.
4. `modifiedLocations` sees every assignment form and `++`/`--`.
5. `dischargeExpression` descends into an assignment's value.
6. **Counterexamples keep the branch value** (`SmtSession.displayAs`). Assuming a condition at the right point
   means it now reads the replayed state, which can be an internal `#`-named symbol the counterexample display
   hides — the Kerridge ALT witnesses lost `r$index = 1` (the `select()` branch taken) because that value is now
   this iteration's `select#k`, not the entry-state symbol the old (wrong-state) assumption happened to show. A
   marker's variables whose current binding is hidden are displayed under their source names; display-only. The
   two quoted diagnostics in `examples/kerridge.md` match again unchanged.
7. In the replay fallback, a marker after the failure point is still assumed when it reads nothing that was
   havoc'd.

**Shipped tests (group `P311 replaying to an obligation`, 7 cases):** R1 refutes with `fails on: f([8] as int[])`,
and the guarded read proves; R2 refutes with `f(1)`, and `i > 1` proves; the short-circuit form refutes and
proves the same way (the `i > 0` refute is only possible if the guard is assumed about the new `i`); `i++` before
`g(i)` refutes. No existing case changed: 2186/2186.

## Phase 312 — `break`  *(shipped — engine change)*

Gap 1 from the LemmaScript port: every LemmaScript loop that leaves with `break` (plus `//@ done_with`) had to be
rewritten to an early `return`. A `break` is an early exit whose continuation is the code after the loop rather
than the end of the method, so it rides the Phase 49b in-body exit machinery with a different continuation.

- **Recognition.** `if (c) break` and `if (c) { s1; …; sn; break }` at the top level of the loop body (an
  `EarlyExit` with `isBreak` and its `lead` statements), and a `break` leaf of the body's final `if`/`else` chain,
  lifted by the Phase 49c desugar exactly as a `return` leaf is — LemmaScript's binary search has the break leaf
  *first* (`if (arr[mid] == target) { result = mid; break } else if …`). The lead may not itself exit or loop.
- **Inside the loop**, nothing new: preservation and progress already run on the path where each exit's condition
  is false, so the breaking iteration need not preserve the invariant or decrease the variant — Dafny's semantics,
  and why the flag rewrite needed an awkward `hi - lo + (result == -1 ? 2 : 1)` measure.
- **After the loop**, from every way out. The postcondition is checked per `break` (`checkEarlyExitPath`: inv ∧
  guard at body entry, the body up to the break with earlier exits not taken, the break's condition, its lead,
  then the code after the loop) as well as from the natural exit. The after-loop region's implicit obligations
  are discharged from each `break` too (inv ∧ guard as entry facts; the body prefix, the break condition as an
  assume marker and the lead as `preceding`) — through Phase 311's replay, which is why 311 came first. `//@
  done_with` needs no counterpart.
- **One bug on the way:** `loopWriteSet` bailed on a `BreakStatement` as "unknown statement", which made the loop's
  write set unbounded and silently dropped every loop-stable `@Requires` from preservation — binary search lost
  `arr.isSorted()` and refuted. A `break` writes nothing.
- **Loud skips:** `continue`; a `break` out of a nested loop (`containsLoopBreak` in `summarizeInner` and the
  nested-loop checks — the inner summary `inner_inv ∧ ¬inner_guard` doesn't cover it); a `break` buried deeper
  than the recognised shapes (the strict body walk still rejects it).

**Shipped tests (group `P312 break`, 12 cases):** LemmaScript's linear search, binary search and isSorted verbatim;
a classic `for` whose `break` skips the update; `while (true)` left only by its `break`; a break lead that leaves
the invariant behind and still proves; refutes for a postcondition wrong only from the break (`fails on:
firstNegative([-1] as int[])`), one wrong only on the natural exit (`firstNegative(new int[0])`), and an after-loop
division safe from the natural exit but not from the break (`f([-1] as int[])`); loud skips for a nested-loop
break, a buried break and `continue`.

**The LemmaScript port** (`examples/lemmascript.md`) now runs LemmaScript's binary search, linear search and
isSorted with their own `result` + `break` loops; the mapping table's `break` row and the "Not ported yet" list
are updated.

**GROOVY-12126, not done here:** recognising `throw LoopControl.BREAK` as a break in `.each`-derived loops (Phase
310 note). That class doesn't exist in Groovy 6, so the code couldn't be tested; it's ready to add once the
change lands.

## Phase 313 — a failing producer: the close has to be reached  *(shipped — a soundness fix to Phase 245)*

Found by checking the ladder against two open upstream PRs. apache/groovy#2987
([GROOVY-12459](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/GROOVY-12459)) is about a producer that throws before
`channel.close()`: `for await` hangs, and the exception stays on the `async` handle that was thrown away.
Phase 245 made an iteration depend on its root's close, but it treated a close as unconditional whenever it
wasn't syntactically inside an if, loop or catch. So it ignored the **exceptional path**, and the hang
compiled clean. A probe confirmed it: `async { out.send(boom()); out.close() }` with `boom()` always
throwing, drained by `for (v in out)`, was silently certified.

- **The check.** When the network analysis finds the close an iteration waits for, and that close is in a
  different process, it walks the closing process (`closeBypass`) for a throw that runs before the close and
  isn't covered. If it finds one, it withholds the certificate with a loud network skip naming the throw. "Can
  throw" means an explicit `throw`, or a call to a method of the enclosing class (implicit `this`, a static
  call, or `C.m()`) that declares `throws`, carries `@ThrowsIf`, or has a body that throws (transitively,
  through further own-class calls). A throw inside a `try` with a catch-everything clause (untyped, `Exception`,
  `Throwable`) doesn't count.
- **Covered:** a `finally` that closes the channel, or a catch-everything `catch` that closes it. The JIRA's
  fixed shape (`try { …; out.close() } catch (Exception e) { out.close() }`) certifies. The catch's close is
  its **twin**: the same close on the failure path. `collectTwinCloses` keeps it out of the recorded uses, so it
  isn't a second, conditional close.
- **A second hole on the way.** The task-side use walk had no `visitTryCatchFinally`, so a close only in a
  task's `catch` counted as unconditional, and a drain waiting on it was certified while hanging on the
  success path. Catches now count as conditional on the task side, as they already did on the main side.
- **Honest boundary.** A library call is assumed to return normally (it's opaque everywhere else in the
  fragment too). Implicit throw-sites (division, parsing, dereference, index) are proof obligations already,
  and discharged they can't throw. A throw in the *same* process as the iteration is out of scope: it exits
  before the wait. Arguments are elided in the message (`someCall(…)`), because a Phase 248-unrolled loop would
  otherwise echo its frozen constants rather than the source. A `throw` with no source position is ignored:
  woven loop `@Invariant`/`@Decreases` checks have none, and they're proved. The first full run withheld 10
  streaming certificates on exactly those before this was added.
- **Not yet:** `close(Throwable)` / `getCloseCause()` from #2987 aren't in the 6.0.0 pin. Once they land, a
  `catch (e) { out.close(e) }` should count as covering too, and the drain claim becomes "finishes, or rethrows
  the producer's failure after the values already sent" (with the propagation through
  `map`/`filter`/`merge`/`split`/`tap` the PR specifies).

**Shipped tests (group `P313 failing producer`, 11 cases):** withheld for the JIRA's own loop shape, a one-shot
send whose argument throws, a transitive thrower, an explicit `throw`, a `throws IOException` callee and an
`@ThrowsIf` callee; certified for a close in `finally`, the twinned catch close, a producer calling a total
method, and a throw the producer catches itself; a close only in a `catch` is the conditional-close skip.
Docs: the drain-discipline subsection of `examples/concurrency.md` (one linked case and its diagnostic) and a
CAPABILITIES row.

**The other PR, #2986** ([GROOVY-12457](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/GROOVY-12457)) is Phase 314, below.

## Phase 314 — parallel-collection callbacks are pool tasks, not processes  *(shipped)*

The other PR from that check: apache/groovy#2986
([GROOVY-12457](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/GROOVY-12457)). A blocking callback in
`eachParallel`/`@Parallel` can hold its ForkJoin worker while a sibling it waits for stays queued. Even with the
fix, a pool of size `n` hosts at most `n` concurrent blockers, and the common pool is still exposed to
contention. The Phase 255 liveness certificates and the Phase 243/277 deadlock certificates assume weak fairness,
which doesn't hold here. The probe was expected to show a scope gap. It showed **a wrong verdict**: the
use walk scans a non-async closure as code of the enclosing process, so a sibling barrier
(`Phaser(2)`, `[1, 2].eachParallel { gate.arriveAndAwaitAdvance() }`) was refuted as "constructed for 2 parties
but only 1 process arrives". The same happened with a `@Parallel` loop (it lowers to `eachParallel` at semantic
analysis) and with callbacks inside a forked process.

- **The check.** `recordParallelUsesIfAny` recognises the callback of the 17 callback-taking `*Parallel` methods
  of `ParallelCollectionExtensions` on both walks (main side and task side). Inside it, every barrier op, channel
  end-use, `select()` and `for (v in ch)` is recorded in `ParCtx.parallelUses`, and marked (`parallelOps`) so the
  per-process recorders pass over it. If there are any, `checkNetworkWellFormedness` withholds the method's
  barrier and network certificates with one loud skip per medium, naming the op and the callback. The skip says
  "the @Parallel loop" when the callback's parameter has the lowering's `$parallel_` prefix, so it echoes the
  source.
- **Why the whole method.** The call blocks its caller until every callback returns, so the rest of the network's
  progress rests on the same pool scheduling.
- **Honest boundary.** Name-based recognition (the receiver isn't type-checked). Media gv doesn't model
  (`CyclicBarrier`, `CountDownLatch`, the PR's own example) carry no claim either way, so nothing is said. A
  callback that blocks on nothing is unaffected. A shape that is certain to deadlock, where the callback waits for
  something its caller does only *after* the call returns (`[1].eachParallel { ch.first() }; ch.send(1)`), is
  skipped rather than refuted. Refuting it is a possible follow-up.

**Shipped tests (group `P314 parallel callbacks`, 8 cases):** withheld for a sibling barrier, a `@Parallel` loop
body (named as such), callbacks inside a forked process, a sibling channel exchange and a drain inside a callback.
Unaffected: a non-blocking `collectParallel`, and a lockstep barrier beside a non-blocking callback (still
certified). A barrier that really is one process short still refutes. Docs: a paragraph closing the weak-fairness
section of `examples/concurrency.md` (one linked case and its diagnostic) and a CAPABILITIES row.

**Found on the way:** a Phase 277 barrier soundness hole, fixed as Phase 315 below.

---

## Phase 315 — barrier counts: every round needs every party  *(shipped — a soundness fix to Phase 277)*

Found while probing Phase 314. With static enrolment the barrier certificate rests on each process's **sync
count**, because every round needs every party. Phase 277 checked only that there were *enough* processes.
Probes showed five shapes compiling clean that hang at runtime:
- two straight-line ones: the method body syncing twice against a task syncing once, and three processes on a
  `Phaser(2)`;
- three non-one-shot ones: a sync in a two-iteration `for`, in a sequential `[1, 2].each { … }`, and in a
  closure that's never called.

The round check never saw them. A round with a single member is skipped (`ids.size() < 2`), and conditional
syncs were passed over silently ("no claim either way"). The scanners counted a non-async closure body as one
unconditional run of the enclosing process.

- **Not one-shot → loud skip.** A barrier op inside an `if`, loop, `catch` or **closure** is conditional. The
  main-side `ParScanner` and the task-side walk now track closure depth for barrier ops. Any conditional op on a
  barrier withholds its certificate (`formatBarrierNotOneShot`), as a non-one-shot channel op always has (the
  channel side was already loud). Like Phase 278's dynamic-enrolment skip, it stops the rest of the method's
  network check.
- **Exactly N processes, unequal counts → refuted** (`formatBarrierRoundShort`): "can never complete round m+1 …
  the method body syncs 2 times but the task forked at line 6 only 1". A finished process doesn't deregister, so
  the round after the fewest never fills. This is certain, whatever the schedule.
- **More processes than parties.** One-shot arrivals that aren't a whole number of rounds are **refuted**
  (`formatBarrierArrivals`): the last round never fills. A whole number of rounds is **skipped** loudly
  (`formatBarrierSurplus`), since which processes meet in which round is the scheduler's call.
- **Fewer processes than parties** is Phase 277's existing refutation, unchanged.
- **Honest boundary.** A `while (true)` lockstep is fine at runtime but now skips: its count is unbounded, and the
  certificate counts rounds. Counting a literal-bounded loop's syncs (the way Phase 248 unrolls channel traffic)
  would certify `for (i in 0..<k)` lockstep. That is now Phase 316. Dynamic enrolment (Phase 278) is
  untouched.

**Shipped tests (group `P315 barrier counts`, 11 cases):**
- refuted: one sync more than the partner, either way round; a surplus process that can never be partnered;
- skipped: surplus processes in whole rounds; a sync in a loop, an `if`, an `each` closure, a closure never
  called, a task's nested closure, and a `while (true)` lockstep;
- certified: three processes in lockstep for two rounds.

All 11 Phase 277 cases are unchanged. Docs: a paragraph in the barrier section of `examples/kerridge.md` (one
linked case and its diagnostic) and a CAPABILITIES row.

---

## Phase 316 — literal-bounded barrier loops are counted  *(shipped)*

The follow-up Phase 315 named. c14 runs its phases in a loop, and after Phase 315 any loop sync was a loud
skip, so even a correct `for (i in 0..<3)` lockstep got no certificate. The Phase 248 unroller already turns a
literal-bounded channel loop into straight-line one-shot traffic before the structural walk, in the method body
and inside forked tasks. It is keyed on a set of variable names: a `for` whose body calls a method on one of
them unrolls.

- **The change.** One line of intent: the Phaser variables (`collectPhaserVars`) join the channel variables in
  that set. A literal-bounded loop that syncs a barrier is then k one-shot syncs, and the Phase 315 count checks
  decide it with no change of their own:
  - a lockstep of loops certifies (a for-in in one process and a C-style `for` in the other is fine);
  - a loop of k against a partner's m ≠ k is refuted at round m + 1;
  - barriers crossed inside the loops are the named circular wait.
- **Boundary, unchanged from Phase 248.** Literal bounds only, at most `CHANNEL_UNROLL_LIMIT` (32) iterations,
  and a body inside the copying fragment. Anything else stays a loop and keeps the Phase 315 not-one-shot skip:
  a symbolic bound, an over-limit loop, `while (true)`, and a sync inside a closure such as `each`.
- **Found, not fixed: values across a barrier.** A method that declares a Phaser is outside the value model
  ("assignment 'gate = new java.util.concurrent.Phaser(2)' is outside fragment"), so an `@Ensures` on a
  barrier-synchronised computation is skipped loudly, not proved. A barrier moves no data, so treating the
  declaration and its syncs as value no-ops would be sound for partial correctness, given PAR disjointness
  (Phase 240). That is now Phase 317.

**Shipped tests (group `P316 barrier loops`, 5 cases):**
- certified: a lockstep of literal-bounded loops;
- refuted: a loop of two against a single sync; loops with different literal bounds; barriers crossed inside
  literal loops;
- skipped: a loop over the unroll limit.

The Phase 315 loop case is now a refutation, so that case moved to a symbolic bound (renamed "a sync in a
symbolic-bound loop withholds the certificate"), keeping a test of the skip. Docs: the barrier-count paragraph
of `examples/kerridge.md` and a CAPABILITIES row.

## Phase 317 — a barrier moves no data: values across barrier rounds  *(shipped)*

The gap Phase 316 found. A method that declares a Phaser was outside the value model ("assignment 'gate = new
java.util.concurrent.Phaser(2)' is outside fragment"), so `@Ensures` on a barrier-synchronised computation was
skipped. That includes the Phase 316 lockstep with work between its rounds, and c14's sync-then-exchange. A
barrier orders processes and reads and writes no program state. With PAR disjointness (Phase 240) holding, the
values a method computes are those of its body without the barrier.

- **The pass.** `ChannelDesugar.desugarBarriers` runs after the network checks, which use the barrier ops on the
  body as written, and before the Phase 118 dataflow desugaring. It drops each Phaser's declaration and every
  statement that is just a call on it, with the result discarded. It works in the body, nested blocks,
  if-branches and `async` arms, rebuilding them with `rebuildAsyncCall` rather than mutating them, since they
  share nodes with the live AST. A bare arm left empty is dropped too: an empty `async { }` would otherwise be a
  "standalone call" the value model refuses.
- **Two claims, independent.** Ordering and progress are the barrier certificate's claim. Values are the value
  model's, partial correctness as everywhere else. A stuck barrier is still refuted next to a value claim that
  proves, and a sync in a branch skips the barrier certificate while the value claim is decided.
- **Honest boundary.** A Phaser referenced any other way, such as its phase number read (`int p =
  gate.arriveAndAwaitAdvance()`) or passed to a call, is left alone, so the value model keeps its loud skip
  rather than seeing a dangling name. A sync inside a loop that survives unrolling isn't dropped (loops carry
  `@Invariant` and the loop encoder keys on the statement), so it keeps the skip too.

**Shipped tests (group `P317 barrier values`, 7 cases):**
- proved: a value computed across lockstep rounds; a reply after a barrier phase, over a parameter; sequential
  code around a sync; a sync in a branch, where the barrier skips and the value proves;
- refuted: a wrong value across lockstep rounds; a stuck barrier beside a value claim;
- skipped: a phase number read.

Docs: a paragraph after the barrier counts in `examples/kerridge.md` (one linked case; the example count goes to
41) and a CAPABILITIES row.

## Phase 318 — loop frame facts: what the loop can't change, it keeps  *(shipped — engine change)*

Gap 3 of the LemmaScript ports (Phase 309's "also met on the way"). Every loop VC but establishment starts from a
fresh state: the invariant, the guard and Phase 64's loop-stable `@Requires` conjuncts. A local the prefix set and
the loop never touches therefore lost its value there. `leftPad` had to restate `n == len - str.length()`;
`int[] r = new int[n]` filled by `r[i] = 0` forgot `r.length == n` (a spurious out-of-bounds and a failed
postcondition); `List out = []` built by `add` got a spurious null-dereference on `out.add`; and `int n =
a.length` didn't bound `a[i]` in the body. Parameters already kept their facts (Phase 64), but locals didn't. Dafny
frames all of these for free.

- **The facts** (`loopFrameFacts`, computed once per site):
  - **Value:** `x == e` for a top-level prefix assignment `x = e`. Neither `x` nor any name in `e` may be written
    by the loop (its guard included) or by the rest of the prefix, or assigned in any closure of the method. `e`
    must be pure (`collectWritesExpr` finds no write) and read only parameters and locals, never fields.
  - **Shape:** for `x = new T[len]`, `[]`, `[:]` or `new C(…)` that the loop doesn't reassign but may write
    into: `x != null`, and for an array `x.length == len` when `len` is itself stable. Content writes are told
    apart by `LoopEncoder.innerFrame` (arrays: element stores; lists: mutators), intersected with the
    conservative `collectWritesStmts`, so a write hidden in an assignment's right-hand side still counts.
  - **No facts at all** when the loop's writes can't be bounded: the Phase 64 default.
- **Where they're assumed:** with the stable `@Requires` in preservation, progress and the for-in per-element check;
  after the loop in the use check; at an in-body early exit; and in the implicit-obligation pass (guard, body,
  after the loop, at each `break`).
- **A trap, caught by a probe before it shipped:** `int m = k; m = m + 1` would have produced the fact
  `m == m + 1`. The right-hand side reads the *old* `m`, so as a fact it's false and proves everything. The
  assigned name is excluded from its own right-hand side's stable set.
- **Boundary:** a local assigned twice in the prefix isn't framed, because neither assignment survives the
  other, so `m == k + 1` isn't proved. Composing successive prefix assignments would close that. Facts come from
  top-level prefix statements only.
- **The LemmaScript ports are verbatim again.** `leftPad` proves with exactly the original's four invariants,
  and `pruneWindow`'s invariant drops its `out != null`.

**Shipped tests (group `P318 loop frame`, 14 cases):**
- proved: leftPad's shortfall, a local copy of a parameter, a filled array's length and nullness, a list built by
  `add`, a local array length bounding the body's index, and the Phase 64 parameter case;
- refuted, the soundness half: a local the loop reassigns, a local whose source the loop writes, a
  self-referencing prefix update, an array the loop reassigns, a list's size, an array length whose source the
  loop writes, and an array's contents;
- the boundary: a local updated twice before the loop.

Docs: `examples/lemmascript.md` (leftPad's prose and both ports), FRAGMENT's loop paragraph, and a CAPABILITIES row.

---

## Phase 319 — Boyer–Moore majority: later loops keep earlier loops' exit facts  *(shipped — engine change)*

Gap 4 of the LemmaScript ports, `majority.ts`. Its invariants count occurrences in a prefix through a recursive
`occOf(arr, x, n)`, which is `arr[0..<n].count(x)` in Groovy. The gap was recorded as "prefix counts have no
axioms", but that was out of date: Phase 208's range count already has base and step axioms, and pass 2's
counting loop proved at once. Probing in layers found two real blockers.

- **The second loop forgot the first.** The postcondition check of the last loop asserted `@Requires`, its own
  invariant and its negated guard, but nothing about `cand`, which the first loop had established. The dumped
  query left `cand` free; with `result = cand` negative it was satisfiable, and Z3 returned UNKNOWN through the
  quantifiers. Phase 207 made every later loop restate such facts (the OpenJML `maintaining` discipline). Dafny
  doesn't: the second loop never writes `cand`, `cnt` or `i`. **The fix extends Phase 318's frame**
  (`frameEarlierLoop`): for an annotated loop in the prefix, each invariant conjunct, and the negated guard, none
  of whose names the current loop, the code between, or a closure writes, is a frame fact everywhere Phase 318's
  facts are assumed. Not for a loop with a `break` (its breaking iteration needn't preserve the invariant or
  falsify the guard), nor across an implicit-this call. Phase 207's "teeth" case still refutes: its dropped fact
  is over an array the later loop writes.
- **The trailing `if`/`else` return.** `majority.ts` ends with `if (2 * occ > arr.length) return cand else return
  -1` after its last loop, which was "unsupported statement IfStatement after loop". `LoopEncoder.returnedBy` reads
  an `if`/`else` (and `else if` chains) both of whose branches only return as the matching ternary. An `if`
  without an `else` falls through, so it keeps the loud skip.
- **Ruled out on the way: a matching loop in the step axiom.** The step `bcount(l,h) == bcount(l,h-1) + …` is
  triggered on `bcount` and mints a fresh `bcount` term each time it fires. I tried Dafny's limited-function
  (fuel) encoding, a twin `bcountL$` the step unfolds into. Neither `majority` nor its refutations needed it, so
  it didn't ship.
- **Unbounded quantifiers.** LemmaScript's `forall(y: int, …)` and `exists(x: nat, …)` have no native Groovy
  spelling. The port ranges them over the array's own values (`arr.every` / `arr.any`). A value that never
  occurs has count 0, so it adds nothing to the `exists`, and `cnt <= i` covers it for the `forall`.
- **Boundaries.** A wrong claim under the quantified count axioms (`result != -1`) comes back "could not decide",
  not with a counterexample: Z3 can't build a model through them, with or without the limited encoding. The
  whole-array `arr.count(x)` of an array and the prefix `arr[0..<arr.length].count(x)` are different functions with
  no bridge, so the port states its postconditions as full-length prefix counts, which is what `occOf(arr, x,
  arr.length)` is.

**Shipped tests (group `P319 majority`, 9 cases):**
- proved: `majority.ts` verbatim; pass 1 alone (its two counting invariants together); pass 2 alone; a later loop
  keeping an earlier loop's exit facts; an `else if` return chain after a loop;
- refuted: not kept when the code between the loops writes them, or when the later loop does;
- skipped: an `if` without an `else` after a loop;
- undecided, the boundary: a wrong majority claim.

Docs: a "Majority vote" section in `examples/lemmascript.md` (one linked case; its "Not ported yet" entry
replaced by the whole-array-count boundary; two rows in its translation table), and the Phase 207 restate rule
reworded in FRAGMENT, CAPABILITIES, `examples/dafny.md` and the P207 group description. Plus a CAPABILITIES row.

## Phase 320 — list building: element facts, findAll, and a write-set bail  *(shipped — engine change)*

Gap 5 of the LemmaScript ports, recorded as "`findAll`, list recursion, element facts after `add`". Probing showed
element facts after `add` already worked: `(0..<out.size()).every { k -> out[k] > 0 }` and the exact
`out[k] == 2 * xs[k]` both proved. What failed `pruneWindow`'s second postcondition was something else.

- **The write-set bail.** The window bound needs the precondition's `t <= now` inside the loop. Phase 64 assumes
  the `@Requires` conjuncts a loop can't invalidate, but its write-set walk (`collectWritesExpr`) treated a list,
  map or array literal as an "unknown expression kind" and bailed to "unbounded writes". So a prefix as ordinary
  as `List<Integer> out = []` dropped *every* loop-stable precondition from preservation and progress. That was
  never unsound, only weaker than it should have been, which is why no case caught it. A literal now writes
  exactly what its elements write. `pruneWindow`'s LemmaScript port carries both postconditions (case renamed
  from "pruneWindow size bound" to "pruneWindow").
- **`findAll`.** `Encoder.tryRecordFindAllAssign`, hooked into `tryRecordFactoryAssign` (so declarations, loop-body
  assignments and returns all see it), binds `src.findAll { t -> p(t) }` to a fresh non-null list with
  `0 <= size <= src.size()`. Every element passes `p` and is drawn from `src`, through a skolem index function
  (`r[k] == src[idx(k)]`), so membership is one universal, not a nested `∀∃`. Membership is what lets `pruneWindow`
  by `findAll` prove its upper bound from the precondition. Not modelled: completeness, order, duplicates. Int
  elements and a single-expression predicate only; anything else stays the loud skip.
- **Still out: recursion that rebuilds a list.** LemmaScript's original `pruneWindow` recurses on `log.slice(1)` and
  rebuilds with `[log[0], ...rest]`. That needs three things this phase didn't add: `drop(n)` as a list value,
  `[x] + rest` concatenation, and a list-valued call result (bound to a local, passed as an argument). Each skips
  loudly today.

**Shipped tests (group `P320 list building`, 12 cases):**
- the literal-prefix fix after a list, an array and a map literal;
- a filter loop's and a map loop's element facts;
- `findAll`: a basic claim, `pruneWindow`, and an indexed local;
- the soundness half: completeness, order, a stronger predicate, a later `add`, and a possibly-null receiver.

Docs: the `pruneWindow` section of `examples/lemmascript.md` (both postconditions, plus the `findAll` one-liner,
two linked cases), its "Not ported yet" narrowed to the recursion, FRAGMENT and README collections, and a
CAPABILITIES row.

## Phase 321 — nonlinear arithmetic beside quantified sums  *(shipped — engine change)*

Gap 6 of the LemmaScript ports, the front page's money-splitting `allocate`: floor each share
`total * w / W`, then hand the leftover back out one at a time, with `ensures sum(\result) === total`. The doc
recorded it as "the solver times out on the nonlinear arithmetic". Probing showed the arithmetic alone was fine:
the floor bracket `q * W <= total * w < q * W + W` proved, and so did a flooring loop's
`s * W <= total * p <= s * W + i * (W - 1)` when nothing else was in the query. Two things were missing.

- **Nonlinear arithmetic beside quantified axioms.** Add `p == ws[0..<i].sum(0)` (the recursive sum axioms are
  universals) and the same loop timed out on preservation and on the postcondition. Z3's nonlinear reasoning and
  its quantifier instantiation don't combine well. `Z3Session.computeCheck` now retries an UNKNOWN query that has
  both (`mixedQuery`) on slices of its top-level conjuncts (`nonlinearSliceProves`):
  - *ground*: the quantifier-free conjuncts plus up to three rounds of each top-level universal's instances at
    the ground terms its trigger matches (`groundSlice`), so the slice is quantifier-free. A universal with no
    pattern (the trigger over `store(a, i, x.intdiv(W))` is refused by `containsForbiddenPattern`) is matched
    by the uninterpreted applications in its body that cover every bound variable, as Z3's auto-patterning would;
  - *linear*: the conjuncts with no nonlinear term, quantifiers kept;
  - failing both, the negated goal is split and each conjunct must discharge on one slice or the other.

  A slice only drops hypotheses or adds instances of universals (any substitution is implied), so its UNSAT is
  the whole query's. Its SAT means nothing, so the retry only ever turns UNKNOWN into VERIFIED. The UNKNOWN
  counter now counts the final verdict. One trap: Z3 numerals are not `APP_AST`s, so the matcher compares
  ground subterms by AST equality first.
- **The range-store sum law.** A store into an array lost every sum over it in a loop body (Phase 69's
  whole-range law is method-body only, and gated on a contract's `.sum()`). Even the linear fill loop
  `r[i] = ws[i]; s += r[i]` with `s == r[0..<i].sum(0)` timed out. `Encoder.emitStoreSumLaw` asserts
  `∀ l, h. sum(store(a, j, v), l, h) == sum(a, l, h) + (l <= j < h ? v - a[j] : 0)`, triggered on the
  post-store sum, from both store executors, gated on a sum term being in play and on `Int` elements.

Not reached: refutation. A model for the recursive sum axioms needs a total `sumArr` satisfying the step for
every range, which Z3's finite models can't express even with every array size pinned small (tried, dropped).
So the first attempt, and other wrong claims in this class, are "could not decide", as Phase 69's skim already
was.

**Shipped tests:**
- group `P321 nonlinear`, 7 cases: the floor bracket and its inexactness (a counterexample, scalar), the flooring
  loop and a too-tight slack (not proved), the fill and bump loops, and a bump by two;
- `LemmaScript port` gains `allocate`, its first attempt (could not decide), and the port without the leftover
  lemma (`result[k]` may be out of bounds).

No existing case changed verdict. UNKNOWN goes from 28 to 35 (the new cases' "could not decide" obligations, and the
precondition-satisfiability checks over their sums), within the ceiling of 40; each obligation the slices prove first
pays the full 2 s timeout, which is most of the added Z3 time.

Docs: the "Splitting money" section of `examples/lemmascript.md` (the port, the lemma, the boundary), two
translation-table rows, "Not ported yet" narrowed to refutation, FRAGMENT's arithmetic and aggregation bullets,
README, and a CAPABILITIES row.

## Phase 322 — the whole-array count meets the prefix count  *(shipped — engine change)*

From the LemmaScript "Not ported yet" list. An array's `a.count(v)` is Phase 12's `count` (an uninterpreted
occurrence count kept by the per-store count law, with no tie to the length), and `a[0..<n].count(v)` is Phase 208's
range oracle `bcount` with base/step axioms. Nothing linked them at `n == a.length`, so a loop that maintained
`c == a[0..<j].count(v)` couldn't conclude `result == a.count(v)` (it timed out), and the majority vote had to state
its postconditions as full-length prefix counts. Lists were never affected: `xs.count(v)` already lowers to
`bcount(xs, v, 0, xs.size())`.

`Encoder.flushCountBridges` asserts `∀v. count(a, v) == bcount(a, v, 0, a.length)` once per array handle,
triggered on either side, so it serves a bound `v` (`a.every { y -> … a.count(y) … }`) and each post-store handle.
It's gated on both spellings meeting in the encoder: a whole count seen first waits (`noteWholeCount`) until a
range count appears. A whole count on its own keeps its historic quantifier profile, which matters because
pulling the range axioms into whole-count-only refutations is what made Phase 208's refutes time out. The
full suite's tallies are unchanged (no existing VC has both spellings).

Seen in passing, not addressed: a whole count with no range count beside it is still unconstrained by the
length, so `@Requires({ a.count(v) == 0 })` doesn't give `a[k] != v`, and the counterexample offered for that is
one the precondition rules out. And the `old.a.count(v)` form across a straight-line store stays undecided:
the store executes before any range count is translated, so Phase 208's range-store law isn't emitted for it.

**Shipped tests (group `P322 count bridge`, 7 cases):**
- the two directions, a bound value, and after a store;
- a counting loop concluding the whole count, and the majority vote with `arr.count(x)` postconditions;
- not over-claimed: a wrong whole count (undecided).

A range count in a `@Requires` makes the precondition-satisfiability check UNKNOWN (no model through the
recursive axioms, as for refutations), so the cases keep range counts out of their preconditions; UNKNOWN headroom
under `PerfBudget.MAX_UNKNOWN` is down to a handful.

Docs: `examples/lemmascript.md` gains the `arr.count(x)` form of the majority postconditions, and the "Not ported
yet" entry is removed; FRAGMENT's count bullet and a CAPABILITIES row.

## Phase 323 — recursion that rebuilds a list  *(shipped — engine change)*

The last list gap of the LemmaScript ports: `pruneWindow` as LemmaScript writes it, recursing on `log.slice(1)`
and rebuilding with `[log[0], ...rest]`. A list-valued call result bound to a local already worked (Phase 225),
so the missing pieces were the list values themselves and how they cross a call.

- **List values.** `Encoder.tryRecordListDerivedAssign`, hooked into `tryRecordFactoryAssign` (so locals,
  returns and loop bodies see it), binds a fresh non-null Int list for `src.drop(k)` (literal `k >= 0`: size
  `max(0, n - k)`, `∀j. d[j] == src[j + k]`) and for a concatenation (`a + b` of list literals and named lists,
  nested freely, or a spread literal `[x, *rest]`): a scalar element is the ground `c[o] == x`, a named segment
  `∀j. o <= j < o + m ⟹ c[j] == seg[j - o]` triggered on `c[j]`, and the size is the segments' sum.
  `listLocalFromCall` now registers its local as a list name, so a call result can be spread or concatenated.
- **List-valued arguments.** `hoistListActuals` binds such an actual to a synthetic list local and passes the
  variable, at the precondition check, in `assumeCalleeEnsures`, and in `dischargeTermination`, where a list
  formal now reads its actual's oracles, so `@Decreases({ log.size() })` sees the dropped list's size.
- **A self-call's list formal clobbered the caller's list.** Phase 226 aliases a list formal's oracles to the
  named actual *by name*, and never restored them. On a self-call the formal `log` is the caller's `log`, so
  after `pruneWindow(log.drop(1), …)` the caller's `log` read as the dropped list (`log[0]` "may be out of
  bounds"). It was harmless while the actual was the same name. The caller's oracles are now saved
  (`Encoder.saveListOracles`) and restored after the `@Ensures` is translated, and on the early returns.

Two soundness fixes found on the way:
- **A spread literal counted as one slot.** `factoryContainerFor` read `[x, *xs]` as a two-element list, so
  `[x, *xs].size() == 2` *proved*. It now refuses a literal with a spread element, which the concatenation model
  takes instead.
- **List arithmetic translated the list as an Int.** `xs + 1` (append), `xs - ys`, `xs * 2`, `xs << x` went
  through the integer dispatch with the list as an `Int` shadow, leaving the result unconstrained, so
  `return xs + 1` was refuted with a counterexample on which it holds. It's now a loud skip.

Not done: `drop` by a symbolic count, `tail()` (which throws on an empty list), and `xs + element`. Also noted:
`listLocalFromCall`'s restore uses `peekSize(name)`, which reads key `name` where `bindSize` writes
`name.size`, so its size restore never fires. Not investigated further.

**Shipped tests:**
- group `P323 list recursion`, 13 cases: `drop` and concatenation values and a wrong `drop` claim, the spread
  literal's size and the claim it used to prove, append still skipping, a recursive length, the caller's list
  after a self-call, recursive `pruneWindow` with a spread rebuild and with an append, a stale entry kept
  (refuted) and `drop(0)` (the measure doesn't decrease);
- `LemmaScript port` gains `pruneWindow recursive`.

The full suite's tallies were unchanged before the new cases.

Docs: `examples/lemmascript.md` leads the `pruneWindow` section with the recursive port, two translation-table
rows, and "Not ported yet" loses the entry; FRAGMENT's list bullet and a CAPABILITIES row.

## Phase 324 — `continue`, and `break` out of a nested loop  *(shipped — engine change)*

The last loop gap of the LemmaScript ports, both loud skips since Phase 312.

- **`continue` is desugared, not modelled.** `ContractExpansionTransform.desugarContinue` rewrites the captured
  loop body before a `for` loop's update is appended: what follows an `if` that may continue moves into both its
  branches, and a `continue` drops the rest of its branch, so `P; if (c) { L; continue }; Q` is
  `P; if (c) { L } else { Q }`. That is exactly a jump to the loop head: the continuing iteration runs the update
  and has to re-establish the invariant, as in Dafny, and every downstream pass sees a continue-free body. It
  applies to `while`, `for`, for-in and do-while. It refuses, leaving the body as it was (so the loud skip
  stands), for a labelled `continue`, one under anything but blocks and `if`s, and a rewrite that would move a
  loop into a branch (nested loops are verified as loops only at a body's top level). A top-level `break` after
  the `continue` ends up inside the `else` and skips loudly as a buried break.
- **A nested loop's `break`.** The inner loop's own preservation and progress already ran on the path where no
  break fires (`symExecBodyWithExits`). What was missing was its summary in the outer VCs: `inner_inv ∧
  ¬inner_guard` is only the natural exit. `LoopEncoder.summarizeWithBreaks` havocs the inner writes (state H) and
  adds one alternative per top-level `if (c) break` / `if (c) { lead; break }`: H as the breaking iteration's
  start, `inv ∧ guard`, the body to the break replayed with earlier exits not taken (`replay`, Phase 311), the
  break's condition, then its lead. A fresh selector picks the alternative, and the bindings are merged as an
  ite over it (`mergeStates`, factored out of `applyIf`). Each alternative runs under the new
  `SmtSession.pushAssertGuard(sel == k)`, so everything its replay asserts holds only on that alternative,
  including the encoder's own facts (a non-null fact, a mint-once axiom: at worst a lost completeness, never a
  leak). A break's state needn't satisfy the invariant. `innerFrame` accepts a `BreakStatement` (it writes
  nothing), and the Phase 109 inner-exit check skips break exits, which have no `@Ensures` of their own.

**Shipped tests:**
- group `P324 continue and nested break`, 13 cases: `continue` in `while`, `for` (the update still runs), for-in
  and do-while, with a lead, from a nested `if`, a wrong one refuted, and one that would move a loop (loud skip);
  a nested break, one whose exact postcondition needs the break's condition, a lead that leaves the inner invariant
  behind, a wrong value from the break (refuted), and an inner `return` beside a break still checked against the
  method's `@Ensures` (refuted);
- `P312 break`: its two loud-skip cases for exactly these features became the shapes that still skip (a nested
  loop's break buried in an `if`, a `continue` ahead of a top-level `break`).

Docs: `examples/lemmascript.md` loses its "Not ported yet" entry and gains a `continue` row; FRAGMENT's loop
paragraph, README's statement list, and a CAPABILITIES row.

## Phase 325 — `continue` ahead of a `break` or `return`  *(shipped — capture change)*
