Phase 324's loud boundary that matters most: the search loop that skips some elements and stops at the one it
wants. Moving what follows `if (c) continue` into the `else` buried a later `if (d) break` / `if (d) return e`,
where neither the Phase 312 break lifting nor the nested-loop break summary looks.

- **A flag, not a branch.** In `ContractExpansionTransform.continueFree`, a top-level `if (c) continue` /
  `if (c) { lead; continue }` (no else, a lead with no exit or loop) whose rest has a `break` or `return` becomes
  `boolean cont#<line>_<col> = c; if (cont) { lead }`, and each later statement is guarded by the flag: an exit
  `if (d) X` becomes `if (!cont && d) X`, a later flag `g = e` becomes `g = !cont && e`, and anything else becomes
  `if (cont) {} else s`, which keeps a tail `if`/`else` chain a chain for Phase 49c's lifting. The `&&`
  short-circuits, so `d` is only evaluated, and its obligations only checked, on an iteration that didn't
  continue. The rest is made continue-free first, so several continues chain. The flag is a body-local, so it is
  re-declared each iteration and needs no invariant, and its `#` keeps it out of counterexamples. Without an exit
  in the rest, Phase 324's branch rewrite stands unchanged.
- **Still out:** a `continue` nested in an `if` ahead of an exit (the old rewrite buries the exit, so loud skip;
  Phase 327 lifts it).
  Separately, and not new: a `for` loop whose body ends in an `if`/`else` chain with a `return` or `break` has its
  update appended after that chain, so the Phase 49c tail lifting doesn't find it (loud skip, with or without a
  `continue`; the `while` form proves). Phase 326 lifts it.

**Shipped tests:**
- group `P325 continue ahead of an exit`, 10 cases: a continue ahead of a break, a search whose break condition
  reaches the postcondition, a return after a continue, two continues ahead of a return/break chain, an exit
  condition that is in bounds only on a non-continuing iteration, a wrong break value and a non-preserving
  continuing iteration (both refuted), a continue ahead of a nested loop's break and a wrong value from it
  (refuted), and a continue nested in an `if` ahead of a break (loud skip);
- `P312 break` drops its "a continue ahead of a break skips loudly" case, which now proves (the first P325 case).

Docs: FRAGMENT's loop paragraph, README's *Out:* list, a CAPABILITIES row.

## Phase 326 — a `for` loop body ending in a `return`/`break` chain  *(shipped — loop-site change)*

The boundary Phase 325 recorded. Phase 49c lifts the exits of the `if`/`else` chain that ends a loop body (each
returning or breaking leaf becomes a top-level `if (pathCond) exit`, ahead of the chain with those leaves
emptied), but only when the chain is the body's last statement. A `for` or for-in loop's update is appended to the
captured body (Phase 59), so the chain never was, and the loop skipped loudly.

- **The update is known.** `LoopSpec.update` records the appended statement at capture. `desugarTailReturns`
  takes it and, when the body ends with it, lifts the chain just ahead and keeps the update last. Sound: a lifted
  exit fires at the chain's entry state and leaves before the update would run (a `break` skips a `for` loop's
  update, a `return` leaves the method), while every continuing leaf still runs it.
- **Nested loops too.** The lifting now also runs on the body of each nested loop when the outer site is built
  (idempotent: an already-lifted body ends in its exit-free residual chain), so a nested loop's chain breaks
  reach `summarizeWithBreaks` as top-level exits, for a nested `while` as much as a `for`.
- **Fixed: a nested `for` loop's init.** `checkNestedEstablishment` ran the outer-body statements before the inner
  loop, but not the inner loop's `init`, so `for (int j = 0; …)` met its invariant with `j` unconstrained: every
  classic `for` nested in a loop was refuted on entry (a false refutation, never a false proof). The init now
  runs before the check.

**Shipped tests:** group `P326 for loop tail chain`, 9 cases: a return/break chain ending a `for` body, breaks
with leads, a for-in body, continues ahead of the chain (Phase 325's flag), a wrong return refuted, the update
still running on the continuing leaf (a step of 2 refutes preservation), a nested `for` loop's chain, and a nested
`for` loop establishing its invariant from its init (and refuted when the init breaks it).

Docs: FRAGMENT's loop paragraph, a CAPABILITIES row.

## Phase 327 — a nested `continue` ahead of a `break` or `return`  *(shipped — capture change)*

Phase 325's boundary: `if (p) { A; if (c) continue; B }; if (d) break` still took Phase 324's branch rewrite,
which moves the exit into both branches of the outer `if`, where the exit lifting doesn't look.

- **A flag set where it continues.** In `ContractExpansionTransform.continueFree`, an `if` that may continue
  (other than Phase 325's top-level `if (c) continue`) whose rest has a `break` or `return` becomes
  `boolean cont#<line>_<col> = false; if (p) { ⟦A; if (c) continue; B⟧ }`, followed by the rest guarded as in
  Phase 325. `flagged` rewrites each branch: an unlabelled `continue` becomes `cont = true` and ends its list,
  and what follows an inner `if` that may set the flag becomes `if (cont) {} else s`, so `B` runs only when the
  iteration didn't continue. It recurses through blocks and nested `if`s and refuses, so the loud skip stands,
  for a labelled `continue`, one under anything else, and a guard that would move a loop into a branch.
- The flag is a body-local declared before the `if`, so it is reset each iteration, needs no invariant, and stays
  out of counterexamples.

**Shipped tests:** group `P327 nested continue ahead of an exit`, 7 cases: a continue nested in an `if` ahead of a
break, one in an `else` that keeps a return from seeing negatives, the rest of the continuing branch skipped
(`s - 1` only when `s != 0`), a continue that doesn't cover the exit and a non-preserving continuing iteration
(both refuted), a nested loop's nested continue ahead of its break, and a nested continue ahead of a loop (loud
skip). `P325`'s "a continue nested in an if ahead of a break skips loudly" case now proves and moved here as the
first case.

Docs: FRAGMENT's loop paragraph, README's *Out:* list, a CAPABILITIES row.

## Phase 328 — `return` in a `.each` closure  *(shipped — capture change)*

Phase 310 made a `return` inside a `.each` closure a loud skip: it ends only that element's call, and reading it
as a method return had "proved" false postconditions. It acts like `continue`, which Phases 324–327 now model.

- **A `continue`, at capture.** `ContractExpansionTransform.eachReturnsAsContinue` copies the closure body's
  if/block spine with each bare `return`, `return k` or `return v` replaced by a `continue`, before the for-in
  spec is built (the real closure is untouched). `.each` discards the value, and a constant or variable has
  nothing left to evaluate. Any other `return` (one that would evaluate an expression, with its own obligations)
  and one inside a nested loop or closure are left alone, so Phase 310's skip still fires, with a message that now
  says what is modelled.
- **Fixed: an `assert` counted as a write.** `collectWritesStmt` didn't know `AssertStatement`, so a body with
  one had an "unbounded" write set: an auto-bounds-only `.each` with an `assert` was taken as accumulating, and a
  postcondition after it skipped loudly. An `assert` writes only what its condition does.
- **Fixed: `eachWithIndex`'s index counted as a write.** The accumulation check removed only the synthetic
  for-in index, not `eachWithIndex`'s user-named one, which its update steps. It now removes whatever the
  update (`LoopSpec.update`, Phase 326) writes.

**Shipped tests:** group `P328 return in a .each closure`, 9 cases: a bare return guarding an assert, a guard that
misses a value (refuted), a constant return in an `eachWithIndex`, a list `.each` with the implicit `it`, a
postcondition after a `.each` that returns, an assert body and an `eachWithIndex` body that are not
accumulations, an accumulating `.each` with a return and a return of an expression (both loud skips). `P310`'s
two `.each` return cases change from loud skips to a refutation (the false `result == 2`, on `f(new int[0], 0)`)
and a proof (`result == 7`).

Docs: FRAGMENT's loop paragraph, README's control-flow list, a CAPABILITIES row.

## Phase 329 — early exits with sequential loops  *(shipped — loop-site change, and a soundness fix)*

Phase 207 verified several annotated loops in sequence, but threw "early exits combined with multiple sequential
annotated loops" as soon as one had a `return` or `break`, so a search loop followed by any other loop skipped
the whole method.

- **Fixed first (unsound before, with a single loop too).** Establishment, the do-while first iteration and the
  prefix exit check assumed every prefix exit's guard false at method entry, then ran the prefix. A guard reads
  the state where it is evaluated: after `x = x + 1`, `if (x == 2) return 0` was taken as `x0 != 2`, which ruled
  out real runs, so `@Ensures({ result != 7 })` over `if (x == 3) return 7` proved (f(2) returns 7), and so did an
  invariant `x != 3` on entry. `walkPrefix` runs the original prefix in order and assumes each exit's guard false
  where it stands, symExec summarising any earlier loop on the way. That is what lets an exit sit after a loop.
- **The skip is lifted.** The last site's prefix is the whole method's up to it, so it checks every prefix exit,
  wherever it sits. An earlier site checks its own in-body returns against `@Ensures`. Its breaks continue into
  the later loops, whose prefix replay summarises it with each break's exit state (Phase 324). Its prefix exits
  are the last site's to check. Phase 310's rule holds: an in-body guard is never assumed false after its loop.
- **An earlier loop that breaks keeps some facts.** Phase 319 dropped all of an earlier loop's exit facts when
  it had a `break`. At a break the state is the iteration's start (`inv ∧ guard`) run through the body up to the
  break and its lead, so a conjunct over nothing written there still holds. `frameEarlierLoop` now keeps those
  conjuncts and drops only the negated guard.

**Known, not new:** a refutation in this shape can print a weak repro. The last loop's use check summarises earlier
loops without replaying the path to them, so the call shown may not reach the failing return, and its
counterexample can name summary variables (`neg$havoc$0`). The verdict is right; the repro is the Phase 310
use-context imprecision.

**Shipped tests:** group `P329 early exits with sequential loops`, 11 cases: the two soundness fixes (a prefix
guard read after the statements ahead of it, refuted on f(2); establishment reading it where it stands, refuted);
a return in the first loop with a sum in the second, and a wrong one (refuted); an exit between the loops reading
the first loop's state, and a wrong one (refuted); the second loop starting where the first broke off; a return in
the second loop; an in-body guard not assumed after its loop (refuted on f(new int[2])); and the break framing's
two limits, a lead that writes a conjunct and the negated guard, both refuted.

Docs: FRAGMENT's loop paragraph, a CAPABILITIES row.

## Phase 330 — several nested loops in one body  *(shipped — loop-site change)*

`verifyNestedLoops` threw "more than one nested loop in the loop body — not yet supported" for a second annotated
loop in an outer body (row-wise matrix work, two passes per row). Everything else already took several: the
outer VCs summarise each nested loop as symExec reaches it, and the obligations pass and Phase 326's tail lifting
iterate over all of them.

- **Each nested loop in turn.** `verifyNestedLoop` is the old single-loop body. Its establishment runs the outer
  body up to the loop (`stmtsBefore`), so the nested loops before it are summarised there and their exit facts
  reach it (`k <= j` from the first loop's `j == n`). Preservation, progress and the loop's returns don't depend
  on its neighbours.
- **A nested return in an earlier sequential loop.** `verifyLoop` passed a null postcondition to the nested
  checks of every outer loop but the last (Phase 207 keeps `@Ensures` for the last site), so a nested loop's
  `return` there wasn't checked. It wasn't a silent pass: the last site can't summarise an outer loop holding a
  nested loop, so the method skipped loudly. It now gets the `@Ensures` whichever site it sits in, and a wrong
  return is refuted, but the correct version still skips at the last loop.

**Shipped tests:** group `P330 several nested loops`, 7 cases: two nested loops in one body; a second whose
establishment needs the first's exit fact; a wrong establishment and a wrong preservation of the second (refuted);
a return in the second, and a wrong one (refuted); a nested return in an earlier one of sequential loops
(refuted).

Docs: FRAGMENT's loop paragraph, README's control-flow list, a CAPABILITIES row.

## Phase 331 — the `test` gate: a repro size cap, and re-based perf ceilings  *(shipped — maintenance)*

The JUnit `test` task (what CI's `check` runs) had been red locally since before Phase 313, while `verify` stayed
green: three failures, none from a loop phase.

- **A counterexample sized near 2^31 exhausted the heap.** `buildFailingCall` renders each array or list
  parameter element by element (`pinnedElements`), and a model is free to size an array at `2147483038`. Under
  `test`'s 2 GB worker heap that threw `OutOfMemoryError`, caught as "internal: Java heap space", so `P202 …
  fulcrum refutes when the best cut is never updated` skipped instead of refuting, and the GC thrash timed out
  `LemmaScript port :: allocate without the leftover lemma`. `verify` passed both only because its JVM takes a
  quarter of physical RAM (16 GB on a 64 GB laptop); `-Xmx2g` on `verify` reproduced it, a bigger `test` heap
  (3 GB, 8 GB) didn't help. CI's Linux Z3 happened to pick smaller models. A failing call is now rendered only when
  every array and list parameter is at most `MAX_REPRO_SIZE` (1000): `new int[2147483647]` is no repro anyone can
  run. `pinnedElements` also indexes with a `long`, so a size past `Integer.MAX_VALUE` can't loop forever.
- **The perf ceilings, re-based.** Phases 313–330 (about 110 cases) took `test` to 8,212 solver checks and 4,910
  distinct VCs, past `MAX_CHECK_CALLS = 8,000` and within 90 of `MAX_DISTINCT_VCS = 5,000`. Re-based ~28–30%
  above, as `PerfBudget` prescribes: 10,500 and 6,400. `MAX_UNKNOWN` stays 40 (36 measured).
- Also: Gradle crashed before running any test, out of memory reading a corrupt previous-results store
  (`build/test-results/test/binary`, from 2026-10-19). That is a regenerable build cache; deleting it fixed it.

## Phase 332 — a repro per caller  *(shipped — reporting fix)*

`allocate without the leftover lemma` reported the same bounds failure twice (the read and the write of
`result[k]`), and the second carried `fails on: allocate(1073751393, new int[0])` beside a counterexample with
`weights.length = 1073741820`. Two identical VCs hit the VC cache, and `Z3Session.check` returned the cached
`CheckResult` object itself. Callers render a result in place: `shown()` swaps the raw counterexample for its
display form (`.size` keys read `.length`, the `?null` flags dropped) and sets `failingCall`. The second caller
rebuilt its repro from the first one's display map, found no `.size` key, and rendered every array parameter as
`new int[0]`. It wasn't just this case: any identical obligation, in the same method or another (the cache is
global), got a wrong repro, and with Phase 331's cap a sound "no repro" was overwritten by a bogus one.

- **The cache keeps a pristine verdict.** `CheckResult.copy()` copies the counterexample maps and notes; the cache
  stores a copy on a miss and hands out a copy on every hit, so each caller renders its own. The verdict, and the
  check counts, are unchanged.

**Shipped tests:** group `P332 a repro per caller`, 3 cases: the read and the write of one element (`f(new int[3],
3)` both times, never `new int[0]`), the same obligation in two methods (each its own call), and an array sized
past the cap getting no failing call (Phase 331). The first two fail against the old cache.

**Seen, not fixed:** that counterexample has `k = 2147483650`, past `int` range, for an `int` local in the second
loop's body; the refutation is genuine (`k` does reach `result.length`), but the value shown can't occur.
*(Fixed in Phase 333.)*

## Phase 333 — loop-written locals in `int` range  *(shipped — soundness of reporting, and two false refutations)*

Phase 332's leftover: `k = 2147483650` for an `int` local. Phase 44c bounds every `int`/`long` parameter and field
to its JVM range, and locals were said to be "bounded transitively via their assignment rhs". That holds in
straight-line code, but not in a loop VC. Preservation, the in-body exits, the post-loop state and the bounds checks
inside the body read a loop-written local at an arbitrary iteration as a fresh value that only the invariant
constrains. With `@Invariant({ k >= 0 })` the solver could pick `k = 2147483648`. That made the counterexample
unreal, and it was a false refutation of claims true for every `int`: `@Ensures({ result <= Integer.MAX_VALUE })`
after a counting loop refuted with `k = 2147483648` (and its `long` twin with a value past `Long.MAX_VALUE`).

- **Bounded at the source.** `collectIntegralNames` records each `int`/`long` param, field and typed local by bit width
  (a name declared with two types in different scopes is dropped). The Encoder asserts the type's range whenever such a
  name's free value is minted: `varForRaw`'s first mint and every `havoc`, so every VC gets it, including preservation,
  which never called `assumeIntJvmBounds`. It is an assumption the JVM guarantees, like the size oracle's
  `0 ≤ size ≤ INT_MAX`. Arithmetic stays mathematical, so the existing gap with wrap-around is unchanged: the bound
  sits on free values, not on `k + 1`.

**Shipped tests:** group `P333 int-range loop locals`, 5 cases: an `int` and a `long` loop local in range after the
loop, an `int` in range at an in-body return (the three refuted before), a wrong bound that still refutes, and the
allocate bump loop's index refutation naming an in-range `k`.

**Seen, not fixed:** that bump-loop refutation now reads `allocate(1, new int[0])` beside `p = 5`, `ws.length = 0`, a
state `ws.sum() > 0` rules out. It is the sequential-loop repro weakness (the earlier loop's writes are havocked and
the repro is built from them), not a range issue.

## Phase 334 — a loop inside a branch  *(shipped — method-level split, plus one unsoundness closed)*

An annotated loop in a branch of an `if` skipped the whole method. `findLoopSites` sees top-level statements only,
so the loop never became a site and the straight-line pass rejected the `WhileStatement`.

- **Split at the `if`.** `branchLoopVariants` finds the first top-level `if` with an annotated loop in a branch (at
  any depth of `if`s inside it) and builds two bodies, `P; assume c; T; R` and `P; assume !c; E; R`, splitting each
  again while one still has such an `if`, so else-if chains and nested ifs come apart too. `verifyBodyVariant` runs
  the per-method checks on each (implicit obligations, then the loops or the straight-line postcondition) with the
  variant published as `ORIGINAL_BODY_KEY`, restored after. The variants cover every path, so this is sound as long
  as the condition is evaluated once with no effect; a condition with an assignment or `++`/`--` is not split.
- **The assume** is an `assert` marked `ASSUME_ONLY_KEY` (the channel ghosts' marker). The loop replay already took it
  as a fact. Three more passes now do: BodyEncoder's path walk and the value-flow scan (as a `Guard`, not an
  obligation), and the post-loop replay.
- **A frame fact.** `loopFrameFacts` keeps an assumed condition when neither the loop nor the prefix after it writes
  what it reads, so preservation and in-body checks see it, and a broken invariant's repro reads `f(1, true)`, not
  `f(1, false)`, which never reaches the loop.
- **Unsoundness closed.** A loop inside a branch of a *loop body* was summarised by `summarizeInner` with its invariant
  assumed, but `verifyNestedLoops` checks only a body's top-level loops, so that invariant was never checked. An inner
  `@Invariant({ i <= 0 })` that contradicts its exit made the branch path vacuous, and `@Ensures({ result == 0 })`
  proved although `f(1, true)` returns 1. `findLoopSites` now refuses that shape loudly.

**Shipped tests:** group `P334 loop inside a branch`, 18 cases (17 since Phase 335 moved the loop-body one): a loop in a then-branch, an else, an else-if chain (two
loops) and a nested if; establishment needing the condition, and failing when it is too weak; preservation, bounds
and postcondition refutations with repros that take the branch, and one from the loop-free arm; loops before and
after the `if`; an early-returning else; the writing condition and the loop-body shape skipping loudly.

**Still out:** a loop inside a branch of a loop body (the same split, applied to the outer body); a writing condition.
*(The loop-body shape is Phase 335.)*

## Phase 335 — a loop in a branch of a loop body  *(shipped — nested-loop checks along a path)*

Phase 334 made this shape loud: the outer loop's VCs summarise the inner loop by its invariant (`summarizeInner`, via
`applyIf`), but `verifyNestedLoops` checked only a body's top-level loops, so nothing proved that invariant. Its
body's obligations went undischarged too: `dischargeRegion` skips annotated loops at every depth, and step 5 of
`verifyLoopObligations` covered top-level inner loops only.

- **The loop and its path.** `branchInnerLoops` walks the outer body into each `if` whose branches hold an annotated
  loop, at any depth of ifs, and returns each loop with its path: the statements before it, with an assume-only
  assert of each branch condition taken (negated on the else side). A writing condition throws, as in Phase 334.
- **The nested checks, along the path.** `verifyNestedLoop` takes the path in place of `stmtsBefore`, so
  establishment runs from outer_inv ∧ outer_guard through the path, branch conditions included. Preservation,
  progress and the inner returns are unchanged.
- **Frame facts.** `assumedPathFacts` keeps each assumed condition that neither the rest of the path, the inner loop
  nor a closure writes. Those are added to the inner loop's stable facts (preservation, progress, in-body returns) and
  to the assumptions its body obligations are discharged under, now also done for these loops.
- **Three deep stays out.** A loop in a branch of a nested loop's body would again be summarised unchecked, so
  `findLoopSites` reports it as "loops nested 3+ deep".

**Shipped tests:** group `P335 loop in a branch of a loop body`, 12 cases: loops in a then-branch, an else and a
nested if; establishment needing the condition; the outer invariant kept through the summary; Phase 334's vacuity
case, now a refutation with repro `f(1, true)`; a broken inner invariant; an out-of-bounds write with a repro that
takes the branch; an inner return against `@Ensures`; a condition the loop writes, not assumed; the writing condition
and the three-deep shape skipping loudly.

**Seen, not fixed:** an inner preservation refutation's repro can leave the outer loop unentered (`f(0, 1)`, `n = 0`):
the inner VCs know neither the outer guard nor the path. That holds for top-level inner loops too.
*(Fixed in Phase 336.)*

## Phase 336 — nested-loop repros enter the outer loop  *(shipped — reporting, plus a do-while unsoundness)*

A nested loop's preservation, progress, in-body returns and body obligations run at an arbitrary inner iteration,
from the inner invariant and guard plus the stable `@Requires`. Nothing tied that state to the outer loop, so a
refutation could pick `n = 0` and render `f(0, 1)`, a call that never enters the outer loop and so doesn't fail.

- **Outer facts at inner iterations.** `outerFactsForInner` returns the outer loop's frame facts (Phase 318: true at
  every outer iteration, so at every inner one) and the conjuncts of the outer invariant and guard, true at outer-body
  entry, over names nothing writes on the way: the statements before the inner loop (its Phase 335 path for one in a
  branch), its init, body and guard, a closure. The invariant is re-parsed contract text with unresolved variables,
  so stability is by name, against the method's params and declared locals only (a field may be written by a call).
  A for-in's per-element clauses (over the loop variable) are left out. They are added to the inner stable facts, so
  they reach preservation, progress and the in-body returns, and to the assumptions of the inner body obligations
  (top-level and branch inner loops). Assuming more true facts can only turn a refutation into a proof the facts
  support, and the outer guard does prove some inner clauses that failed before.
- **Unsoundness closed: do-while nested establishment.** `checkNestedEstablishment` assumed outer_inv ∧ outer_guard,
  but a do-while's first pass runs before either is checked. `@Invariant({ k < n })` on an inner loop under
  `do { … } while (k < n)` proved with `n = 0`. It is now also checked from the loop entry (`walkPrefix`, as Phase 88b
  does for in-body exits). The outer facts above are frame facts only under a do-while.

**Shipped tests:** group `P336 nested-loop repros`, 7 cases: inner preservation and bounds refutations whose repros
enter the outer loop (`f(1, 1)`, `f(new int[0], 1)`); the outer guard proving an inner clause; an outer fact the
outer body overwrites, not assumed; the do-while first pass refuting with `f(0)` and a correct inner invariant
under a do-while verifying; an instance method with a field. G379's bounds case now reads `f(new int[0], 1, true)`.

**Still weak:** the sequential-loop repro (Phase 333's `allocate(1, new int[0])`), where a later loop's state comes
from an earlier loop's havoc. *(Phase 337.)*

## Phase 337 — repros that meet `@Requires`, and loop-summary names  *(shipped — reporting)*

The plain sequential cases already rendered good repros (`f(1)`, `f(new int[0], 1)`): the earlier loop's exit facts
reach the later one. The weak ones had two causes. The allocate bump-loop refutation printed
`allocate(1, new int[0])` beside `ws.length = 0`, under `@Requires({ … ws.sum() > 0 })`. The bounds check drops the
quantified and aggregate conjuncts of the precondition to keep Z3 out of a quantifier+NIA dead end (Phase 91b;
with them, this query is "incomplete quantifiers"), so the model was free to break them. A loop summary's havocked
values showed under internal names: `s$havoc$0 = 1, i$havoc$1 = 1`.

- **The repro is re-checked against the whole `@Requires`.** `reproUnderRequires` runs in `buildFailingCall` when the
  precondition has a quantified or aggregate conjunct (the only ones a VC drops). It pins the rendered arguments
  (scalars, booleans, array and list sizes, and elements up to 64) and checks the full precondition. Met, or
  UNKNOWN: the call stands. Broken: the scalars and sizes alone are tried, and the elements of a model that meets
  it replace the rendered ones, re-checked in turn (`new int[2]` under `a.every { v > 5 }` becomes `[44, 6] as int[]`).
  Neither: no failing call, and the note "no failing call: these arguments break the @Requires, which this check
  assumed only in part (it may not be reachable)". allocate in fact never fails there; the refutation means the
  slack bound is missing.
- **Auxiliary sessions.** These checks decide no obligation, so `Z3Session.auxiliary` gives them a 500 ms timeout,
  no Phase 321 sliced retry, and no count as an UNKNOWN verdict (the check itself counts).
- **Names after a loop.** `shown()` displays the latest `x$havoc$N` of each variable as `x (after a loop)`.

**Shipped tests:** group `P337 sequential-loop repros`, 7 cases: allocate's repro withheld with the note; elements
rebuilt from a precondition model; a quantified precondition whose repro already meets it, kept; `s (after a loop)
= 1` in place of `s$havoc$0`; later-loop preservation, bounds and postcondition repros.

## Phase 338 — a loop after a nested outer loop  *(shipped — loop-summary write set)*

Phase 330's leftover: an annotated loop after an outer loop that holds a nested loop (a row-wise pass, then a plain
one) skipped the method with "nested loop writes a field/collection or unbounded construct — not yet supported". A
later loop replays the earlier ones as summaries, `summarizeInner`: havoc what the loop writes, assume its invariant
and negated guard. Its write set comes from `innerFrame`, which bailed on any loop statement in the body.

- **A nested loop's writes.** `innerFrameStmt` now accepts an annotated loop (one carrying a `LoopSpec`) as writing
  what its init, guard and body write. The guard must write nothing (`guardWritesNothing`: no assignment or
  `++`/`--`, read-only calls only), since `innerFrameExpr` reads assignments, not conditions. The nested loop's own
  correctness is not assumed here: it is verified at its own site (Phase 330), and the summary only havocs.
  An unannotated loop still bails, so it skips loudly as before.
- Frame facts, `frameEarlierLoop` and the obligation replay share `innerFrame`, so a fact the nested loop overwrites
  (`t = 5`, counted up inside) does not reach the later loop, while one nothing writes does.

**Shipped tests:** group `P338 a loop after a nested outer loop`, 10 cases: a nested outer loop then a plain loop
(nonlinear `s == n * m` reaching it), its wrong postcondition, a wrong inner invariant still caught, an overwritten
fact refuting and an untouched one framed, array contents carried, an early return in the later loop, three loops,
two nested outer loops in sequence, and an unannotated inner loop skipping loudly.

## Phase 339 — a `break` inside a non-tail `if`  *(shipped — break flag, plus a branch-merge fix)*

A `break` was modelled only as a top-level `if (c) break` / `if (c) { lead; break }`, or as a leaf of the body's
tail `if`/`else` chain (Phases 312/326). One buried under another `if`, or followed by more of its branch, skipped
the loop: "unsupported statement BreakStatement", or in a nested loop "a `break` in a nested loop is modelled only
as a top-level …".

- **The break becomes a flag** (`ContractExpansionTransform.desugarBreak`, after `desugarContinue` and before a
  `for` update is appended). For an `if` that holds a loop `break` in any other shape: `boolean brk#L_C = false`
  before it; inside, each `break` becomes `brk = true`, and what follows an inner `if` that may set it is guarded
  by `if (brk) {} else s` (Phase 327's `flagged`, for breaks); then `if (brk) break` after the `if`. The iteration
  leaves at the same point with the same state, and the `for` update is still skipped. Breaks inside a `switch`
  belong to it and are left alone; an `if` that also returns is left to the tail lifting (rewriting a
  return-and-break chain buried its returns); a labelled break leaves the body unchanged, a loud skip.
- **Fixed: a write lost in the branch merge.** `iteCombineMap` skipped a name with no binding at the `if`'s
  entry ("truly fresh on both sides"), even when one branch wrote it. A scalar unread before the `if` (`r`, outside
  the invariant) has no entry binding, so `if (i == 1) { r = i }` merged to nothing and `r` read as its free value
  afterwards: sound, since a free value over-approximates, but `r == 1` at a later `break` did not prove, with or
  without the flag. The entry value is now the name's free value (`varFor`, what a later read gets) when its sort
  matches, so the merge is `r = c ? i : r`.

**Shipped tests:** group `P339 break inside a non-tail if`, 11 cases: a break under another `if` with more of the
body after it, in a nested loop, in an `else` (nested and top-level, with statements after it); the postcondition
from the break state, and one the break state misses; the rest of the branch after the break not run; a `for`
update skipped; a write in an `if` before the exit reaching the break state; an inner break's state refuting the
outer claim; a labelled break skipping loudly. G357's two "buried break skips loudly" cases now verify.

## Phase 340 — a nested loop writing a field or collection  *(shipped — loop-body stores, plus three fixes)*

A nested loop that assigned `this.count`, called `m.put(k, v)` or `xs.set(i, v)` skipped the method: "nested loop
writes a field/collection or unbounded construct". A bare field, a field array element and a list `add` already
worked. Two layers refused the other three: `innerFrame` (the summary's write set) and the loop engine itself, which
could not execute them as body statements in any loop ("assignment to a non-variable target", "unsupported
statement in loop region").

- **The stores they are.** `LoopEncoder.asStore` rewrites `this.f = v` to `f = v` (the name a bare `f` reads),
  `m.put(k, v)` on a map to `m[k] = v` (Phase 186's map store), and `xs.set(i, v)` on a list to `xs[i] = v`, before
  `applyAssign`. `innerFrame` takes the same writes: `this.f` as a scalar, `put`/`set` as content writes (havocked
  like an array or map, size kept), their arguments write-free.
- **`List.set` bounds.** `set(i, v)` throws outside `[0, size)` but carried no obligation, in straight-line code too
  (`xs[i] = v` did). `ObligationCollector` now synthesises the `get(i)` index site for a two-argument `set` on a
  `List`-typed receiver (a `BitSet`'s `set(int, boolean)` excluded by type).
- **Fixed: no frame facts around a nested loop.** `collectWritesStmt` read a nested loop's raw `loopBlock`, where
  groovy-contracts weaves its invariant checks; those calls made the write set "unbounded", so `loopFrameFacts`
  returned nothing for every outer loop holding a nested loop (`out = []` lost `out != null`, so `out.add(i)` in the
  inner body raised a false NPE). An annotated loop now contributes its `LoopSpec`'s init, guard and body.
- **Fixed: a void method's `@Ensures` after a loop** skipped with "no return value after loop". `resultExpr` returns
  null for a void method and `result` is left unbound.

**Shipped tests:** group `P340 nested loop writing a field or collection`, 16 cases: `this.count` in a nested loop
(bounded and exact `n * m`), a bare field, wrong claims and a field fact the nested loop changes refuting; a list
built in a nested loop, a list field, a map `put`, list `set` in bounds; an overwritten map key and list element
refuting the old value; an out-of-bounds `set` refuting in a nested loop and in straight-line code; a field array;
a void `@Ensures` after a loop, and a wrong one refuting.

**Still out:** `xs << v` in a loop body ("unsupported statement in loop region"), in any loop. *(Phase 341.)*

## Phase 341 — `xs << v` on a list  *(shipped — the left shift as the add it is)*

A statement `out << k` skipped in any loop ("unsupported statement in loop region") and in straight-line code
("statement with no modelled effect"); `out.add(k)` worked in both.

- **The adds it makes.** `Encoder.leftShiftAdds` reads a left-nested chain `xs << a << b` on a variable as
  `xs.add(a)`, then `xs.add(b)`. The loop engine applies them through `applyListMutationInLoop` when `xs` is
  list-typed (`isListTyped`: a list parameter or field, or a local declared with a `List` type, which `listNames`
  did not include). The straight-line walk emits them as the mutation steps a written `add` makes, when the
  receiver's declared type is a `Collection`, so a `Set`'s `<<` inserts (the replay dispatches on the receiver).
  `innerFrame` counts the chain as a list write, so an outer loop's summary havocs the list's contents and size.
- **Not an add.** A `StringBuilder`'s `<<` appends text, a `File`'s writes, an `int`'s is a shift whose value the
  statement discards: none is rewritten, and each still skips loudly.

**Shipped tests:** group `P341 list << in a loop body`, 12 cases: appending in a loop (sizes and elements), a wrong
size refuting, a chain, a nested loop, the outer summary havocking the list, straight-line code, a list parameter, a
set parameter inserting and a wrong set claim refuting, and a `StringBuilder` and an `int` shift skipping loudly.

## Phase 342 — a set mutated in a loop body  *(shipped — set semantics in loops; an unsoundness closed, a bigger one found)*

`st << k` in a loop body skipped. The probe showed worse: `st.add(k)` in a loop was accepted and modelled as a list
append. `applyListMutationInLoop` stored into the list oracles (`arrayFor`, `sizeOf`) and the set model
(`setFor`, its membership and cardinality) never changed. So `@Invariant({ st.isEmpty() })` was preserved through
`st.add(k)`, and `!st.contains(0)` through `st.add(0)`: silent false proofs. A true `contains` invariant failed.

- **A set's own store.** For a set name (`Encoder.isSetName`), `add`/`remove` apply the straight-line replay's
  encoding: `store(s, e, 1/0)` and the cardinality law (`|s'| = |s| + (e ∈ s ? 0 : 1)`). `clear`, `addAll` and the
  rest return false (a loud skip); `clear` had set the list size to 0 and left the set alone. `xs << v` takes the
  same path for a set. `summarizeInner` havocs a mutated set's own model too, so an outer loop's summary of a nested
  loop that adds to it does not keep its old contents.

**Shipped tests:** group `P342 set << in a loop body`, 11 cases: membership kept after `add` and `<<`, the size
bound, the two false proofs now refuting, a duplicate add not growing the set, a wrong claim, `remove`, a set field
(kept and refuting), and `clear` skipping loudly.

**Found, not fixed: `@Requires` assumed in non-entry states.** Probing the nested case turned up a long-standing,
general false proof (present at `8c1ff8f`, about 80 commits back). The post-loop check (`checkUse`'s coarse
context), the in-body exit checks (`checkEarlyExitPath`) and the loop-region obligations (`dischargeSeeded`)
assert the whole `@Requires` over the current state's symbols. A parameter, field or collection the prefix or the
loop writes is then tied to its entry value. With `@Requires({ x == 0 })`:
  - a loop doing `x = x + 1`, then `return x`, proves `result == 0` (`f(0, 1)` returns 1);
  - `x = 5` before the loop contradicts the entry fact (a frame fact `x == 5` against `x == 0`), so every claim
    after the loop proves (`result == 99`);
  - an in-body `if (k == 1) return x` proves `result == 0` (it returns 1);
  - a body bounds check `a[x]` reads `x == 0` and misses the overrun;
  - `@Requires({ st.isEmpty() })` / `xs.isEmpty()` survives a loop's `add`.
Preservation and progress filter `@Requires` to the conjuncts the loop cannot invalidate (Phase 64,
`loopStableRequires`); these contexts do not, and none of them filters the prefix's writes. The fix is to assume,
in every non-entry context, only the conjuncts over names nothing between entry and that point writes (the prefix,
earlier loops, the loop itself), keeping a content-only write's shape facts (`a.length`, `a != null`). It costs
proofs that lean on a written parameter's `@Requires`, so it is its own phase. *(Fixed in Phase 343.)*

## Phase 343 — `@Requires` is about the entry state  *(shipped — soundness: a long-standing false proof closed)*

Phase 342's finding. `@Requires` constrains the entry values; three contexts asserted all of it over the symbols of
a later state: `checkUse`'s coarse post-loop context, `checkEarlyExitPath` for an in-body exit, and the loop-region
discharges of `verifyLoopObligations` (guard, body, after-loop, break regions, nested bodies), plus the nested
establishment at an outer iteration. Preservation and progress used Phase 64's `loopStableRequires`, but a nested
loop's site had an empty prefix, so it saw only its own writes.

- **One filter, everywhere it applies.** Each non-entry context assumes `loopStableRequires(req, site)`; the entry
  contexts (establishment, the prefix replay, a do-while's first pass, the region before the first loop) keep the
  whole precondition. A nested site carries its `outer`, whose prefix and body are the writers that matter.
  `checkUse` decides first (`prefixReplayable`) whether it replays the prefix from entry, then asserts accordingly.
- **What survives a write.** A conjunct is kept when each of its names is one of:
  - a class reference;
  - a value-type parameter (primitive, boxed, `String`) never reassigned. A callee can mutate what a parameter refers
    to but never reassign the caller's variable, so this holds even past unknown calls;
  - a parameter or field the (bounded) write set misses;
  - a parameter never reassigned, used only for its nullness, an array's `length`, or a list's `size()` when only
    `set` mutates it (`onlyShapeUses`). A field needs a bounded write set for that too, since a call could reassign it.
  "Reassigned" is syntactic: `=`, `op=`, `++`/`--`, a declaration, `this.f = v`, or any assignment in a closure.
- **The write set was too eager to give up.** `%` is `Types.REMAINDER` in Groovy 6, not `MOD`, so every loop body
  using it had an "unbounded" write set and no loop-stable `@Requires` at all. The remaining pure operators and
  static calls on `Tuple`, `Math` and the boxed types now write nothing but their arguments.
- **Repros for written parameters.** The failure model holds a written parameter's value at the failure, not its
  input (`f(1, 1)` for the post-loop `x = 1`). `reproUnderRequires` now also runs when `@Requires` mentions a written
  parameter: it pins what the writes can't have changed and takes the rest from a model of `@Requires` (`f(0, 1)`,
  `f([], 1)`), or withholds the call with Phase 337's note.

**Changed case:** P-ring's "loop body with framed write verifies" leaned on the entry `head < tail` at every
iteration; its invariant now carries it (`head + 1 - done <= tail`).

**Shipped tests:** group `P343 @Requires is about the entry state`, 10 cases: a parameter incremented in the loop, one
set before it, an in-body return, a body bounds check, a set and a list a loop adds to, a set a nested loop adds to, a
reassigned array parameter, preservation after a prefix write (all refuting with repros that meet `@Requires`), and
an array stored into keeping its length and nullness.

**Noted, not fixed:** an alias (`int[] b = a; b[0] = 5`) writes `a`'s contents under another name, which the
syntactic write set misses (as Phase 64's filter always did); an uncontracted call in a loop body skips loudly, so
it cannot carry a stale fact through.

## Phase 344 — `break` and `continue` before a nested loop  *(shipped — exit rewrites, plus an unsoundness closed)*

A `continue`, or a `break` buried in an `if`, that a nested loop followed left the body unchanged ("unsupported
statement ContinueStatement/BreakStatement in loop region"): the rewrite would have put the loop in a branch, and
nested loops were verified only at a body's top level. Phase 335 changed that, so the refusal was stale. A top-level
`if (c) break` or `if (c) return e` before a nested loop skipped the same way.

- **The flag guards the loop.** `continueFree` sends an `if` that a nested loop follows down the flag route (Phases
  325/327) rather than copying what follows into both branches, which would duplicate the loop; `flagged` and
  `breakFlagged` drop their `containsLoop` refusal. The loop lands in the `else` of `if (flag) {} else`, a loop in a
  branch of a loop body.
- **An exit before the loop isn't taken on the way in.** The walks to a nested loop (its establishment, the outer
  facts it inherits, its body's obligations, the branch-loop paths) replay the outer body with `symExec`, which
  refuses an exit. `pastExits` turns each top-level exit `if` on the way into an assume-only `!c`.
- **Fixed (unsound before, since Phase 335): a branch's assumptions held on both paths.** `LoopEncoder.applyIf` ran
  each branch's statements with plain `assertExpr`, so a nested loop's summary (`inv ∧ ¬guard`) or an `assert` in one
  branch constrained the other path too. A loop in the then-branch whose invariant says `k == 1` made the
  else-branch's `s = -5` "preserve" `s >= 0`, and an `assert k == 1` in a branch did the same. Each branch now runs
  under `pushAssertGuard` of its condition (Phase 324's mechanism for break summaries).

**Changed cases:** G369's "a continue that would move a loop into a branch" and G372's "a nested continue ahead of a
loop" verify now (both claims are true).

**Shipped tests:** group `P344 break or continue before a nested loop`, 14 cases: a continue before a nested loop, its
wrong count refuting, the continuing iteration skipping the nested loop and a claim that it ran refuting; a continue
nested in an `if`; one followed by a break; a buried break before a nested loop in its branch, and a claim as if the
loop ran on the breaking iteration refuting; a top-level break and a return before a nested loop, and a wrong claim
at that return; the two fixed unsoundnesses (a loop and an `assert` in one branch); three-deep nesting still
skipping loudly.

## Phase 345 — for-in over a range  *(shipped — the commonest counting loop)*

A for-in was modelled only over a named collection, so `for (i in 0..<n)`, probably the commonest Groovy counting
loop, skipped the method ("unsupported statement ForStatement"), with or without an `@Invariant`.

- **A counting loop.** `buildLoopSpec` desugars `for (x in lo..<hi)` / `lo..hi` to `int x = lo; while (x < hi) {
  body; x = x + 1 }` (`<=` inclusive), with `x` itself the counter rather than a hidden index bound to an element:
  an `@Invariant` over `x` is then a loop-head invariant, as for a classic `for` (groovy-contracts checks it at body
  entry, which the head covers). The auto invariant `lo <= x <= hi` (`hi + 1` inclusive) and variant `hi - x` give
  safety and termination with no hand-written invariant. `(lo..<hi).each { x -> … }` takes the same path.
- **Ranges can run backwards.** Groovy iterates a range whose upper bound is below its lower one downwards (`0..<-2`
  is `[0, -1]`, `1..0` is `[1, 0]`), which the counting loop doesn't model. `LoopSpec.rangeForward` (`lo <= hi`) is
  checked as its own VC in the establishment's entry state, top-level and nested (`checkRangeForward`), then assumed
  for the invariant's establishment. An inclusive range also needs `hi < Integer.MAX_VALUE`: its counter reaches
  `hi + 1` at exit, which Phase 333's `int` bound would make an infeasible, vacuous exit state.
- **What the desugar relies on, checked syntactically.** The range is evaluated once, and its iteration ignores
  writes to `x`: a body that assigns `x`, or writes (assigns, stores into, calls a method on) a name the bounds
  read, leaves the loop uncaptured, and the skip now says why (`ContractExpansionTransform.LOOP_SKIP_KEY`, read by
  BodyEncoder's unsupported-statement skip).
- **Auto-only accumulation check.** `autoOnlyBodyAccumulates` excluded a for-in's synthetic index but not a range
  loop's counter, so `(0..<n).each { assert … }` skipped; the update's writes are excluded now. Its message no
  longer says the invariant is "not attachable to a `.each`" for a for-in, which can carry one.

**Shipped tests:** group `P345 for-in over a range`, 19 cases: counts over `0..<n` and literal bounds, an untyped
variable over `0..<a.length`, a prefix sum, an inclusive `1..n`, `continue`/`break`, nested and sequential range
loops, `(0..<n).each` and a false assert in it; a wrong invariant; ranges that may run backwards (`0..<n`, `1..n` at
0, `0..n - 1` at 0 beside an off-by-one store, a nested `0..<i - 1`, an inclusive range to `Integer.MAX_VALUE`);
and the loud skips (the body assigning the variable, writing a bound, accumulating with no invariant).

**Still out:** `<..` / `<..<` ranges, `(lo..hi).step(k)`, `n.times { }`, and `.eachWithIndex` over a range.

## Phase 346 — a library call in a loop body  *(shipped — overload choice, honest repros; a bigger unsoundness found)*

`s = s + Math.abs(i)` in a loop body under `0 <= i` failed to preserve `s >= 0`, with `fails on: f(1)`, though
`f(1)` returns 1, and the havocked value displayed as `s (after a loop)`.

- **The overload needs the argument's width.** `java.lang.Math` specs both `abs(int)` and `abs(long)`; Phase 219's
  typed lookup declines when the argument's kind is unknown, and `staticNumericKind` knew only `scalarTypes`
  (parameters and fields). A local's width is now taken from `integralNames` (Phase 333, conflicting declarations
  already dropped), and a for-in's variable is noted there too. So the spec applies in loop bodies, after a loop
  (`return Math.abs(i)` skipped as "outside the fragment") and over straight-line locals.
- **An untranslatable value is labelled, and its repro withheld.** `LoopEncoder.rebind` havocs a right-hand side the
  encoder can't translate; it now mints it as `x$unmodelled$n`, shown as `x (unmodelled)`. The model picks such a
  value freely, so no run is known to produce it: `shown()` withholds the failing call with a note naming it.

**Shipped tests:** group `P346 a library call in a loop body`, 9 cases: `Math.abs` in a loop body, into a body
local, `Math.max`, after a loop, in a guard, in a range for-in, over a straight-line local; a claim the spec doesn't
give refuting with a real call; and a contracted call's havocked result withholding the call.

**Found, not fixed — a call's side effects are dropped (unsound, long-standing).** A same-class call used as a value
is modelled without its writes:
- an uncontracted method is a "pure function" when it merely has no contract (`PureEvaluator.resolve`), so
  `int bump() { count = 99; return 1 }` makes `s = s + bump()` keep `count == 0`, in straight-line code and loops;
- a contracted method with no `@Modifies` is assumed to write nothing, and nothing checks it does: `int s =
  clobber(a)`, with `clobber` storing `a[0] = -1`, keeps `a[0] == 0`.

Only a call as a statement in a loop body skips loudly. *(Fixed in Phase 347, the hybrid: a declared frame wins,
an absent one is inferred, an unbounded one skips loudly.)*

## Phase 347 — a call is framed by its writes  *(shipped — soundness: the call-frame hole closed, the hybrid rule)*

Phase 346's finding. A same-class call used as a value dropped its side effects three ways: `PureEvaluator.resolve`
made any contract-free method a pure function; `assumeCalleeEnsures` read a callee with no `@Modifies` as writing
nothing ("a null @Modifies frames everything"); and the Phase 116 combiner inlining replaced a call to a method with
`@Ensures({ result == E })` by `E` whatever its body did. The rule now, Paul's hybrid:

- **A declared `@Modifies` wins.** It is frame-checked, so trusting it at call sites is sound. `@Modifies({ [] })`
  declares that nothing is written; groovy-contracts rejects an empty closure (`@Modifies({})`: "must contain a
  field reference, parameter reference, or list of references"), an upstream tweak worth making. The frame check
  now compares the declaration with the inferred write set (transitive, list mutators and `++` included), falling
  back to the old partial visitor when that can't be bounded.
- **Absent, the frame is inferred** (`calleeWrites`, memoised on the node): the loop engine's write collector run
  over the callee's body, filtered to its fields and parameters. It follows same-class calls (a written formal
  maps to the actual, which must be a plain variable), a closure's body, `switch`/`try`/`throw`, casts, GStrings,
  spreads, ranges, groovy-contracts' `==>`; an unknown method is read as writing its receiver (unless the
  receiver's type is immutable — a `String` parameter can't be mutated), a registry spec by its `@Pure` or declared
  frame, the SAM shorthand `cs(r)` on a callable in scope as pure, and an unknown static call (a library call with
  no spec) as unbounded. These extensions apply only while a callee's frame is inferred (`INFER_MODE`): a loop's
  own write set keeps its earlier, narrower reading, because bounding a loop that used to be unbounded puts its
  loop-stable facts into every loop VC, and that changed a refutation tuned without them (P253's merge order timed
  out at 8 s with the channel facts in scope). A bodiless callee — a registry skeleton, an interface method — keeps the trusted reading
  "nothing" unless it declares otherwise.
- **Unbounded is loud.** A call whose frame can't be bounded (`xs << x`, a multiple assignment, a written formal
  passed `this.a`) skips with "call 'm(…)' whose writes can't be bounded from its body — declare @Modifies on m".
- **Where calls are framed now.** Straight-line `int s = f()`, `s = s + f()` and `2 + f()` (the Phase 309
  return-expression hoist, `hoistValueCalls`, shared with assignment right-hand sides), call statements, and loop
  bodies: `LoopEncoder.rebind` hoists each call the encoder can't translate through the `LoopCallHandler`, which
  mints the result in the callee's return sort (a `String`-returning `glue(acc, x)` keeps its `@Ensures`) — a
  same-class call it can't model is loud, a library or cross-class call keeps its opaque reading. A same-class
  static call statement is a `StaticMethodCallExpression` after STC, which the loop engine now takes too.
- **Purity is "writes nothing".** `PureEvaluator.resolve` and the combiner registration both require an empty
  frame; a contract-free writer is framed at its call site and its result is opaque.
- **Display:** a callee's framed location shows as `count (after a call)`; hoist temporaries are hidden.

**Changed cases:** G047's Phase 7 insertion sort and G048's natural-guard twin proved only through the hole (their
`insert` has no `@Modifies`, and its `@Ensures` says nothing about `a[i]`): under the inferred frame the
postcondition refutes, honestly — the version with the frame and the bound lemma is Phases 14/24. G390's "unmodelled
call result" case now verifies (the call's `@Ensures` reaches the loop body).

**Shipped tests:** group `P347 a call is framed by its writes`, 19 cases: a pure helper still unfolds; a writer
leaves the fields it doesn't write alone (straight-line and loop); `@Modifies({ [] })`; a `@Requires`-only helper as
an opaque value; the contracted writer as a declaration, a statement, inside an expression, a reassignment, and
through a helper it calls; array-parameter stores by contract-free and contracted callees; a declared frame
honoured, and one the body breaks refused; writers in loop bodies as values and statements, instance and static;
an unbounded body skipping loudly.

**Still out:** the frame of a cross-class call (`obj.m()` on an object parameter, Phase 194's demote-to-skip
boundary), and aliasing. A frame check that can't bound the body is silent (the old partial visitor), as before.
*(The silent frame check is Phase 348.)*

## Phase 348 — an unchecked frame is loud  *(shipped — the one silent corner of Phase 347's rule)*

Phase 347's rule trusts a declared `@Modifies` at every call site because the frame check stands behind it. But
when the body's writes couldn't be bounded, that check fell back to the old partial visitor and said nothing — so
a `@Modifies({ this.count })` over a body with `l << x` passed, and every caller went through the declaration
unchecked. The loud-unsoundness tenet says the gap must announce itself.

- **The collector records why it gave up.** `unbounded(why)` is the write collector's exit for every construct it
  can't follow: the first reason wins, it is kept only while a callee's frame is being inferred (`INFER_MODE`; a
  loop's write set is a plain `false`, as before), and `calleeWrites` memoises it beside the write set
  (`INFERRED_WRITES_REASON_KEY`, kept even for a walk nested in another's, since it names a real construct). The
  reasons name the construct in the developer's spelling: `the operator '<<' in '(l << x)', which could mutate its left operand`;
  `multiple assignment 'def (a, b) = [x, x]'`; `a synchronized statement`; `static call 'Util.tweak(…)' with no
  @Pure or @Modifies spec`; `call 'fill(…)' writes its parameter 'a', but the argument 'new int[1]' isn't a named
  variable`; and a helper's own reason rides up through the call that uses it: `call 'weird(…)': the operator
  '<<' …`.
- **The frame check reports it.** `Reporter.formatModifiesUnchecked`: "Cannot check the @Modifies clause [count]
  of 'bump': its body's writes can't be bounded — ‹reason›. Callers trust the declared frame, so make the body one
  whose writes can be read off it (declare @Modifies on the callee it uses, or rewrite the construct)." The partial
  visitor still runs, and what it can see outside the clause rides in the same message ("The partial check already
  sees it write 'other', outside the clause") — one message, because STC keeps one error per anchor position, so a
  second error on the method node is dropped silently. (That dedup is also why the inferred route reports the
  first offender only; the next appears once it is fixed.)
- **The call-site skip names it too.** Phase 347's "call 'weird(…)' whose writes can't be bounded from its body —
  declare @Modifies on weird" now carries the construct between: "… from its body: the operator '<<' in '(l << x)',
  which could mutate its left operand — declare …".
- **A collector gap the flag found at once:** the whole-corpus run flagged every DFS body in the suite (G155, G172)
  — `if (u !in visited)` bailed, since Phase 347 taught the collector `in` but not `!in`. The negations and the
  other pure comparisons (`!instanceof`, `<=>`, `===`, `!==`, `=~`, `==~`) are now followed in infer mode. Five
  frames that had passed in silence are checked.
- **Posture, unchanged:** the declaration is what callers go through. The last shipped case has `weird` declare
  `@Modifies({ [] })` over a `<<` body: `weird` is flagged, and its caller still proves `count == 0` past the call.
  Sound by declaration, with the flag as the one place a wrong declaration would be caught.

**Shipped tests:** group `P348 an unchecked frame is loud`, 9 cases: an unbounded body flagged with the construct
named, and the same body with plain assignments bounded and checked; a helper's reason carried up; the partial
check's offender in the same message; a sibling-class static; a writer passed `new int[1]`; a `synchronized` block;
the Phase 347 call-site skip naming the construct; the declared frame trusted by the caller while the body is
flagged. G391's unbounded-callee case expects the new wording. *(The unbounded construct in these cases was `l << x`
until Phase 349 gave `<<` a bounded reading; it is a multiple assignment now.)*

**Still out:** the Phase 347 items (cross-class frames, aliasing). A bounded reading of `<<` on a nameable
receiver (an append writes its receiver; an int shift writes nothing, so "writes the receiver" over-approximates
both soundly) would turn the commonest flag into a checked frame — a small follow-up. *(Phase 349.)*

## Phase 349 — `<<` writes its receiver  *(shipped — the commonest flag becomes a checked frame; an append resizes)*

Phase 348's follow-up. `xs << v` is an append on a collection and a shift on an int; "writes its left operand,
unless that is of immutable type" covers both soundly (the shift writes nothing, so recording it is a harmless
over-approximation), and is the rule the collector already applied to an unknown method's receiver. So, while a
callee's frame is inferred (`INFER_MODE`; a loop's own write set is untouched), `Types.LEFT_SHIFT` goes through
`recordReceiverWrite`: the operand's base name is recorded (a local is filtered out later), a chained `log << a << b`
or a call result on the left contributes its own writes. `@Modifies({ this.log })` over `log << x` is now checked
and passes; `@Modifies({ [] })` over it is a violation; a contract-free `push(xs, v) { xs << v }` has the frame
`{xs}`.

**An append resizes.** Phase 229 deliberately kept a collection's size across a call ("the shipped mutators are
size-preserving, and the implicit size stability is a true, load-bearing fact") — true of a registry spec, and
false of a body that appends: with the frame alone, a caller kept `xs.size() == 0` past `push(xs, n)`, by `<<` or
by `add`, contract-free or under a declared frame. The collector now notes the size-changing writes beside the frame
(`WRITE_SIZE` → `INFERRED_SIZE_KEY`, read by `calleeSizeWrites`): `<<`, any recorded mutator not in
`SIZE_PRESERVING` (`sort`, `swap`, `fill`, `reverse`, `shuffle`, `set`, `putAt`, `setLength`), an unknown method on
the receiver, and a same-class callee's resized formal mapped onto the actual. At the call site, a bodied callee
that may resize a location whose size oracle exists havocs it — `havoc$xs.size()$n`, shown `xs.size() (after a
call)` — with `old.xs.size()` pinned at the call and the caller's own `old$…` size restored after. A registry spec
keeps the Phase 229 reading (no body to read; its mutators preserve size), an array's length is never havoced, a
body that can't be bounded resizes every collection its declared frame names. A declared frame says WHAT is
written; whether the body resizes it is still read off the body.

**Shipped tests:** group ``P349 `<<` writes its receiver``, 16 cases: a list field appended within / outside the
frame; chained appends; a `StringBuilder` field; an appended `Set` parameter as a write; a shift on an int parameter
and on an int local as no write; a helper appending to a local writing nothing visible; a contract-free appender
framed by the caller, with the list's size and elements unknown after; a contract-free `add` and a declared-frame
`add` resizing; a declared-frame element store and a registry sort keeping the size; an append in a helper's loop.

**Still out:** the Phase 347 items (cross-class frames, aliasing). A map's size is havoced with the rest of the map
(its key set is), so nothing new there; a `StringBuilder`'s `length()` has no size oracle to havoc.
*(The cross-class frame is Phase 350.)*

## Phase 350 — a cross-class call is framed by its writes  *(shipped — soundness: the receiver's state after a call)*

The last "still out" of Phase 347. A call on a class-typed PARAMETER, `c.bump()`, had two readings, neither
right. As a statement, Phase 45 havoced every field of the receiver and never assumed the callee's `@Ensures` (its
recorded limit). As a value, `int x = c.bump()`, it took the generic call framing: the callee resolved on the
receiver's class (Phase 133's lookup), but its frame was read as if same-class — its field `count` became the
CALLER's `count` (havoced, when there was one; its `@Ensures` `count == old.count + 1` asserted about that
variable), and the receiver's own `c$count` stayed at its entry value, so `c.count == 3` verified past the
increment. The probe showed both; the second is Phase 194's residual (b).

- **The receiver context.** In `assumeCalleeEnsures`, a call whose receiver names an object parameter and whose
  callee lives on that parameter's class (or a superclass) is a cross-class call: a written field maps to the
  receiver's entity `c$field` (Phase 45's naming, so the caller's reads of `c.field` see the havoc), a written
  formal to its actual as before, and the callee's `@Ensures` is translated under the receiver
  (`Encoder.translateWithUnderReceiver`: bare `count` is `c$count`, `old.count` the snapshot pinned at the call,
  `result` and the formals from the bindings). After the havoc the receiver's class invariants are re-assumed
  (Phase 45's step 2 — the callee preserved them on exit). A callee without `@Ensures` gives an opaque result
  and exactly its frame; a getter's `@Ensures({ result == count })` reads the receiver's field.
- **The statement form goes the same way.** `applyCrossClassCall` tries this route first; its all-fields havoc
  remains the fallback for a callee with no body and no contract (a library type). Phase 45's "the callee's
  `@Ensures` is currently not assumed cross-class" is closed.
- **Through a helper.** The collector reads a call on a sibling-typed parameter by its callee's frame
  (`siblingReceiverClass` / `collectSiblingCallWrites`): a written field is the receiver, a written formal the
  actual, an empty frame nothing. So `twice(c) { c.incr(); c.incr() }` has the frame `{c}`, and a written OBJECT
  parameter at a call site means its fields: they are havoced and its invariants re-assumed. `peek(c) { c.get() }`
  has an empty frame and leaves them alone.
- **A sibling class's static.** A contract-free static on another class of the compilation unit unfolds as a
  function when its frame is empty (`PureEvaluator.siblingClass`, symbol `Util$tweak`); a writer stays opaque. The
  collector reads such a static by its frame too (a written formal maps to the actual; the sibling's own fields
  are named `Sib$field`, no caller location, so they drop out as invisible). A library static with no spec is
  unbounded as before.
- **The Phase 194 alias boundary stands,** in both routes and for a helper writing through an object parameter:
  another parameter of the same class demotes to the loud skip.

**Changed case:** G392's "a static call on another class has no frame" used a sibling class's static, now bounded;
it uses `System.identityHashCode` (no registry spec).

**Shipped tests:** group `P350 a cross-class call is framed by its writes`, 18 cases: the value call and the
statement call havocing the fields the callee writes; the callee's `@Ensures` reaching the caller and a wrong claim
against it refuting; a same-named caller field left alone, and the callee's `@Ensures` binding to the receiver;
a getter's result; an opaque result without `@Ensures`; the invariant re-assumed after a contract-free writer, and
refuting without it; a callee writing only its formal; an unbounded callee loud; the alias boundary; a same-class
helper writing through an object parameter, and one only reading it; a sibling static unfolding, not when it
writes its own class, and one storing into an array argument.

**Still out:** a call on an object FIELD or LOCAL (`this.c.incr()`, `Counter d = c; d.bump()`) — the receiver
context is per object parameter; aliasing; a cross-class call in a loop body keeps its opaque reading (the loop's
write set is unbounded there, so the loop skips loudly anyway). *(The field and the local are Phase 351.)*

## Phase 351 — a call through any receiver lands on that receiver  *(shipped — soundness: four mislocated frames)*

Phase 350's follow-up, and a soundness fix as much as a feature. The call framing reads a callee's fields as the
CALLER's same-named locations unless the receiver is a modelled object parameter — right only when the receiver is
the caller itself. The probe found it proving false claims four ways:

- **an object field** — `c.incr()` on `Counter c` assumed Counter's `hits == old.hits + 1` about A's own `hits`;
- **a local alias** — `Counter d = c; d.bump()` havoced the caller's `count` (if any) and left `c$count` at its
  entry value, so `c.count == 3` held past the increment;
- **a parameter of the caller's own class** — `o.incr()` on `A o` framed and assumed `count == old.count + 1`
  about `this.count`, true only when `o` is `this`;
- **another class's static** — `Util.set7()` with `@Ensures({ total == 7 })` was assumed about A's `total`.

And a fifth, quieter one: a receiver of another class resolved its callee on the CALLER's class first, so with a
same-named method on both, `c.incr()` was A's `incr` — A's field havoced, Counter's `@Ensures` never assumed.

**What changed.**

- **An object field is a receiver** (`collectObjectParams`): a field of another class's type — static only, in a
  static method — that this method never reassigns and no parameter shadows is modelled like an object parameter:
  `c.count` reads `c$count` (it was outside the fragment), its class invariants are assumed on entry, calls through
  it are framed onto it (Phase 350), and the Phase 194 alias boundary covers it (a field and a parameter of the same
  class may be one object). `this.c.incr()` is the same receiver.
- **A local alias is its receiver** (`collectObjectAliases`, `TypeEnvironment.objectAliases`): a local declared
  `T d = r`, `r` a modelled receiver, declared once and never reassigned, IS `r` — for calls (statement and value),
  the callee's `@Requires` discharge, field reads in the encoder, and a written object at a call site.
- **Every other explicit receiver is loud** when its callee writes or reads its own fields (a parameter of the
  caller's class, a fresh object, a call result, a reassigned field or local): "call 'o.incr(…)' writes its
  receiver's field 'count', but 'o' isn't a receiver the verifier models (an object parameter or field, or a local
  holding one) — the caller can't name that field", or "… has an @Ensures over its receiver's field …". A callee
  that touches no field of its own stays framed as before. Carrier receivers (Phase 133) bind their own fields and
  registry specs are receiver-independent (Phase 220); neither is affected.
- **A foreign static writes its own statics:** they are no location of the caller's, so they drop out of the frame;
  an `@Ensures` over them is loud (the caller can't name `Util.total`). A static of a superclass is the caller's.
- **A receiver of another class resolves on that class** and its superclasses before anything else
  (`resolveContractedCallee`); the caller's class is searched only for `this`, implicit-this and its own statics.
- **The write collector follows a local reference** (`localAliasSources`): a local assigned a parameter or field by
  name, transitively (`b = a; c = b`), writes it, so `put0(a) { int[] b = a; b[0] = 5 }` has the frame `{a}` (the
  collector's recorded blind spot, now down to aliases through other expressions). Only a reference counts: `int
  n = x` copies a value. And a parameter of immutable type in the frame is dropped — it can only be reassigned
  (`x = x + 1`), which never reaches the caller (before, the caller's argument was havoced: imprecise, not unsound).
- **Display:** an object receiver's own handle (`c = 0`) is hidden; its fields show as `c$count`.

**Probed, not changed:** a contract-free helper whose body declares a local (`int n = x; return n + 1`) doesn't
unfold as a function, so a postcondition over its result refutes; and a field named `count` with `old.count` in a
caller's contract shows a stray `count.size()` in counterexamples (the `.count` list dispatch). Both are older than
this slice, recorded as follow-ups. *(The stray size is Phase 352 — not the `.count` dispatch after all; the helper
with a local is Phase 353.)*

**Shipped tests:** group `P351 a call through any receiver lands on that receiver`, 19 cases: a field call
havocing the field object's state, its callee's `@Ensures` reaching the caller, and not landing on the caller's
same-named field; `this.c`; a reassigned field loud; a field and a parameter of one class at the alias boundary; a
local alias as a value call, a statement call, with the `@Ensures` off the caller's field, and as a read; a
same-class parameter loud; a fresh object loud; the receiver's class resolving first; a foreign static leaving the
caller's static alone, and loud with an `@Ensures` over its own; helpers aliasing an array and an object parameter;
a helper copying a value and one reassigning its int parameter leaving the caller's argument alone.

**Still out:** a fresh object as a receiver (`new Counter().incr()`, `Counter d = new Counter()`: a constructor's
effect isn't modelled, so loud); an alias through any other expression (`T d = cond ? a : b`, a getter — Phase 357); a field
the method reassigns; aliasing in general, which stays the documented non-goal behind Phase 194's boundary.

## Phase 352 — an old scalar field has no size  *(shipped — counterexample hygiene)*

Phase 351's recorded follow-up, and the diagnosis there was wrong: the name `count` had nothing to do with it. Any
field read as `old.f` showed a stray `f.size() = 0` (`hits.size()`, `size.size()`). The Phase 40 entry snapshot pins
`old.f.size()` for every field the postcondition's `old` names, so `old.xs.size()` survives an `xs.add(…)`; its
comment called the bind "harmless for non-sized fields", and for proofs it is. But minting the size oracle
declares an `f.size` variable, and the counterexample display lists every model variable it can name.

The snapshot now pins the size only for a field that can have one (`isScalarField`): a primitive, a boxed number,
a `Boolean` or a `Character` is skipped; anything else (a List, an array, a String, an unknown type) keeps it.

**Shipped tests:** group `P352 an old scalar field has no size`, 5 cases: an `int`, a boxed `Integer` and a field
named `size` read through `old` refuting with no stray size, and a List field's `old.xs.size()` still proving, with
a wrong claim about it still refuting.

## Phase 353 — a helper with locals unfolds  *(shipped — Phase 8a's bounded unfolding beyond one expression)*

Phase 351's other follow-up. Phase 8a defines a contract-free helper to the solver by inlining its body
(`f#(args) == body[params ↦ args]`, fuel-bounded) — but only a single-expression body: `{ e }` or `{ return e }`.
Anything else left the call an uninterpreted function, so `inc(x) { int n = x; return n + 1 }` refuted
`result == k + 1`, as did the statement form of `factorial` (`if (n <= 0) return 1; return n * fact(n - 1)`), which
the code's own comment named as not inlined.

- **The fold** (`PureEvaluator.foldStatements`): the body runs forward under a substitution — formals ↦ actuals,
  then each local ↦ its current value, already substituted. A declaration or a plain reassignment (of a local or a
  parameter) updates it; `return e`, or a trailing expression (Groovy's implicit return), is the value; an `if` is a
  ternary over its two continuations (each branch's statements, then the rest), so an `if`/`return` chain and an
  `if`/`else` that assigns a local both fold. A nested block flattens. `int r;` binds `r` to a hidden unknown, so a
  read before assignment never captures a name from the caller's scope. Anything else — a loop, a `switch`, a
  `throw`, a compound assignment, a path that falls off the end — refuses, and the call stays uninterpreted (sound),
  as before. A budget of 64 statement visits bounds the `if` duplication.
- **The collector** reads `int r;` (an empty initialiser) as writing nothing, in infer mode: it used to give up, so
  such a helper wasn't even a function (and Phase 348's reason text was a raw `<not implemented yet…>`).
- **A soundness fix found on the way** (since Phase 350): an inlined body is translated in the CALLER's scope, so
  a sibling class's helper reading its own static (`Util.tweak(x) { x + base }`) read the caller's `base` — with
  `A.base == 0`, `result == k` verified, the truth being `k + 5`. A sibling helper whose unfolded body names a field
  of its class is no longer inlined (`mentionsField`); one over its parameters still is.

**Shipped tests:** group `P353 a helper with locals unfolds`, 13 cases: a local copy, a reassigned local and a
reassigned parameter unfolding, and a wrong claim refuting; an `if`/`return` chain proving and its counterexample
the missed branch; an `if`/`else` assigning an uninitialised local; the statement-form factorial by fuel and its
symbolic recursive step; a folded helper in a caller's contract; a loop still opaque; the sibling helper reading its
own static refuting, and one over its parameters unfolding.

**Still out:** a loop, `switch` or compound assignment (`n += 1`) in a helper body; a sibling helper over its own
fields (opaque, not inlined). *(The compound assignment is Phase 354.)*

## Phase 354 — compound assignment in a helper and a body  *(shipped — the fold's last plain-statement gap; `%=` fixed)*

Phase 353's fold refused `x op= e`, `n++` and `--x`, so a helper using one stayed an uninterpreted function.

- **The fold** reads `x op= e` as `x = x op e` (`+ - * / intdiv % ** << >> >>> & | ^`; Groovy's `?=` is not folded)
  and `x++` / `--x` as a statement as `x = x ± 1`. An expression that still assigns or increments once substituted
  (`return n++`, `(n = 5) + 1`) refuses (`hasEffect`): its value isn't a pure term without the evaluation-order
  semantics the body encoder gives statements, so the call stays uninterpreted — sound, and for `return n++`
  incomplete. A closure's own statements are left to the closure.
- **A Groovy 6 spelling bug in bodies:** `%=` is `REMAINDER_EQUAL` (as `%` is `REMAINDER`, Phase 343), which
  `Encoder.compoundBaseOp` didn't know, so `r %= 3` in a method or a loop body was "a statement with no modelled
  effect" and the method skipped. The body desugar now takes the same operators as the fold (`%=`, `intdiv`'s
  compound, `**=`, the shifts and the bitwise compounds), each lowered through the binary operator's existing
  translation. Whole corpus unchanged.

**Shipped tests:** group `P354 compound assignment in a helper and a body`, 13 cases: `n += 2` unfolding and a wrong
claim refuting; `x *= 3` on the parameter; `n++` / `--x` statements; a compound assignment in a branch; `%=`, `&=`
and String `+=` in helpers; `return n++` staying opaque; `%=` and `&=` in method bodies; `%=` in a loop body with
an invariant proving, and a wrong bound refuting.

**Still out:** a loop or `switch` in a helper body; `?=` (elvis-assign). *(The loop is Phase 355.)*

## Phase 355 — a loop in a helper  *(shipped — a helper's loop summarised by its own verified invariant)*

Phases 353/354 fold a contract-free helper's straight-line body into its defining expression; a loop still left the
call an uninterpreted function. A loop can't fold into a closed expression, but its exit state can be described.

- **The summary** (`PureEvaluator.foldLoop`): a loop carrying `LoopSpec` (an `@Invariant`) and a variant (an explicit
  `@Decreases`, or a range for-in's automatic one) runs its `for` init into the substitution, then gives each
  variable the body writes a fresh name (`$loopK$c`, hidden from counterexamples). The facts at exit — every invariant
  and the negated guard, over those names — go out beside the defining expression (`unfoldBody(c, facts)`), and the
  encoder asserts each it can translate with the call's definition. The fold continues after the loop, so
  sequential loops and a loop followed by more code compose.
- **Why it is sound.** Loop verification runs for every method with an annotated loop, contracted or not, so the
  helper's own checks prove the invariant established and preserved and the variant decreasing — for every input,
  since a contract-free helper has no `@Requires` (one would make it a contracted method, whose `@Ensures` is the
  route). So an exit state exists and satisfies the facts. The VARIANT is the load-bearing part: without proven
  termination there may be no exit state, and `¬guard` over a variable the loop doesn't write (`while (x > 0) {}`)
  would contradict, making every caller proof vacuous — so a loop with no variant keeps the call opaque.
- **Path conditions.** Establishment is proven only on the path that reaches the loop, so each fact is guarded by
  the fold's path condition (`¬pc ∨ fact`): a loop in `if (x > 0)` adds nothing at `pos(-3)`. Asserted
  unconditionally, its `0 <= i ∧ i ≥ x … i == x` would contradict there.
- **What refuses** (the call stays opaque): a loop that breaks, returns or throws (the exit isn't `inv ∧ ¬guard`);
  writes anything but plain `int`/`long` variables (`a[i] = v`, `xs.add(v)`: only scalars get fresh names, so a
