  list's contents would be read at entry); calls a method on an object; nests a loop or a `switch`/`try`; comes from
  `.each`; or a collection for-in.
- **The posture this exposes.** A helper's loop is verified for every argument, so its invariant must hold for all
  of them: `i <= x` fails on entry for a negative `x`, and the helper reports it. `hi = Math.max(x, 0)` is the idiom
  (a contracted helper with `@Requires({ x >= 0 })` and an `@Ensures` is the other route).

**Shipped tests:** group `P355 a loop in a helper`, 15 cases: a summed loop's result non-negative, and a claim the
invariant doesn't give refuting; an exact invariant's closed form, symbolically and at a constant; two sequential
loops; a `while` counting down; a range for-in with its automatic variant; a loop in a branch guarded by it, and the
other branch proving nothing extra; no variant, a `break` and a list mutation each leaving the call opaque; and a
wrong invariant, a non-decreasing variant and an invariant failing for some input each reported at the helper.

**Still out:** a loop that breaks or mutates a collection, a nested loop, and a `switch` in a helper; closed
evaluation (`PureEvaluator.tryEvaluate`) still doesn't run loops, so a constant argument goes through the summary.
*(Closed evaluation of loops is Phase 356.)*

## Phase 356 — a helper loop evaluated at constants  *(shipped — the closed evaluator runs loops; two older bugs fixed)*

Phase 355's follow-up. The closed evaluator (Phase 8a, `PureEvaluator.tryEvaluate`) turns a contract-free helper call
whose arguments are all constants into its value by running the body. It ran straight-line code, `if` and recursion;
a loop was not evaluable, so `total(4)` stayed an uninterpreted function unless a Phase 355 invariant summarised it —
and an unannotated loop has none.

- **Loops run for real:** `while`, `do`/`while`, a classic `for (init; cond; update)`, a `for (x in lo..hi)` over a
  forwards range, and an annotated loop from its `LoopSpec` (init, guard, body, update — the raw statement carries
  groovy-contracts' woven invariant checks, which the evaluator can't run). Unlabelled `break` and `continue` are
  control signals caught by the innermost loop; a `for`'s update runs after a `continue`, as in Java. A collection
  for-in, an `.each`, a backwards range and a labelled jump are not evaluable. Termination needs no argument here:
  the step budget bounds every iteration, and running out is "not evaluable", so the call falls back to the symbolic
  routes (the Phase 355 summary, or an uninterpreted function) — sound either way.
- **The statement forms the fold already had** (Phases 353/354) evaluate too: compound assignments, `x++` / `--x` as
  statements, and `int r;` (unbound until assigned, so a read before is not evaluable). And `n.intdiv(d)` (truncating,
  as Java's `/` on ints) and `Math.max` / `min` / `abs` — the clamp idiom Phase 355 recommends for a helper's bounds.
- **`%` was not evaluable:** Groovy 6 parses it as `REMAINDER` (the Phase 343 spelling), which the evaluator didn't
  know — `x % 7` with `x` constant was an uninterpreted call.
- **The step budget was one per method:** the evaluator is built once per method and `tryEvaluate` never reset its
  20,000-step budget, so one call that exhausted it — easy once loops run — left every later call in the method
  unevaluable. Each top-level evaluation now gets the whole budget.
- **A helper named like a GDK built-in was shadowed in contracts:** a contract's `sum(4)` reads `this.sum(4)`, and
  the method-call dispatch tried its GDK aggregation handler first, taking it for a list fold over `this` — heavy
  axioms and a solver timeout. A new first-tier handler, `tmcOwnHelper`, routes a call on implicit-this or `this`
  that resolves to a contract-free helper of the class (or a sibling's static) to the helper, ahead of the built-ins;
  a translation that fails hands on to them, as before.

**Shipped tests:** group `P356 a helper loop evaluated at constants`, 12 cases: an unannotated loop at a constant and
a wrong constant refuting; a `while` with a `break`; a `continue` in a classic `for`; a `do`/`while`; a range for-in
with a `Math.max` bound; an annotated loop from its specification; a digit sum with `%` and `intdiv`; a call in a
caller's precondition; a helper named `sum` in a contract; an argument past the budget falling back, and not
using up the budget for a later call.

**Still out:** a loop over a collection, or one that mutates one, in a closed evaluation (the evaluator's values are
integers and booleans only); a labelled `break`/`continue`.

## Phase 357 — an alias through an expression  *(shipped — soundness: two silent frame holes closed)*

A contract-free helper's frame is inferred from its body (Phase 347), and a write through a local counts for what
the local holds (Phase 351) — but only a local assigned a parameter or field **by name**. `int[] b = f ? a : c;
b[0] = 5` left the frame empty, so a caller's `@Ensures({ a[0] == 0 })` across `put0(a, c, true)` verified, falsely;
so did a cast, an elvis and a `def` local. A probe for the wrap-up of Phase 356 found it.

- **A local's sources come from any right-hand side** (`aliasSources`): a variable; both branches of a ternary or
  elvis; a cast's operand; the owner of a field or element read (`h.arr` → `h`, `xss[i]` → `xss`). A fresh value —
  a literal, `new`, a list/map/array literal, or a call returning a new collection (`collect`, `findAll`, `toList`,
  `clone`, …) — aliases nothing. A for-in variable aliases its collection's elements. A local of value type (`int n =
  f ? x : y`) copies, so aliases nothing.
- **A source the inference can't name is loud:** a call's result (`int[] b = id(a)`) or a view (`xs.subList(0, 1)`)
  may be any parameter or field, so a write through such a local makes the frame unbounded, with the reason "a write
  through the local 'b', assigned from 'xs.subList(0, 1)', which may alias a parameter or field" (Phase 348's loud
  skip at the call site, and its unchecked-frame report on a declared `@Modifies`).
- **Rebinding is not writing through:** in callee inference a plain `b = v`, a declaration and a for-in variable are
  recorded as rebindings (`REBIND`). A rebound field or parameter is still written, as before; a rebound local is
  not, so `List rest = pruneWindow(…)`, only read, keeps the recursive LemmaScript port's frame empty — without this
  the loud rule above made it unbounded. The aliasing is flow-insensitive: a local ever assigned an opaque source and
  ever written through is loud even if rebound in between.
- **Fixed, older: a helper's write to an object parameter's field was dropped.** `recordTarget` recorded `h.n = 5`
  (and `h.n++`, `h.n += 1`) as a write of a field `n` of the helper's own class — which has none, so the write fell
  out of the frame, and the caller kept `h.n == 0` across the call. In callee inference a field write through any
  base other than `this` or a class now records the base, recursively (`h.inner.n`, `xs[0].n` → `h`, `xs`), and the
  caller havocs the object's fields (Phase 350). A declared `@Modifies({ k })` on such a helper now fails its check.
  Phase 351's `Box b = h; b.n = 5` had worked only because the declaration of `b` was itself counted as a write of `b`.

**Shipped tests:** group `P357 an alias through an expression`, 16 cases, 11 of which compiled cleanly before: a
ternary alias refuting the caller and an array outside both branches staying framed; an elvis, a cast and a `def`
alias; a view and a call's result loud; a call's result only read keeping the frame; a value-typed local copying; an
object parameter's field written, incremented and written through a local; an object ternary meeting the Phase 194
boundary; a declared frame missing the written object and one naming it; a for-in variable aliasing its collection.

**Still out:** `a.clone()` and other unknown methods on a receiver are still read as writing it (sound, imprecise —
`clone` and the GDK copies: Phase 358);
flow-sensitive aliasing; aliasing in general, the non-goal behind Phase 194's boundary. A local array alias in a
method's own body (`int[] b = a; b[0] = 5; return a[0]`) is unchanged: not linked, so a spurious bounds warning, not
a false proof.

## Phase 358 — a copy is a read, a user method is not  *(shipped — precision, and soundness: two silent write holes closed)*

Phase 357's follow-up. The write collector decides what a call writes by its method name: a mutator (`add`, `sort`,
…) writes its receiver, a name on the read lists (`LOOP_PURE_READS`, and `INFER_PURE_READS` in callee inference)
writes nothing, and anything else is read as writing its receiver (Phase 347) — or, in a loop's write set, as
unbounded.

- **A copy is a read:** `clone`, `toSorted` and `toUnique` join the read lists, and `grep`, `findResult(s)`,
  `countBy`, `indexed` and `collectNested` the callee-inference one (`unique()` and `sort()` mutate, so stay out;
  `reverse()` mutates a `StringBuilder`, so stays out too). Before, `int[] b = a.clone(); b[0] = 5` in a helper
  havocked the caller's `a`, `xs.toSorted()` its size, and a loop taking a clone dropped every loop-stable
  precondition over the original.
- **Fixed, older: a user method named like a library read was a read.** The read lists name library methods, but
  the test was on the name alone, so a sibling class's own `int size() { n = n + 1; … }` called on a parameter was
  taken as `List.size()`: nothing written, in a helper's inferred frame (the Phase 350 sibling-frame branch came
  after the read-list test) and in a method body loop's write set, which kept `h.n == 0` loop-stable across
  `h.size()`. Both verified a false `@Ensures({ h.n == 0 })`. `pureRead` now refuses the name when the receiver's
  declared type — or a supertype — is a class compiled from source that declares the method itself; the call then
  takes the sibling's own frame (a pure `size()` still frames nothing), the receiver-write fallback, or, in a loop,
  the bail. The same test guards Phase 343's written-parameter and size-preserving visitors. A receiver with no
  declared type (a `def` local, a call's result) may be of any class, so there any class of the compilation unit
  declaring the name is enough to refuse it.
- **Fixed, older: an unknown method on a receiver with no name wrote nothing.** Phase 347's fallback records an
  unknown method's receiver as written — but a receiver that isn't a name (`id(h).size()`) contributed only its own
  expression's writes, though `id(h)` is `h`. Now, by Phase 357's `aliasSources`, a fresh receiver (`new T()`, a
  literal, a copy) still writes nothing visible; anything else makes the frame unbounded, loudly ("a call on
  'A.id(h)', which may be a parameter or field and may write it"). `xs << v` returns `xs`, so a chained
  `log << a << b` writes `log`, as before.

**Shipped tests:** group `P358 a copy is a read, a user method is not`, 11 cases: a helper writing a clone keeping the
original, and writing the original still refuting; clearing a sorted copy keeping the size; a loop taking a clone
keeping a loop-stable precondition; a sibling's own writing `size()` in a helper, through a local and in a method body
loop and through a `def` local (each compiled cleanly before); a call on a call's result loud (compiled cleanly
before); a sibling's own writing `clone()`; a sibling's reading `size()` framed by its body.

**Still out:** a receiver declared as an interface or library type that a source class implements (`List<T> xs`
holding a user `List`) is still read by the library's contract (Phase 359); `reverse()` and the other receiver-type-dependent
names stay writes.

## Phase 359 — a call is framed by what it may dispatch to  *(shipped — soundness: virtual dispatch in frames and values)*

Phase 358's follow-up. A call's frame came from the method its receiver's DECLARED type names — a library read by
name, or a source method by its body (Phases 347, 350). A virtual call runs the receiver's runtime override, so:

- a `Comparable<Box> c` parameter holding a `Box` whose `compareTo` writes `n` was the library's read — nothing
  written — and a caller's `@Ensures({ b.n == 0 })` across `cmp(b, b)` verified, falsely;
- a `Base h` parameter holding a `Sub` was framed by `Base.get()`'s body, missing `Sub.get()`'s write — in a
  helper's inferred frame, through a same-class call inside `Base` (`twice()` calling `get()`), and at a call in the
  caller's own body (`h.get()`).

The world is closed over the compilation unit, as for sibling frames (Phase 350): a class compiled elsewhere is a
library class, read by its supertype's contract. `overriders(m)` lists the instance methods of the same name and
arity that a class of the unit extending or implementing `m`'s class declares, and:

- **the collector** adds them to a call's candidates (same-class and sibling calls), so their frames are unioned in,
  formals mapped to actuals by position; a field only a subclass declares stays caller-visible in the base method's
  frame;
- **a library-typed receiver** with unit overrides (`libraryReceiverOverrides`) is framed by those overrides onto
  the receiver — the library's own method by its contract, a read — so a reading `compareTo` keeps the frame; in a
  loop's write set it is not a pure read (Phase 358's `userDeclared` takes unit subtypes too), so the loop bails;
- **the call site** (`assumeCalleeEnsures`) unions the overrides' frames into the callee's, an override's formals
  renamed to the callee's by position (`Sub.put(int[] b)` overriding `Base.put(int[] a)`); an override whose writes
  can't be bounded leaves the call unmodelled, loudly: "call 'get(…)' may dispatch to Sub.get(…), whose writes can't
  be bounded from its body".

The `@Ensures` assumed at the call stays the callee's: an override inherits it (groovy-contracts), and one that
redeclares it is held to Phase 120's behavioural-subtyping check.

- **Fixed, older: an overridden helper's body was its value.** The closed evaluator (Phase 8a, `PureEvaluator.resolve`)
  inlined a contract-free, frame-empty same-class helper as its call's value — `foo() { get() }` proved
  `result == 0` from `Base.get() { 0 }`, though a `Sub` receiver runs `Sub.get() { 1 }`. An instance method a class
  of the unit overrides is no function now: its call is opaque (or, in a contract, outside the fragment, loudly).

**Shipped tests:** group `P359 a call is framed by what it may dispatch to`, 10 cases, 7 compiling cleanly
before: a `Comparable` holding a class whose `compareTo` writes; a base-class parameter holding a writing subclass,
directly and through a same-class call in the base; a call on a base-class parameter in the caller; an override
writing its differently-named parameter; an unbounded override loud; a reading override, and a reading `compareTo`,
keeping the frame; an overridden helper's body not its value (compiled cleanly before), and one never overridden
still inlined.

**Still out:** a subclass compiled in another unit (the closed world — Phase 360); a collection subclass with fields (`class Bag
extends ArrayList`) is outside the fragment, so loud. A subclass in another unit may override a helper the closed
evaluator inlines, by the same closed-world boundary.

## Phase 360 — an overridable body is no contract  *(shipped — soundness: the open world, slice 1 of 3)*

Phase 359's follow-up. Its overrides are those of the compilation unit; a subclass compiled elsewhere — an app
extending a verified library class, months later — can override a method unseen, and Groovy classes and methods
are open by default. Every contract-free instance method's body was therefore an unwritten contract: read as the
call's frame (Phase 347) and, when frame-empty, as its value (Phase 8a). An app's `class Offset extends Counter {
int get() { count + 100 } }` broke a library's proved bounds check `a[c.get()]`, with nothing at runtime to catch
it, since `get()` has no contract for groovy-contracts to check.

Three designs were weighed: (A) record each relied-on body in the class file and check a later checked unit's
overrides against it; (B) the open world — trust a body only where it can't be overridden; (D) B by default, with an
opt-in closed-world option whose every reliance is a ledgered trusted fact (Phase 216), plus A's check where the
later unit is checked. D was chosen, in three slices; this is the first, B.

- **`openToOverride(m)`:** a body is trusted only for a static, private or final method, a constructor, or a
  method of a closed class — final, an enum, a record, or sealed with every permitted subclass closed in turn (a
  `non-sealed` one reopens the hierarchy). Otherwise `modifiedNames` is unknown — the call is loud, naming the
  method: "'Counter.incr(…)' can be overridden by a subclass compiled elsewhere, so its body isn't its frame — make
  it or its class final (or sealed), or declare @Modifies on it" — and `PureEvaluator.resolve` refuses it as a
  function, so its value is opaque.
- **A declared contract is what an override is held to** (Phase 120's behavioural subtyping when the subclass is
  checked; groovy-contracts at runtime), so `@Modifies` restores the frame, and `@Ensures` with `@Modifies({ [] })`
  the value.
- **The corpus:** 55 cases relied on an open body — the Phase 347–359 framing groups, and a few older ones (P14
  sort, P24, P25, P45, P237, the inheritance group). Each had its example classes closed — `final`, or `sealed` over
  `final` subclasses where the case is about a hierarchy — so it says what it said before, with the exact solver
  check count (9,756) of the closed-world run.

**Shipped tests:** group `P360 an overridable body is no contract`, 9 cases: an open class's writer loud (verified
before); a final class, a final method and a declared `@Modifies` trusted; an open helper's body neither frame nor
value (verified before), a private one inlined, and an open one's `@Ensures` with `@Modifies({ [] })` restoring the
call; a sealed hierarchy of final classes closed, and a `non-sealed` subclass reopening it (compiled cleanly before).

**Next (slices 2, 3):** a `closedWorld: true` checker option (Phase 362) that trusts open bodies again, each reliance a
TrustLedger entry (`report` lists the obligations a subclass author takes on, `deny` fails the build); then stamping
the reliances into the class file, checked against a later checked unit's overrides.

**Still out — found by this phase's probe, and the next soundness item: a property read through a user getter
(Phase 361).**
`b.n` from another class is modelled as the field `b$n`, but Groovy reads it through `getN()`. A class that declares
its own getter — even a final one, `int getN() { n = n + 1; return n }` — makes `int x = b.n; int y = b.n` differ,
and the verifier proves `x - y == 0`; under the open world a subclass's `getN()` override is the same hole.

## Phase 361 — a property read is its getter  *(shipped — soundness: accessors, measured)*

Phase 360's recorded follow-up. Phase 45 modelled `b.n`, for an object parameter `b`, as the field `b$n`. The
runtime was measured first (a `@TypeChecked` / `@CompileStatic` probe with a subclass overriding `getN()`):

| read | runs |
|---|---|
| `b.n` from another class, `@TypeChecked` or `@CompileStatic` | the getter — a subclass's override included |
| `o.n` on a peer, inside the class | the getter |
| `this.n`, bare `n` | the field |
| `p.n` on a public field, a subclass declaring `getN()` (`@TypeChecked`) | the subclass's getter |

So a user getter that writes (`int getN() { n = n + 1; return n }`) made `int x = b.n; int y = b.n` differ while
the verifier proved `x - y == 0`, and — under Phase 360's open world — a subclass compiled elsewhere may give any
open class such a getter.

- **`propertyAccessorReason(t, n, write)`:** `x.n` (`x` not `this`) is the field only when `t`'s class is closed
  (Phase 360: final, enum, record, closed sealed) and no class of its hierarchy — superclasses and permitted
  subclasses — declares a getter (`getN`, `isN`) or, for a write, a setter beyond a `@Generated` one or a trivial
  `return n` / `n = v`. Otherwise the reason names the open class or the accessor.
- **Reads:** the encoder's object-field read returns no term — outside the fragment, and nothing later may take it
  up (an uninterpreted function would make two reads agree). A postcondition skip now appends the reason
  (`Reporter.READ_NOTES`): "precondition '…' is outside fragment: 'Box' can be subclassed elsewhere, and Groovy
  reads 'n' through the getter 'getN', which a subclass may override — make the class final (or sealed)".
- **Helpers:** a read through such a getter is a call that may write, and a write through a user setter may write
  anything, so either makes the inferred frame unbounded, with the same reason.
- **Field writes in a method body** (`b.n = 5`) were already outside the fragment, so are unchanged.
- **The corpus:** 28 cases read fields of an open class from outside (P45, P89, P194, P350, P351, P357, P358) and
  had their example classes closed, as in Phase 360; P360's open-class cases now claim about an array, so they still
  test the method rule. The solver check count is unchanged (9,775).

**Shipped tests:** group `P361 a property read is its getter`, 8 cases, 5 compiling cleanly before: two reads
through a writing getter; a helper reading through one; an open class's field read, with the reason; a sealed
hierarchy whose subclass declares a getter; a helper writing through a user setter (loud — conservative: that setter
writes only its receiver); a trivial getter, a generated one on a final class, and a trivial setter, all the field.

**Still out:** a user setter is not read for its own frame (one writing only its receiver is loud though sound);
a user getter is not read as a value (a `@Ensures` on it is not used for `b.n`); `closedWorld: true` (Phase 360's
slice 2) will relax the open-class rule for code that opts in (Phase 362).

## Phase 362 — the closed world, opted into and ledgered  *(shipped — slice 2 of 3)*

Phases 360/361 made the open world the default. The cost is real — reasoning about another object's state needs
its class closed — and some code knows better: its subclasses are its own, or framework proxies (Spring, Micronaut,
Hibernate, Mockito) that subclass and delegate, where `final` would break the framework. Such a class opts back in:
`@TypeChecked(extensions = 'verification.VerifyChecker(closedWorld: true)')`, read per class (an enclosing class's
annotation covering a nested one) by the `inferLoops` option's parser, now `verifyOptionEnabled`.

- **What it relaxes:** `openToOverride` is Phase 360's test (now `overridableElsewhere`) and not the closed world,
  so an overridable body is again the call's frame (Phase 347) and, frame-empty, its value (Phase 8a); and an open
  class's field is read as the field (Phase 361), its unit subclasses' accessors scanned instead of permitted ones.
- **What it keeps:** the unit is still seen — an override a unit class declares (Phase 359) and a user accessor
  anywhere in the unit's hierarchy (Phase 361) count as before.
- **The ledger (Phase 216):** a new kind, `closed world`, recorded where a proof relies, anchored at the relying
  method — a call's frame (`reliedFrame`, at the collector's candidates and the call site, not wherever a frame is
  merely computed, so the method under check is never its own reliance), an inlined value (`PureEvaluator.resolve`),
  an equational combiner's inlining (its `MethodNode` now kept with the equation), and a field read. Each names the
  subclass author's obligation: "a subclass compiled elsewhere must write no more", "… must not override it", "…
  must not declare getN()". `VERIFY_TRUST=report` lists them, `deny:world` fails on them; the harness `trusted:`
  summary counts them.
- **Docs:** TOOLING.md's ledger section gains the option, with the kind token `world`; the README's knobs note it.
- **Harness:** `tcw(…)`, the `tc` header with the option.

**Shipped tests:** group `P362 the closed world, opted into and ledgered`, 8 cases: an open class's writer framed and
ledgered; its fields read as fields, ledgered; an open helper's body as its value, ledgered; the method under check
not ledgered as its own reliance; `deny` failing at the relying method; an override in the unit and a getter a unit
subclass declares still caught; the option per class.

**Next (slice 3):** stamp the reliances into the class file, so a later unit compiled with the checker has its
overrides checked against them — the unchecked subclass remains the residual, now a ledgered one (Phase 363 for
3a; the carriers were refined to two: skeleton files and, optionally, annotations).

## Phase 363 — an override is held to its ancestor's skeleton  *(shipped — slice 3a; three older holes closed)*

Slice 3 was refined into two carriers for the reliances (a relied-skeleton file, the JDK-specs dialect; and,
optionally later, a class-file annotation) over one model: **a reliance is a contract nobody wrote** — a frame is a
`@Modifies`, an inlined value an `@Ensures` with `@Modifies({ [] })`, a field read a trivial getter's `@Ensures`. So
checking a later unit's override is contract inheritance, which already existed for source ancestors. 3a is the
consumer, built and tested first against hand-written skeletons.

- **A precompiled ancestor's skeleton is an ancestor declaration** (`skeletonDecl` in `superAndInterfaceDecls`):
  `SpecRegistry.ancestorContract` returns the relied skeleton's method (`relied/<fqn>.groovy`, under `VERIFY_SPECS`
  or `META-INF/groovy-verify/`), else the spec skeleton's — never ledgered, since the override is proved against
  it. Its `@Requires`/`@Ensures`/`@Modifies` are inherited through `findContractText`; a `@Pure` one inherits as
  `@Modifies({ [] })` (`declaredModifies`). The frame check names the skeleton.
- **An inherited `@Ensures` is a postcondition to prove:** the verification gate looked at the method's OWN
  `@Ensures` only. A source ancestor's reaches the method anyway, through groovy-contracts' inheritance transform,
  so this is new for skeleton ancestors only.
- **Fixed, older: a precompiled method has no body, but was read as writing nothing.** `modifiedNames` gave every
  bodiless method the skeleton's "nothing" — right for a skeleton, and for a source abstract method whose unit
  overrides are unioned (Phase 359), but not for a library method: a helper calling an inherited one (`fill(a)` from
  a subclass of a precompiled class) wrote nothing. Now its own class's skeleton is its frame (ahead of the open-world
  test, since a checked override is held to it), and without one the call is loud: "'LibCounter.fill(…)' is compiled
  elsewhere, with no contract or skeleton giving its frame — supply a skeleton … declaring @Modifies".
- **Fixed, older: `super.m(…)`** recorded `super` as the written name — no caller-visible location, so dropped. It
  now resolves on the superclass, non-virtually.
- **Fixed, older: a same-class method named like a library mutator** (`fill`, `add`, `sort`, `append`, …) was read
  by the mutator list as writing its receiver `this` — dropped — instead of by its own frame; the twin of Phase 358's
  read-list hole. The mutator reading now applies only to a method no same-class call or user class declares.
- **Fixed: a skeleton without imports said nothing** — CET resolves contract annotations' simple names through the
  imports, so an un-imported `@Ensures` was silently dropped; the skeleton dialect now star-imports
  `groovy.contracts`.
- **Harness:** `specs:` / `relied:` case keys (fqn → skeleton text) written to a temporary `VERIFY_SPECS` directory
  for one compile, the registry's cached entries evicted around it (`SpecRegistry.evict`); and a precompiled
  "library" class, `fixture.LibCounter`, in the test sources, so a case's source is a later unit.
- **Also found:** an applyCrossClassCall fallback (Phase 45: an unresolvable callee havocs the receiver's fields)
  ignored the arguments; it is now loud when handed a mutable one. (Unreached by this phase's cases, which resolve.)

**Shipped tests:** group `P363 an override is held to its ancestor's skeleton`, 11 cases, 7 compiling cleanly
before: an override writing outside a relied frame, and one within it; a spec skeleton's `@Pure` as an empty frame;
an inherited `@Ensures` refuted on the override and met; a source interface's `@Ensures` proved on an implementer, as
before; a same-class instance method named like a mutator framed by its body; a helper calling an inherited
precompiled method loud, directly and through `super`; a skeleton framing it, exactly.

**Still out:** inherited fields of a precompiled class are not modelled (`n.count` with `count` declared by the
library class is outside the fragment — loud); 3b, the writer of relied skeletons (Phase 364); 3c, the annotation
carrier.

## Phase 364 — a library writes what its proofs relied on  *(shipped — slice 3b)*

Phase 363 holds a later unit's overrides to a relied skeleton; this writes them. Under `closedWorld: true`, each
reliance on a member of a class compiled in the same unit is now recorded structurally as well as ledgered
(`recordFrameReliance`, `recordValueReliance`, `recordFieldReliance`, beside the Phase 362 `trustClosedWorld`
calls), and when a class's checking ends the unit's reliances are written to the output directory — the compile's
`targetDirectory`, so Gradle's classes dir and the jar — as `META-INF/groovy-verify/relied/<fqn>.groovy`:

- **a frame** as `@Modifies({ [this.count, a] })` (a formal by name, a field as `this.f`);
- **a value** as `@Ensures({ result == (<body>) }) @Modifies({ [] })` when the body is one expression — the file
  is parsed back (`SpecRegistry.parseForLint`) and, if it doesn't parse, written again with `@NoOverride` instead —
  and as `@NoOverride` when it isn't. `@NoOverride` is new to the 3a consumer: an override of a member so marked is an
  error unless it only delegates (`super.get()`), since "returns what the base body returns" can't be checked for a
  body no expression states;
- **a field read** as its getter, `@Ensures({ result == (n) }) @Modifies({ [] }) int getN()`, and a write as its
  setter, `@Ensures({ n == v }) @Modifies({ [this.n] }) void setN(int v)`.

A reliance on a class compiled ELSEWHERE stays ledger-only (its relied file is its own library's). An in-memory
compile (no output directory) ledgers each class's reliances as unwritten — "relied skeleton not written: the
compilation has no output directory, …" — so `deny:world` still fails on them.

- **Finding them in the later unit:** relied skeletons are resources of the library on the COMPILE classpath, which
  the checker's own loader needn't see; `SpecRegistry` now reads them through the compile's class loader
  (`COMPILE_LOADER`, set per method from the source unit), and caches them per loader, so a long-lived daemon never
  reuses a relied skeleton from an older build of the library.
- **Tests:** `ReliedSkeletonTest` (JUnit, two units): a closed-world library compiled to a classes directory writes
  the expected files (and none for a class nothing relied on); compiled against it, a checked override writing
  more, changing a relied value, or shadowing a relied field with a getter fails, one within its frame and a
  delegating one pass, and an unchecked subclass is not checked — the residual.

**Shipped tests:** group `P364 a library writes what its proofs relied on`, 4 cases: an in-memory compile ledgering
its reliances as unwritten, and one relying on nothing ledgering nothing; a relied `@NoOverride` holding an override,
unless it delegates. And `ReliedSkeletonTest`, 7 tests.

**Still out:** a class that loses all its reliances keeps a stale relied file until the classes directory is
cleaned (over-strict, never unsound — Gradle's full recompile cleans it; incremental Groovy compilation may not);
a subclass compiled without the checker (the residual, now ledgered, stated in the jar, and checkable by anyone who
runs the checker); 3c, the class-file annotation carrier, only if shading (which may drop `META-INF`) matters.

## Phase 365 — a soundness sweep  *(shipped)*

A probe sweep of ~150 shapes neighbouring Phases 357–364 — traits, interface `default` methods, closures and
callables, constructors and initialisers, overloads, default arguments, varargs, nested and inner classes, statics,
field shadowing, in-place JDK/GDK mutators and views, exceptions — found four families of silent holes. Traits,
default methods, constructors, the collection layer and closures stored or passed on were already loud or refuted.

- **Overloads resolved by name and arity.** `resolveContractedCallee` took the first same-arity overload, so for
  `h(a)` on an `int[]` the frame of `h(Object)` (empty) stood in for `h(int[])`'s, and with contracts its `@Ensures`
  and `@Modifies`; `PureEvaluator` evaluated `h(long)`'s body as the value of `h(1)`, which runs `h(int)`. A call now
  resolves to the method STC chose (`stcTarget`: the call's `methodTarget` / `DIRECT_METHOD_CALL_TARGET`), matched by
  erased signature; with no target and several same-arity overloads up the hierarchy (`ambiguousOverload`) — the
  PureEvaluator's case, which carries no types — none is assumed. A carrier operator (`Encoder.singleArgMethod`)
  likewise declines an overloaded name. The frame collector already took the union of the overloads.
- **Fields another class owns.** A frame names fields bare, read as the writing method's class's (or, through a
  receiver, the receiver's). So `A.n = 1` written from class C was recorded as C's `n`, and dropped for a caller in A;
  a static nested class's bare `n = 1` (the outer static), and an inner class's `n = 1` or `A.this.n = 1` (the
  enclosing instance's field), were read as locals; `C.s()` calling `A.setN(1)` was framed `A$n` (Phase 350's name
  for a sibling's static) and dropped as invisible; and a superclass method writing the static its subclass caller
  inherits was framed as the receiver's field `c$k`. Now a write to a static of another class of the unit is
  recorded as `Sib$field` (`foreignStaticName`) and kept in the frame (`unitStatic`), and a caller whose class or
  superclass owns it reads it under its own name (`callerOwnStatic`) — in `assumeCalleeEnsures`, in the collector,
  and in the frame check (which names it `A.n` for a method of another class). An enclosing instance's field is
  unbounded, loudly ("a field of A, which a frame of A.In can't name").
- **A written formal handed `this`.** `c.w(this)`, where `w(A a)` writes `a.n`, havocked a variable named `this`,
  leaving the caller's fields framed. Now loud, in the collector and at the call ("which is passed 'this' — the
  caller's own fields").
- **An unknown call writes what it is handed.** Phase 347 read an unknown method as mutating its receiver "and
  nothing else nameable", but `r.nextBytes(b)`, `s.getChars(0, n, dst, 0)`, `rdr.read(buf)`, `q.drainTo(ys)`,
  `f.accept(b)` and `c.call(b)` fill their arguments; and `collect`, `collectEntries`, `collectMany`,
  `collectNested` and `toArray` are reads only without a collector argument. Each mutable argument of an unknown
  call is now written and may be resized (`recordArgumentWrites`, beside the receiver), a read name's collector
  overload is no read (`collectorOverload`), and a callable called by name (`k(b)` on a closure field or parameter)
  writes its arguments too. A constant, an immutable-typed value or a closure literal is no write.

**Shipped tests:** group `P365 soundness sweep`, 26 cases, 22 verifying before: an overloaded callee's frame,
value, `@Ensures` and `@Modifies`, and on another class's receiver; another class writing the caller's static,
through an instance method and by calling back into the caller's class; a nested class writing its outer static;
a superclass's write to an inherited static; an inner class's and `A.this.n`'s writes to the enclosing instance
(loud); a written `this` (loud); `nextBytes`, `getChars`, `read`, `toArray`, `accept`, a closure field, `collect(dst)`,
`collectEntries(map)` and `drainTo`. And four that still prove: the chosen overload's `@Ensures` (refuted before), a
same-named static of another class, a plain `collect { … }`, an immutable argument.

**Boundaries, stated:** a `@TypeChecked` call still dispatches through the metaclass at run time, so a metaclass
change or category made by code outside the proof (`C.metaClass.get = { -> 1 }`, `use (Cat) { … }`) can replace a
method's behaviour, even a final class's; every proof assumes the statically chosen method runs (`@CompileStatic`
callers dispatch directly). An instance method of a final class is framed by its body but its value is still opaque
(over-strict). A `Sib$field` written through a chain of calls is havocked under that name by a caller that can't
read it, harmlessly.

## Phase 366 — a contract-layer sweep  *(shipped)*

Phase 365 swept how calls are framed; this sweeps what a method's own body and its contracts are taken to mean —
`old` snapshots, `result` aliasing, side effects inside contracts, class invariants, loops calling framed helpers,
`instanceof` patterns, exceptions — about 60 shapes. `old` (arrays, lists, maps, fields, through helpers) and the
loop engine's use of helper frames were already sound. Two families were not.

- **A container alias in the method's own body.** The encoder keeps an array, collection or map by NAME (its
  element, size and nullity oracles), so `int[] b = a` gave `b` oracles of its own: `int[] b = a; b[0] = 1` proved
  `a[0] == 7`, and `int[] b = a; a[0] = 1; b[0]` read 7. (This is what the "spurious bounds warning" on such a `b`,
  recorded earlier as over-strict only, was hiding.) The same held for a field assigned a parameter, a ternary of
  names, a call that may return its argument (`ys = id(xs)`), and an `instanceof` pattern variable. Phase 351 gave
  objects an alias model; this is the container half, and it is loud: `containerAliasHazard` finds each
  container-typed local, parameter or field assigned something that may share its contents (Phase 357's
  `aliasSources`; an opaque value reaches the names it mentions and the fields), and `mutatedNames` the names the
  body mutates (a store, field write or `++` base, a mutator's receiver, an argument a call may write — a unit
  callee by its frame); an alias with either side mutated skips the path, early-exit and loop checks
  (`guardContainerAlias`), naming the assignment. A read-only alias is a faithful copy: it now shares its source's
  oracles (`int[] b = a; b.length > 0 ? b[0] : 0` proves; it refuted before). A call whose non-overridable callee
  only returns fresh values (`returnsFresh`) aliases nothing; `intersect` joins the fresh-result methods, and a
  collector overload (`collect(dst) { … }`, which returns `dst`) leaves them.
- **A helper's pattern variable.** `if (o instanceof int[] b) b[0] = 1` in a helper wrote a "local": the frame
  dropped it. Now the pattern variable aliases what it tests, in the inference (`patternVariable`) as in the guard.
- **Contracts that write.** groovy-contracts evaluates a contract when it checks it, so one calling a method that
  writes changes the state the proofs assume — a callee's `@Requires({ bump(a) })` rewrote `a` at every call while
  the caller's proof framed it. A contract (`@Requires`, `@Ensures`, a class `@Invariant`) calling a method of the
  unit that writes, or whose writes can't be bounded, or a collection mutator, is now an error on the contract
  (`contractPurityCheck`), anchored on the annotation.

**Shipped tests:** group `P366 contract-layer sweep`, 16 cases: a store through a local alias, a read through one
after a store into the original, a ternary of names, a call returning its argument, a field assigned a parameter,
a pattern variable, a loop through an alias (all loud, all verifying before); a read-only alias and a fresh call
result that prove; a helper's pattern variable over an array and a list (refuted, verifying before); a writing
`@Requires`, `@Ensures`, callee `@Requires` (whose caller verified before) and `@Invariant` (errors); a contract
calling a pure method, fine.

**Still out:** the alias is loud, not modelled — two names for one container whose contents change aren't proved
through; implicit bounds obligations on an alias still see its own length (a spurious warning, sound); a callee's
`old.x` on a non-parameter in a static method is a groovy-contracts restriction.

## Phase 367 — the trusted base, audited against the runtime  *(shipped)*

The shipped JDK skeletons (`META-INF/groovy-verify/specs/`, 55 methods over 13 classes) and the method-name tables
the frame inference reads (the pure-read lists, the fresh-result list, the pure static classes) are trusted: never
proved, consumed at every call. `SpecAuditTest` (JUnit, four tests) now runs each against the runtime it describes.

- **Skeletons:** each method is found on the runtime class by its skeleton signature (or, for a skeleton whose
  formals are widened to `Object` or narrowed to exact types, the one runtime method they fit) and run on the cross
  product of edge-heavy inputs (`MIN_VALUE`/`MAX_VALUE` and their neighbours, ASCII and non-ASCII chars, empty and
  mixed-type lists, unsorted arrays, `LocalDate.MIN`…) that its `@Requires` admits — 14,743 runs. Each `@ThrowsIf` arm
  is checked in its stated direction (an exhaustive arm both ways, a sufficient one only forward), the `@Ensures` on
  every normal return (with `result` and `old`, the receiver's members for an instance spec), and the frame: an
  argument or receiver outside `@Modifies` (all of them, for `@Pure`) must be unchanged, and a framed collection keep
  its size (Phase 229's assumption). Mutation-checked: a wrong total spec (`abs`), an over-wide throw arm (`floorDiv`)
  and a mutator marked `@Pure` (`sort`) each fail it.
- **Name tables:** every read name is called on sample receivers (lists, sets, maps, strings, arrays, builders,
  numbers, an iterator) with sample arguments (none, indices, closures, comparators, collections); a receiver or
  argument changed is a failure. Every fresh-result name must return neither its receiver nor an argument, nor a view
  (writing the result mustn't change the receiver). Every public static of each pure static class with a mutable
  parameter is run, and must leave its arguments unchanged.

**Found and fixed:**

- `Collections.frequency(c, o) == c.count(o)` was **false** whenever the needle's boxed type differed from the
  elements' (`frequency([5L], 5)` is 0, `[5L].count(5)` is 1 — `equals` against Groovy's `==`), and the int model can't
  tell them apart: `frequency(xs, 5)` over a `List<Long>` proved `result == xs.count(5)`. The skeleton now names
  **exact formals** — `frequency(Collection<Integer> c, Integer o)` and a `Long` twin — and the registry's typed lookup
  (`SpecRegistry.accepts`, `exactFormal`, `typeKey`) matches a formal written as a boxed type, or with type arguments,
  only to an actual of exactly that type (and never to an unknown one); callers now pass the actuals' type arguments.
  `List<Integer>` with an `int` needle links as before.
- `map.get(key, default)` — `get` is on the read list, but the GDK's two-argument form puts the default in when the
  key is absent: a helper calling it was framed as writing nothing. Now that arity writes (`WRITING_ARITY`).
- `Character.toChars(cp, dst, i)` — `Character` is a pure static class ("writes only what its arguments do"), but this
  one fills `dst`. Now its arguments are written (`STATIC_ARG_WRITERS`), and a loop's write set, which can't name
  them, bails.

**Shipped tests:** `SpecAuditTest`, 4 tests; group `P367 the trusted base audited`, 7 cases, 5 verifying before:
`map.get(key, default)` writing and resizing a helper's map, `toChars` writing a helper's array, and `frequency`'s link
across mismatched boxed types, both ways; and two that still prove, a plain `map.get(key)` and `frequency` over a
`List<Long>` with a `long` needle.

**Boundaries, stated:** the audit samples — inputs a generator doesn't produce (an unspecced type, a value outside
the edge sets) go untested, and the name tables are audited on common receivers, not every type a name can reach. A
map whose reads write is beyond any name table: `[:].withDefault { 0 }` inserts on `get`, so a helper reading one is
framed as a read (a runtime-type property the static types don't show).

## Phase 368 — the encoder's built-in semantics, audited against the runtime  *(shipped)*

Phase 367 audited the skeletons and the name tables; most of what the verifier assumes about Groovy is neither, but the
encoder's own translations. `EncoderAuditTest` (JUnit; its own task, `./gradlew encoderAudit`, run by CI as a separate
step — about two minutes, kept out of `check`) checks them against the runtime: 128 probe expressions —
integer arithmetic and its wrap, `%`, `mod`, `intdiv`, `/`-then-truncate, `Math.floorDiv`/`floorMod`, shifts and
bitwise ops, long arithmetic and narrowing, comparisons, ranges and `in`, Groovy truth and Elvis, casts, list / array /
string methods with their edge cases (empty, negative and out-of-range indices) — each run on an edge-value grid
(`MIN_VALUE`, `MAX_VALUE`, 31/32/33, empty and mixed lists, `''`…) for its runtime value V, about 2,500 points. At each
point the verifier, pinned there by `@Requires`, is asked to prove `result != V`: a proof is the encoder believing a
value the runtime doesn't produce. Its twin `result == V` is the precision check; a point where the runtime throws must
draw some diagnostic. The probes run under `@CheckOverflow` (the strong claim: the JVM's wrap); a second test runs the
wrapping probes without it and requires each wrong value the math-int default proves to be a point where the
`@CheckOverflow` twin reports an overflow — so the documented assumption (README, Phase 44) is the default model's
*only* divergence. Mutation-checked: reverting the cast fix fails it at 11 points.

**Found and fixed:**

- **A cast was transparent.** `x as boolean` translated as `x`, so `@Requires({ x == 7 }) @Ensures({ result != true })`
  proved — at every non-zero point. A cast to `boolean` is now Groovy truth (`Encoder.groovyTruth`: non-zero, non-empty,
  non-null; an unmodelled kind is a loud skip), and an integer `as String` its decimal text (it had compared an int
  with a string).
- **`@CheckOverflow` gaps.** `MIN_VALUE.intdiv(-1)` wraps exactly as `MIN_VALUE / -1` does, but only `/` carried the
  obligation; `x << k` is `x * 2^k` and wraps like `*`; a narrowing cast (`(int) l`, `l as int`, to short / byte / char)
  wraps outside the target's range and was the identity. All three are now overflow obligations (`OverflowSite` ops
  `div` for `intdiv`, `shl` for a literal shift count — a non-literal count is a loud skip — and `narrow:<type>`
  ranged by the target). A `<<` on a collection is an append, and draws none.
- **`last()`** throws on an empty list, and only `first`/`head`/`pop`/`removeLast` carried the non-empty obligation.

**Recorded, not changed:** Groovy's lenient indexing — `xs[5]` is `null` past the end, `xs[-1]` and `a[-1]` count from
the end, `max()`/`min()` of an empty list are `null` — is read as Java's strict indexing: a bounds obligation that the
runtime never throws, so wrong values there are proved only beside a loud warning (over-strict, never silent).
`Math.floorDiv`/`floorMod`'s spec states only the throw, so its value is opaque (precision); a spec's `@ThrowsIf` is a
survival fact, not a call-site obligation, so a call that always throws (`floorDiv(x, 0)`) draws no diagnostic
(partial correctness — it never returns). *(Closed in Phase 370.)*

**Shipped tests:** `EncoderAuditTest`, 2 tests; group `P368 the encoder audited`, 11 cases, 5 verifying before (a
boolean cast's wrong value, `intdiv`, `<<` and a narrowing cast under `@CheckOverflow`, `last()` on a possibly-empty
list), and 6 that prove, two of them new (`(x as boolean) == (x != 0)`, refuted before; `x as String`, skipped before).

## Phase 369 — cleanup: what the diagnostics say, and two audit findings  *(shipped)*

Loose ends from Phases 365–368, each wrong or misleading output a user met.

- **A failing call with a non-null object argument.** `renderArg` fell back to `null` for any object type, so
  `g(C c)` under `@Requires({ c != null })` read `fails on: g(null)` — a call the precondition forbids. A non-null
  object now renders as `new C(…)` with the properties the model fixed (`new C(count: 5)`, from Phase 45's
  `c$count`), when its class has a visible no-arg constructor; otherwise the call is withheld rather than shown
  wrong. And the counterexample names an object parameter's field as the source spells it, `c.count = 5` — only a
  real field (Phase 89's `a$id` identity symbol is no field, and keeps its name).
- **Groovy's negative indices.** `xs[-1]` is the last element and `a[-2] = v` stores into the last but one (measured
  by the Phase 368 audit); the encoder read index −1. A negative CONSTANT index is now `size − k` in every path that
  translates an index — the read, a straight-line or loop store, and the bounds obligation, which reads
  `0 <= xs.size() - 1` (`Encoder.indexTerm`, `negativeConstant`). A non-constant index is unchanged: still bounded
  below by the obligation, so never mis-read.
- **A list subscript out of range doesn't throw.** Past the end `xs[i]` reads `null` (and a negative one counts from
  the end); the warning said `Possible IndexOutOfBoundsException`. The value model still needs `[0, size)`, so the
  obligation stands, but a list subscript's head now says what would happen — "List index may be outside [0, size):
  there the subscript reads null (or, when negative, counts from the end) rather than throwing, which the verifier
  doesn't model" — and its repro asserts no exception. `get(i)`, an array subscript and a negative constant (which
  does throw on an empty list) keep the exception. Four cases' expectations moved with it; one of them, the `-1`
  sentinel into `xs[i]`, is the clearest: Groovy returns the last element there, it never throws.
- **Applying a callable writes what it is handed.** `call` and `apply` are on the read list ("applying a callable
  doesn't write the callable"), and so their arguments were never written: a helper's `f.apply(b)` was framed as
  writing nothing — a silent hole, found here. Their mutable arguments are now written, as an unknown call's are
  (Phase 365) (`CALLABLE_APPLY`).
- **A closure literal's class is no override.** The class Groovy generates for a closure literal (`A$_g_closure1`,
  a `Closure` subclass) stood in, by Phase 359's dispatch rule, as an override of every `Closure.call` in the unit —
  so a helper's `c.call(b)` was unbounded with the reason "call 'call(…)': call 'doCall(…)': a call on
  'error.getStackTrace()'". Generated callables are no longer overriders (`generatedCallable`); a closure's effects
  are its body's, counted where the literal is.

**Not done, and why:** `@Modifies({ A.n })` — declaring a write to another class's static, which Phase 365 made a
frame-check error — is rejected by groovy-contracts' own transform ("@Modifies elements must be field references
(this.field) or parameter references"), so the stock annotation can't express it. It is the second item for the
groovy-contracts `@Modifies` JIRA, beside `@Modifies({})`.

**Shipped tests:** group `P369 cleanup`, 11 cases: the built object argument and its field's spelling; `xs[-1]`,
`a[-2]` and a store through `a[-1]` proving (bounds warnings before); `xs[-1]` on a possibly-empty list; a list
subscript's head and `get(i)`'s; `f.apply(b)` writing (verifying before) and an immutable argument not; a closure
literal handed to a helper (the `doCall` reason before).

## Phase 370 — a spec's `@ThrowsIf` is an obligation at the call  *(shipped)*

A registry spec's `@ThrowsIf` arm was only a survival fact (Phase 222): past the call, its condition is false. Nothing
checked it AT the call, so `Math.floorDiv(x, y)` was silent where `x.intdiv(y)` warned of division by zero, and
`floorDiv(x, 0)`, which always throws, drew nothing (the Phase 368 audit's note).

- **The obligation.** Each spec'd call with arms is a site (`SpecThrowSite`, collected by the `ObligationCollector`
  through `specThrowSiteFor`), discharged like a division's: the arms' conditions, with the formals replaced by the
  actuals, must be unsatisfiable under the path's facts. So `@Requires`, guards, loop invariants and the value-flow
  replay all discharge it. A refutation reads `Possible ArithmeticException: Math.floorDiv(x, y) throws when y == 0`,
  `obligation: !(y == 0)`, with a failing call and a repro asserting the arm's exception. An arm outside the fragment
  is a loud skip, never assumed false. The registry is peeked (`SpecRegistry.peek`) before it is consumed, so a call
  without arms ledgers nothing new.
- **A handler covers it.** An arm whose exception a surrounding `catch` covers is defined behaviour (Phase 193). The
  curated coverage gained the two exceptions the specs throw beyond the built-ins: `IllegalArgumentException` (itself)
  and `NoSuchElementException`, both also under `RuntimeException`/`Exception`/`Throwable`.
- **Deliberate throwers are exempt.** For `Objects.requireNonNull`, `Objects.checkIndex` and the `Math.*Exact` family,
  the throw is the point: a check written as a method, or arithmetic that throws where the operator would wrap.
  Calling one is a deliberate throw, as a `throw` statement is, so there is no obligation; its arms still give the
  survival facts after it (`THROWING_GUARDS`). `Integer.parseInt` is there too, because the built-in numeral
  obligation (Phase 54) already covers its arm. `SpecAuditTest` checks every entry names a shipped skeleton with arms,
  so a renamed spec can't leave an entry that quietly exempts another call.
- **The method's own `@ThrowsIf`.** A woven guard (the default) runs at entry, so its condition is false throughout
  the body. That is now an entry fact for every implicit obligation, built-in or spec'd. Before, a division the guard
  had already ruled out still warned. A declared, unwoven throw makes an obligation of the same (or a covered)
  exception the method's contract where its condition holds. Both apply only to a condition over parameters the body
  never reassigns, the entry state it speaks of.

One existing case moved: `Long.parseLong(s)` on a possibly-null `s` now warns at the call, and its survival fact still
keeps the `s.length()` after it quiet (now asserted with `refute:`).

**Found, not changed:** in a loop body, an implicit obligation's failing call is built from the parameters alone, so it
may not enter the loop. A `floorMod(i, y)` (or `i % y`) in a `for (i < n)` body, under `@Requires({ n >= 0 })`, shows
`fails on: f(0, 0)`, a call that never reaches the body. The warning is right (`y` may be zero) but the repro is not.
This is older than Phase 370 (the built-in `%` does the same), and it is the next reporting item. *(Phase 371.)*

**Shipped tests:** group `P370 spec throws`, 14 cases, 6 verifying before: `floorDiv` by a possibly-zero divisor and by
zero, `max` of a possibly-empty collection, `nCopies` of a possibly-negative count, a declared throw of another exception
(all compiled cleanly before), and a woven guard ruling out a division (warned before). Plus discharge by `@Requires`, a
guard, a handler, a supertype handler, a loop invariant; the deliberate throwers; a declared throw. And `SpecAuditTest`'s
fifth test, `throwingGuardsNameSpecsThatThrow`.

## Phase 371 — a loop's failing call is a run from entry  *(shipped — reporting, and a soundness hole closed)*

An obligation in a loop is checked at an arbitrary iteration: the invariant's for an annotated loop, a summary's for
an unannotated one. That state needn't be reachable, and the failing call came from its model's parameters alone, so
a `floorMod(i, y)` in a `for (i < n)` body showed `fails on: f(0, 0)`, a call that never enters the body.

- **A witness from entry.** In a loop region the check runs as before with its diagnostics held. On a refutation it is
  re-sought along exact paths from method entry (`loopEntryPaths`): the statements before the loop, then each of its
  first eight iterations (guard, body), ending at the region's point, which is the guard about to be evaluated, an
  iteration begun, or the loop left by its guard. A loop on the way, an earlier one or one nested in the body, is
  unrolled the same way (`expansions`), and up to 32 paths are tried, shortest first. A path is replayed exactly
  (`replayExact`): each statement as it runs, an early exit asserted not taken, each branch condition in full. The
  region's facts (the invariant, the guard) are asserted too; they can only filter runs, never admit one that isn't
  real. The first path that refutes is reported, and its call is a run that gets there. If none does, the original
  diagnostic is reported with its call withheld and a note ("no failing call: the failure is at a loop iteration the
  check reaches through the loop's summary, not from entry, and no run of its first eight iterations gets there…").
  Witness sessions are auxiliary (Phase 337) and run only on a refutation.
- **Soundness: an unannotated loop's body is checked at every iteration.** With no `@Invariant`, a loop's obligations
  fell to `dischargeRegion`'s statement-wide fallback, which checked the body in the state BEFORE the loop:
  `int i = 0; while (i < n) { s = 100.intdiv(i - 3); i++ }` proved the divisor non-zero from `i == 0`, and `f(4)`
  throws. The same held for an index the loop moves (`a[i]` checked at `a[0]`), a divisor the loop writes, and a
  do-while's later passes. A classic `for` escaped only because its counter is declared in the loop (so it was free).
  Now `dischargeUnannotatedLoop` checks the guard and body with everything the loop writes havocked (a marker in the
  replay, `HAVOC_LOOP_KEY`) and, in the body, the guard holding. The region after the loop follows as before. A
  for-in over a collection havocs its loop variable and isn't unrolled.
- **Display.** A loop summary havocs every name's size slot as well; `x.size (after a loop)` is now shown only for a
  name that has a size.

- **Channel programs keep their own witness.** A method that names a channel (a desugared pipeline, or processes under
  rely/guarantee) isn't re-sought: its processes are closures and its receives ghost cursors, which no sequential replay
  runs, and its calls stand on those models' witnesses (the Kerridge gallery's `overRead(0)`, the trip count at which
  it hangs). The first measurement, without this, withheld five of their calls.

Across the corpus (outside this phase's own cases), loop refutations now find a witness from entry, and one withholds
its call: an over-strict bounds warning on an unannotated counting loop that no run fails. Three existing cases kept
their expected calls only once earlier and nested loops were unrolled too (Phase 337's sequential repro, Phase 336/340's
nested ones). No `ok:` case gained a warning from the soundness fix.

**Boundary:** a failure first reachable after the eighth iteration keeps its warning without a call, even when the
invariant's model happened to give a right one (`f(10)` for a divisor `i - 9`). A for-in over a collection, a loop in a
branch on the way, and a closure all end the search there. Channel programs aren't searched (above).

**Shipped tests:** group `P371 loop repros`, 11 cases, 8 verifying before. Silent before: an unannotated loop's divisor
at its fourth pass, an index it moves, a divisor it writes, a do-while's second pass. A wrong call before: `f(0, 0)` now
`f(1, 0)`, and `f(new int[0])` on a counting loop that never fails, now withheld. A failure past the eighth iteration
(the boundary), and a run that leaves the loop. Plus a body guard still discharging, an annotated loop's call entering
it, and a later iteration's failure.

## Phase 372 — a closure runs when it is called  *(shipped — soundness: a silent hole across closure iteration)*

A sweep after Phase 371's finding, which was a loop body checked in the state before the loop. The same shape held for
every closure: a site inside a closure literal was discharged with the statements before the closure, so in the state
where the closure is WRITTEN. It runs later, perhaps many times, after its own writes and the method's later ones.
Measured against the runtime, every one of these compiled cleanly and throws: `int d = 1; 3.times { s = 100.intdiv(d); d-- }`, and the
same body under `upto`, `downto`, `step`, `collect`, `findAll`, `inject`, `any`, `every`, `sum`, `reverseEach`, a map's
`each`, a stored `Closure c = { … }` called after `d = 0`, and `{ xs.get(0) }` called after `xs.clear()`. Only a `.each`
/ `eachWithIndex` escaped, as the loop Phase 310 desugars it into.

- **The fix.** Each site inside a closure literal is checked with every captured name it may read changed havocked
  first (`closureHavoc`, consulted in `dischargeObligationUnder`, so every pass gets it). That covers the names the
  closure itself writes (an earlier call's), those written by any statement after it (a later call's), those an
  enclosing loop writes, and those any closure in the method writes (it may be called in between). The write sets are
  the frame inference's (`collectWritesStmts`: a pure read like `get` writes nothing, a callee its frame), per statement,
  falling back to the crude targets, plus every instance field through a this-call, only for a statement it can't
  bound. A `.each` desugared to a loop is left to the loop. A channel method is left to rely/guarantee (Phase 371's rule).
- **Its failing call is withheld**, with the note "no failing call: the failure is inside a closure, in a call whose
  arguments and captured state the check takes as unknown rather than following from entry". That holds for every site in
  a closure, havoc or not: a closure parameter is free too, and `2.times { int k -> 100.intdiv(k - 3) }` showed
  `fails on: f()`, a call that never fails. Havocked values show as `d (when the closure runs) = 0`.
- **A closure literal local is never null** (Phase 277's constructor rule): `Closure c = { … }; c()` drew a
  null-dereference warning on `c()`.
- **Display.** A havocked size shows as the source spells it (`xs.size() (when the closure runs)`), not the oracle's
  `xs.size`.

No corpus case moved: none relied on the hole, and no `ok:` case gained a warning.

**Boundary:** a closure's calls aren't followed, so its warnings come without a failing call, and a captured name the
closure's caller can't change by then (written only before it) keeps its value. A `.each` loop's witness comes from
Phase 371.

**Shipped tests:** group `P372 closure iteration`, 10 cases, 8 verifying before. Silent before: `times`, `collect` and
`inject` writing what they read, a stored closure after a later write, `xs.clear()` before the call. A wrong call before:
`fails on: f()` for a closure parameter that never reaches the failure. A false warning before: a closure literal local's
`c()`, twice. Plus a captured value nothing writes and an `.each` loop keeping its call.

## Phase 373 — what a statement writes inside it  *(shipped — soundness: silent holes in evaluation order)*

A sweep after Phase 372, over the shapes where a statement writes more than its top-level target, or runs in more than
one order. A site was checked in the state BEFORE its statement, with the statements before it replayed, so a write
inside the statement, or inside a try or switch, never reached the sites that read it. Measured, every one of these
compiled cleanly and throws: `if ((n = m) >= 0 && 100.intdiv(n) > 0)` with `m = 0`, the same read in the if's body,
`int x = b ? (d = 0) : 1; 100.intdiv(d)`, the elvis form, `int x = i++ + i; 100.intdiv(i - 1)`, a try block's
`d = 0; return 100.intdiv(d)`, a catch or a finally reading what the try block wrote (after a return too), a case body
entered by falling through from `case 1: d = 0`, and a closure parameter's `c()` (or a `Consumer`'s `accept(this)`)
followed by `100.intdiv(count)` — the call was taken to write nothing, and `@Ensures({ count == 1 })` over `c()` proved.

- **Writes inside a statement.** `Encoder.nestedTargets` names what a statement assigns or increments besides its
  top-level target, and `isCallableCall` a call of a closure or a functional interface's method (Runnable, Callable,
  Comparator, `java.util.function.*`, `@FunctionalInterface`). For a statement's own sites those names are havocked
  first (`hiddenWrites`); a callable's call may write anything it reaches (`callableReach`: this object's fields and the
  statics, each parameter of a mutable type and an object parameter's fields, and what any closure in the method
  writes). Not when the callable runs last (`c()`, `int x = c.call()`): its receiver and arguments are evaluated before
  its body. Replayed later, such a statement is refused (`LoopEncoder.refuseHiddenWrites`) and havocked whole; the
  value-flow pass stops at it.
- **Try and switch by their structure** (`dischargeTry`, `dischargeSwitch`). A try block runs in order; a catch is
  entered after any prefix of it, so what the block writes is havocked there; a finally runs after the block or a catch,
  by any exit, so what both write is havocked there. A case body is entered by its match or by falling through, so what
  the cases falling into it write is havocked there.
- **Frames.** A callable's call makes a method's inferred frame unbounded ("a call of the callable 'f', whose body may
  write anything it reaches — declare @Modifies"), unless the callable is a local bound only to a closure literal,
  whose writes its declaration already counts. Phase 369 had bounded it by the arguments: that let
  `h(Function<Integer, Integer> f, int[] b) { f.apply(1) }` leave `a[0]` unwritten for `g(f, a)`, though `f` may hold
  `a` itself. The postcondition engine skips over such a call the same way.
- **The failing call is withheld** after any of these havocs, with a note ("no failing call: the failure rests on what a
  statement writes inside it …"): the state there is not followed from entry, and `fails on: f(-2147483648)` (default
  arm), `f(false)` (the ternary arm that writes nothing) and others were calls that don't fail. Havocked values say
  where they come from: `d (in the finally) = 0`, `(in the catch)`, `(after a fall-through)`, `(after the try)`,
  `(after the switch)`, `n (after a nested write)`, `count (after a callable's call)` — they all read "(after a loop)".
- **A GString literal local is never null**: `GString g = "${-> …}"; g.toString()` drew a null-dereference warning.

**Changed cases:** G413's "applying a function may write its argument" and "a closure literal handed to a helper" now
expect the unbounded frame's reason, and "… an immutable argument isn't" (`ok:`, unsoundly) is renamed "… nor does an
immutable argument bound it" and expects it too.

**Boundary:** these states aren't followed from entry, so their warnings come without a failing call; a write inside a
statement havocs the name for all of that statement's sites, including those evaluated before the write. The
postcondition engine still skips a nested assignment, a finally, a fall-through or a callable's call, loudly.

**Shipped tests:** group `P373 evaluation order`, 18 cases. Silent before: 12 — the finally (after a return and after
normal completion), the try block's order, the catch, the fall-through, the assignments in a condition and in an if's
condition read in its body, the ternary and elvis writes, the increment in an operand, a closure parameter's call and a
`Consumer`'s. A wrong call or label before: after a switch (`f(-2147483648)`), after a try ("after a loop"). A wrong
proof before: the postcondition over `c()`. A false warning before: the GString. Plus an increment in an index and in a
stored value, kept.

## Phase 374 — the exact ways a statement runs  *(shipped — witnesses, and a hoist that ran a conditional increment always)*

Phase 373 traded calls for soundness: every failure behind a nested write, a finally, a fall-through or a switch lost
its `fails on:` call, though most are a plain call from entry (`f(0)` for a finally reading `d = n`, `f(1)` for a case
falling into the divide). The havocked check still decides the obligation; on a refutation, the call is now sought
the way Phase 371 seeks a loop's: along exact paths from entry, through each of the statement's ways.

- **Evaluation order** (`EvalOrder`, new). A statement writing inside its expression is lowered into straight-line
  assignments in the order Java evaluates it: `(n = m) >= 0 && 100.intdiv(n) > 0` is `n = m`, assume `n >= 0`, then the
  divide. A value read before a later write to what it reads is snapshotted into a `$eoN` temp; `&&`, `||`, a ternary
  and an elvis branch into one path per way, each with its condition assumed (a value that isn't a condition, the elvis
  operand, by its Groovy truth, `(x as boolean)`). For the statement's own sites, the lowering stops at the site and
  keeps only the ways that reach it; the conditions the region assumed of the statement are in it, so they are dropped.
- **Try and switch.** A try is run through to its finally (a final `return`'s value evaluated first; an early return in
  it not taken); a finally's sites take the try block's way. A switch is entered at each case, with its match assumed
  and no earlier case's, or by none (the default, or past the switch), and runs the arms it falls through until one
  breaks; an arm leaving by a return ends that way. Only constant cases have an exact entry: a range keeps the note.
- **Composed with Phase 371.** A loop region's exact tail, and its unrolled entry iterations, are lowered the same way:
  `int x = (i == 2) ? (d = 0) : 1` in a loop body gives `fails on: f(3)`.
- **No witness for a catch** (no exception is followed) or a callable's call (its body is unknown): their note stays.
  A witness attempt that the replay can't take is no witness; it never stops the check. An exact witness whose model
  is empty depends on nothing, so a method with no parameters shows `fails on: f()`.
- **Soundness: an increment under a short circuit.** `Encoder.expandIncDecStatements` hoisted every `i++` in a
  statement, the right operand of `&&`/`||` included, where it runs only when the left lets it: `int i = 0; boolean t =
  b && (i++ >= 0); 100.intdiv(i)` read `i == 1` for `b == false` and compiled cleanly, and `@Ensures({ result == 1 })`
  over `i` proved. Such a statement is no longer hoisted: Phase 373 havocs it, and the lowering gives `fails on: f(false)`.
  A ternary's arms were already refused.

**Changed cases:** G417's ten cases whose call Phase 373 withheld now expect it (`f(0)`, `f(1)`, `f(true)`, `f()`);
its catch case keeps the note.

**Boundary:** a catch's sites, a callable's reach and a switch over non-constant cases keep the note. A path is
sought among at most 32 per site (64 tries with a loop's entries). The postcondition engine still skips these
statements, loudly.

**Shipped tests:** group `P374 exact witness`, 11 cases. Silent before: an increment under `&&` and under `||`. A wrong
proof before: a postcondition over the `&&` increment. A call withheld before: a ternary arm's increment, a try in a
try, a switch with no default, a string switch falling through, a finally after an early return not taken, a nested
write in a loop body. Plus an always-evaluated increment (still hoisted) and a range switch (its note kept).

## Phase 375 — a re-assigned array holds the new array  *(shipped — soundness: an external report from the ClearSplit port)*

Reported from the ClearSplit port: a conservation theorem written as a fold, `bal = afterExpenseRow(bal, …)` in a loop
with the invariant `bal.sum() == 0`, still verified with its key precondition deleted. Reproduced at Phases 372–374
alike, and wider than the report: re-assigning an array (or list) local rebound only its scalar handle, so its
contents, length and nullity kept reading the array it held BEFORE. In a loop, `v = grow(v)` (`result.length ==
a.length + 1`) preserved a false `v.length == m`; `v = w` kept v's own length; `v = inc0(v)` kept `v[0] == 0`; a list
parameter's `xs = grow(xs)` and `xs = ys` kept `xs.size()`. Straight-line, `v = grow(v); v.length` proved a false
`@Ensures({ result == m })`. And the callee's facts never reached the caller's array: an array formal read its own
oracles (`a.length` in `grow`'s contract wasn't `v.length`), so the TRUE invariant `v.length == m + i` was refuted.

- **Fresh oracles on re-assignment** (`Encoder.freshArray`, used by the loop replay's `rebindArray`, the prefix replay's
  `replayArrayAssign`, and the path and value-flow passes' `arrayReassign`): a re-assigned array or list name gets
  fresh contents, length and nullity, and loses any factory record, then:
  - a contracted call (`listLocalFromCall`, Phase 225's list route, now taking arrays) assumes the callee's `@Ensures`
    with `result` read as the name; an argument naming it is read through a snapshot of it as it was before the call
    (`snapshotArray`, `withActualSnapshot`) — minted first, the fresh oracles would be the argument's too;
  - an allocation or literal is recorded, reading the old state first (`v = new int[v.length + 1]`), its nullity and
    size bound rather than asserted of the old handles; a non-int allocation's contents are fresh;
  - another array name is aliased (`aliasArray`): its length and nullity always (an array's length never changes),
    its contents only while neither is written through (a store rebinds only one name's contents here). A list
    alias shares its size only then too. The path pass's own alias stays Phase 366's, which skips loudly;
  - anything else leaves them fresh (unknown).
- **An array formal reads its named actual**, as a list formal does (Phase 226): `a.length`, `a[i]`, `a.sum()` in a
  callee's contract are the caller's array's.
- **A stale factory record made a proof vacuous:** `List<Integer> v = [1, 2]; v = grow(v)` folded `v.size()` to 2
  through the literal, against the callee's `result.size() == a.size() + 1`. The contradiction proved `@Ensures({
  result == 42 })` once the argument read the snapshot; the record is now dropped with the old oracles.
- **A replayed allocation is recorded:** a callee precondition's prefix replay havocked `int[] v = new int[m]`, so
  `g(v)` under `@Requires({ a.length > 0 })` was refuted for `m > 0`.

**Boundary:** an invariant or postcondition over an array's `.sum()` across such a call, the reported shape itself,
is now reported but undecided (`Could not decide … (solver: timeout)`): refuting it needs a model of the sum's
quantified axioms, which the callee's own `result.sum() == a.sum() + 1` also times out on. A list local aliased before a
loop (`List<Integer> v = xs`) is still refuted at loop entry, as before. An array field re-assigned in a loop
(`data = grow(data)`, `this.data = …`) is covered. The report's second finding, a call-site precondition over a field
argument's length under a class invariant (`@Invariant({ data.length == n })`, `bump(data, i)` needing `i < a.length`),
is still refuted, the invariant not reaching the call. A re-assigned field's non-nullity now comes from the callee's
contract only: `data = bump(data, i)` under an invariant `data != null` needs `@Ensures({ result != null … })`, where
before the field's old non-null fact was kept.

**Shipped tests:** group `P375 array re-assignment`, 14 cases. Silent before: a false invariant across `v = grow(v)`, an
element fact across `v = inc0(v)`, an array alias and a list alias in a loop, a list parameter re-assigned from a call
in a loop. A wrong proof before: the straight-line false postcondition. A false refutation before: the true array and
list invariants, the true straight-line postcondition, a callee precondition over `new int[m]`'s length, a list's true
size after `v = grow(v)`. Plus guards: an alias whose source is written (skipped loudly), an allocation sized by the
array it replaces, a list literal re-assigned from a call on itself.

## Phase 376 — a call site sees the class invariant  *(shipped — completeness: the ClearSplit port's second finding)*

A callee's `@Requires` was checked at a call site (`verifyCallSite`) from the caller's own `@Requires` alone: unlike
every other check, it never assumed the class invariants at entry. Under `@Invariant({ n >= 0 && data != null &&
data.length == n })`, `void direct(int i) { data = bump(data, i) }` with `@Requires({ 0 <= i && i < n })` was refuted
for `bump`'s `i < a.length` with `data.size() = 0, n = 1`, a state the invariant rules out; so was `g(cap)` under
`@Invariant({ cap > 0 })`. ClearSplit's mutable `Ledger` couldn't call its pure step functions because of it.

- **The invariants are assumed at a call site** (`assumeClassInvariants`, as every other pass does): entry facts, before
  the prefix replay moves the fields. Not in a constructor, which hasn't established them.
- **A `this.f` argument is the field** (`namedLocation`): its length, contents and nullity are tied to the formal's,
  as a bare `f`'s are, and `data = bump(this.data, i)` reads it through Phase 375's pre-call snapshot.

**Boundary:** only the caller's own class's invariants; an argument's class invariant is still Phase 45's, for a
class-typed parameter. Under Phase 375, a re-assigned field's non-nullity comes from the callee's contract, so `bump`
needs `result != null` for the invariant's `data != null` to hold at exit.

**Shipped tests:** group `P376 call-site invariant`, 7 cases. A false refutation before: an array field's length under
the invariant, passed bare, as `this.data` and through a local alias, and a scalar field's bound. Plus guards: an index
the invariant doesn't cover, a field written before the call, and a constructor, which assumes nothing.

## Phase 377 — a list alias keeps its size  *(shipped — completeness: a gap Phase 375 left)*

Phase 375 made a re-assigned name share an alias's contents (and, for a list, its size) only while neither is written
into — and counted every call argument as a write. So `List<Integer> v = xs` before a loop calling `v = grow(v)` gave
`v` a fresh size at the alias, and the loop invariant `v.size() == xs.size() + i` failed on entry; a false invariant was
refuted there too, not where it is false. `new ArrayList<Integer>()` before such a loop failed the same way: the list
constructors weren't modelled at all (a straight-line `v = new ArrayList<Integer>(xs)` was skipped as outside the fragment).

- **In-place writes by the callees' frames** (`inPlaceWritesOf`, handed to the encoder as `inPlaceWritesSupplier`): a
  store `x[i] = …`, a call on `x` other than a pure read, and an argument a same-class callee's frame writes (its formal
  in the frame, or a frame it can't bound, or an override elsewhere); any other call's argument still counts, unless
  the call is a pure read. Read lazily, at an alias: read when the encoder is made, the callees' frames were inferred
  before their bodies' later rewriting and memoised unbounded (seven trace-loop cases, P197–P201, caught it).
- **List constructors** (`tryRecordListConstruction`): `new ArrayList()`, `new LinkedList()` and an int capacity are a
  new empty, non-null list; `new ArrayList(xs)` of a list is a copy — its size and elements, a separate object, so a
  later `xs.add(1)` leaves it as it was.
